# Advances in Business Strategy and Competitive Advantage (ABSCA) Book Series

Patricia Ordóñez de Pablos (Universidad de Oviedo, Spain)ISSN: 2327-3429 |
| --- | --- |

### Mission

Business entities are constantly seeking new ways through which to gain advantage over their competitors and strengthen their position within the business environment. With competition at an all-time high due to technological advancements allowing for competition on a global scale, firms continue to seek new ways through which to improve and strengthen their business processes, procedures, and profitability.

The Advances in Business Strategy and Competitive Advantage (ABSCA) Book Series is a timely series responding to the high demand for state-of-the-art research on how business strategies are created, implemented and re-designed to meet the demands of globalized competitive markets. With a focus on local and global challenges, business opportunities and the needs of society, the ABSCA encourages scientific discourse on doing business and managing information technologies for the creation of sustainable competitive advantage.

 
| 

### Coverage

*   Small and Medium Enterprises
*   Strategic alliances
*   Economies of Scale
*   Balanced Scorecard
*   Entrepreneurship & Innovation
*   Resource-Based Competition
*   Differentiation Strategy
*   Business Models
*   Adaptive Enterprise
*   Core Competencies

*   Bryan Christiansen  
    Tactical Systems LLC, USA
*   Agnieszka Piekarz  
    Independent Researcher, Poland

Recent global events involving cybersecurity breaches such as that at the credit scoring company Equifax which exposed the private data of over 145 million consumers in the United States have raised serious concerns everywhere, including the field of international business. Other recent examples include the online travel agency Orbitz (880,000 records compromised), the search generator Yahoo (3 billion user accounts compromised), and Statistics Canada which lost or mishandled hundreds of sensitive census and employee files (Amerding, 2018). Clearly the situation is now very critical on a gigantic scale.

Cybersecurity involves the methods to protect computer systems against online threats, and the increasing societal dependence on information technology has pushed the industry to the forefront as one of the most urgent challenges facing the global community today. Poor cybersecurity is the primary reason why hackers are able to penetrate safeguards in business computers and other networks, and the growing global skills gap in cybersecurity simply exacerbates the problem.

ISACA (2018), the international professional association focusing on Information Technology (IT) governance, estimates there will be a global shortage of two million cybersecurity professionals by 2019. This sobering statistic mirrors the same message from other authoritative sources such as International Data Corporation (IDC), a global market intelligence firm based in Massachusetts, USA which focuses on technology. Since 20 percent of all organizations receive fewer than five candidates for each advertised security-related positions, the size of the challenge is self-evident. Nations and companies with weak cybersecurity forces are exposed to cyber espionage which, in turn, disrupts critical infrastructures such as healthcare, trade, power generation, transportation, banking, and distribution.

These facts all influence international business risk immensely. The World Economic Forum’s (2018) Global Risks Report for 2018 includes cyberattacks and data breaches in the Top Five most likely and damaging risks in terms of overall impact on global business. The following pages cover a broad spectrum of the cybersecurity field ranging from cybersecurity talent gaps and banking risk management to cybersecurity education and social networks. Below is a brief listing of all 15 chapters.

Chapter 1 models the projected processes and outcomes of the global cybersecurity talent gap through multiple means: a review of the literature, general systems theory, social network analysis, game theory, and abductive logic from up-to-date data. Many experience cybersecurity talent gaps at a local, experienced level. They see positions that go unfilled or filled with people without the requisite skills; they see data and identity compromises, projects that are stymied, and heightened risks. They must address this gap locally by educating individuals through the talent pipeline, supporting learning and training programs, cross-training employees into cybersecurity endeavors, placing classified ads / head-hunting and hiring ever-more-expensive talent, and so forth. They tap outside vendors to support the work. For those in the proverbial trenches, understanding this global labor market challenge at a bird’s-eye view may be helpful.

Chapter 2 examines a Business Transformation Framework and Enterprise Architecture Framework for managers in business innovation. During the last decade, security strategies have not been efficient due to global insecurity and financial crises because businesses depend on security standards, cyber and information technology evolution, enterprise architecture, business engineering, and multilevel interoperability. The chapter provides a Business Transformation Project (BTP) for the reader to consider.

Chapter 3 explores the cyber security risks the banking system may encounter. The status of banking systems, which includes a number of online services, in Turkey with respect to cyber security risks and the current risks are assessed and presented along with possible solutions. This study analyzes e-payment systems (online banking and e-trade/the use of debit/credit cards) and the supply chain, the backbone of the e-finance system, with respect to national cyber security risks.

Chapter 4 highlights the current state of art of existing research over access control in increasingly decentralized environments, and to argue how the subject of access control is more relevant than ever before, with increasing research opportunities emerging. In this chapter, the authors analyze the current state-of-art of access control mechanisms and systems over decentralized applications with a focus on enterprise ecosystems, analyze the current challenges and opportunities the new technological landscape offers – specifically, over the application of blockchain-based technologies in access control – and propose new research directions for the future.

Chapter 5 considers a number of exemplary issues that are considered worthy of inclusion in the development of future cybersecurity workers. The global shortage in skilled labour for cybersecurity and the risk it presents to international business can only be solved by a significant increase in the numbers of skilled personnel. However, as the nature of risks proliferate and bifurcate the training of such, personnel must incorporate a broader understanding of contemporary and future risks. That is, while technical training is highly important, it is contended that future cybersecurity experts need to be aware of social, political, economic, and criminological issues. Accordingly, an overview is given of the issues of the ‘dark side of the net’ that cause problems for global cybersecurity and international business risk. The issues are discussed so that from these a skill set can be articulated which will attend to (and mitigate against) potential threats.

Chapter 6 proposes a Cyber Security Competency Model that integrates learning theories (cognitive, affective, and psychomotor), learning continuum hierarchy (awareness and training), and cyber security domain knowledge. Employing a literature search of scholarly and practitioner works, together with cyber security standards from governmental and non-governmental organizations, the chapter integrates cyber security domain knowledge, learning theories, and learning continuum hierarchy to design a model of cyber security competencies suitable for use in educating individuals and the general workforce. This theoretical based approach to designing cyber security awareness and training programs will produce skilful individuals and workforce can mitigate cyber attacks in the global business environment.

Chapter 7 provides aspiring cybersecurity students a clear understanding of the various educational pathways they can choose to achieve their goals. The authors describe educational categories and include an assessment of each that students will want to consider based on their own situation. They also discuss how the study of cybersecurity can be accomplished from a computer science, engineering, and business perspective. Students with STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Mathematics) skills can accomplish their goals in numerous cybersecurity roles including cyber engineer, architect, and other technical roles. Finally, students with cyber business interest can accomplish their goals with a focus on strategy, compliance, awareness, and others. Organizations need employees with all these skills. This chapter concludes with the recommendation for continual learning, the value of networking and the encouragement for students to start now creating a cyber career.

Chapter 8 surveys a strategy to minimize risk and increase productivity in varied environments using the tool WhatsApp Messenger which is a cross-platform mobile messaging application that allows mobile phone owners to exchange messages without having to pay for short message services (SMS). Shrewd entrepreneurs are employing this service to grow their businesses in global markets. WhatsApp can be applied to build capability in emerging economies where the usage of smartphones has doubled recently. The technology can be applied to collect data which can be interpreted to make organizational sense in the new digital world. In this chapter, the author makes a brief survey of WhatsApp to postulate its dynamism in penetrating global markets.

Chapter 9 investigates online calling cards and professional profiles in cybersecurity in social media. Presently the demand is very high for people to work in various cybersecurity professions, and that demand may well continue into the near-term. While there are more formal trails for employment—such as higher-educational pathways—performance in cybersecurity competitions, participation in professional conferences, and social media presentations may all offer less conventional paths into cybersecurity hiring. Through a convenience sample across a number of social media platforms and bottom-up coding, this work explores some aspects of cybersecurity professional profiles (“calling cards”) available on the open Social Web and what may be learned about respective skills and capabilities from these glimmers of the person(s) behind the profiles. These profiles are assessed based on a 2x2 axis with focuses on (1) target skills and (2) personhood attributes. From these analyses, some tentative insights are shared about the cybersecurity calling cards and how informative they may be for recruitment and retention of cybersecurity workers.

Chapter 10 covers the Wannacrypt ransomware attack and recommends ways to avert future occurrence. Cyber attack has become a global phenomenon organizations, government agencies, and business entities must contend with as cyber criminals frequently target their operations. The Wannacrypt ransomware attack was unleashed on the global community in early May, 2017 with a devastating effect. The attack described as the largest in internet history disrupted major organizations and affected over 200,000 computers in 150 countries.

Chapter 11 explains the so-called weakest link in cybersecurity: the electronic “hive mind” or groupthink. If people are the “weakest link” in cybersecurity because of their psychological make-up and hard wiring—their socialized desire to trust and cooperate with others, their cognitive biases and misperceptions, their preferences for convenience, their general going with System 1 inattention instead of System 2 attention and thinking—this begs the question of whether the same micro-scale cognitive limits found in individual users are also present on a mass scale. There have been discovered problematic unthinking leanings in group decision-making: obedience to authority, bystander effects, groupthink, and the Abilene paradox, among others. Using a range of often-mass-scale data sources and data analytics tools, research questions were asked around three areas: (1) the level of sophistication of the cybersecurity electronic hive mind towards cybersecurity issues, (2) the gap between the non-expert members and the expert members in the hive mind, and (3) whether the extant hive mind was more reflective of mob unthinkingness or deliberation and wisdom.

Chapter 12 contends with multidimensional mappings of political accounts for malicious political socialbot identification. Malicious political socialbots used to sway public opinion regarding the U.S. government and its functions have been identified as part of a larger information warfare effort by the Russian government. This work asks what is knowable from a Web-based sleuthing approach about the four following factors: the ability to identify malicious political socialbot accounts based on their ego neighborhoods at 1, 1.5, and 2 degrees; the ability to identify malicious political socialbot accounts based on the claimed and linked geographical locations of their accounts, their ego neighborhoods, and their #hashtag networks; the ability to identify malicious political socialbot accounts based on their strategic messaging (content, sentiment, and language structures) on respective social media platforms; and the ability to identify and describe “maliciousness” in malicious political socialbot accounts based on observable behaviors on that account on three social media platform types: (1) microblogging, (2) social networking, and (3) crowd-sourced encyclopedia content-sharing.

Chapter 13 studies information security threats in Romanian public and private organizations. Along with the incontestable benefits for the modern society, information and communication technology developments induce new vulnerabilities. Mobile computing devices, cloud computing, but also privacy issues are just a few elements that should be considered when shaping the modern information security that is essential to our modern way of life. Since information security risks are rapidly evolving and taking new forms, the real benefits of information and communication technologies may be exploited only if trust is built on every layer of responsibility. This study makes radiography of the present main information security threats faced by Romanian organizations, as well as of the attitude of Romanian organizations towards information security, as resulted from a research and detailed survey questionnaires performed by the authors. Following the results of this research, the authors propose action to improve the security posture of Romanian organizations, as well as knowledge, capabilities and decision-making of business managers.

Chapter 14 attempts to understand the effects of cybercrime to Zimbabwe’s peace and security. In the 21st century, cybercrime has become an international threat. This has necessitated many states to enact legislations and other measures to curb cybercrime. Primary data was gathered through key informant interviews, while documentary search was used to review scholarly literature on the subject. Key informants for the study were drawn from institutions that deal in combating cybercrime. Zimbabwe does not have adequate and effective legislative instruments to combat cybercrime. Cybercrime is a threat to peace and security as it can be used to bring down critical infrastructure and disrupt communication networks of the country. Some of the measures identified to curbing cybercrime include prevention and awareness; training and development; development of new technology and introduction of new laws, and updating of current and introduction of new legislations.

Chapter 15 is based on a study which sought to understand the threats of cyber warfare in Zimbabwe. The effects of cyber warfare, cyber intelligence mechanisms in place and the status of the harmonization of laws and collaboration of SADC countries in efforts to address cyber threats were also covered. Qualitative research methodology was used to conduct the study. A total of fifteen key respondents drawn from information technology experts, academia, top military personnel and lawyers participated in the study which revealed that Zimbabwe was vulnerable to cyber warfare due to increased use of technology and failure to keep up with technological advancements. The study noted that the current legislation in place does not explicitly address cyber warfare threats but focuses more on cybercrime. The study recommended that Zimbabwe should enact effective legislation to curtail cyber warfare in order to enhance cyber security. Investment in cyber security in terms of research and human capital development should also be prioritized.

In this era of global hypercompetition, nations and organizations alike are experiencing unprecedented stress to remain sustainable in the 21^(st) century. The current cybersecurity chaos which has befallen international business entities such as eBay, Target Stores, Heartland Payment Systems, and JPMorgan Chase in recent years cannot continue much longer without serious consequences worldwide. We trust this publication shall shed additional light on the global cybersecurity challenges now facing us all to provide future research that can be put into applied practice.

# Chapter 1

*   Shalin Hai-Jew  
    Kansas State University, USA

ABSTRACT

Many experience cybersecurity talent gaps at a local level. They see positions that go unfilled or filled with people without the requisite skills; they see data and identity compromises, projects that are stymied, and heightened risks. They have to address this gap locally by educating individuals through the talent pipeline, supporting learning and training programs, cross-training employees into cybersecurity endeavors, placing classified ads/head-hunting and hiring ever-more-expensive talent, and so on. They go to outside vendors to support the work. For those in the proverbial trenches, understanding this global labor market challenge at the 30,000-foot level may be helpful. This work models the projected processes and outcomes of the cybersecurity talent gap through multiple means: a review of the literature, general systems theory, social network analysis, game theory, and abductive logic, and up-to-date data.

INTRODUCTION

In a typical workday, the cybersecurity talent gap in the global labor markets is patently clear. There are news reports of various data compromises in cities that have had their data encrypted and controlled by ransomware. There are data spills with private data shared broadly. On the Dark Web are businesses selling people’s credentials for others to exploit. And within work places are smaller fires—phishing attacks, malware attacks, disappeared memory devices, misplaced laptops with sensitive data, and others. Those who can afford to hire top-flight talent and purchase top-shelf technologies attempt to create a secure cyber-environment. Those who cannot afford to do so are left exposed and must focus on lower-cost methods for recovery. In many senses, the “cyber-technological haves” are also the most vulnerable because of the wiredness of their societies and their early adoptions of cybertechnology.

A Broad Vulnerability

“Cyber,” broadly speaking, touches virtually every aspect of modern life. In a typical day, people may use resources on the Internet and Web for the following: intercommunications, work, news consumption, entertainment, banking, library services, health management, research, and others. The Internet of Things (IoT) stands to broaden the reliance on cyber in people’s homes, healthcare, transportation, commerce and shopping, and other systems. Less obviously, they rely on infrastructure that relies on cyber (cyber-physical systems): electricity, transportation (e.g., GPS, scheduling, sensor networks), manufacturing, commerce, military systems, and others. The deep integration of cyber in contemporary lifestyles means that the potential cyber “attack surface” is wide and deep, and cyberattacks based on found and created vulnerabilities may be high-impact, disruptive, and even potentially devastating.

Cybersecurity

Cybersecurity may be conceptualized as the so-called “security value chain,” which includes five elements:

Deter -> Protect -> Detect -> Respond -> Recover

Each step of the chain is important to strive for a holistic context of security. Therefore, security is created through a mix of policies, laws, law enforcement, technologies, surveillance, and social norms, among others. These various elements provide actual defense-in-depth (the uses of various defensive lines at all levels for a stronger collective defense), and they challenge any nation-state, criminal organization, hacker collective, or individual to really consider cost-benefit calculations before they would take actions to compromise cybersystems or cyber elements in systems.

The Definition of Necessary Skills

Information security professionals, based on the 2013 Global Information Security Workforce Study, do well to have the following skills to be successful in the field (in descending order): “broad understanding of the security field (92%), communication skills (91%), technical knowledge (88%), awareness and understanding of the latest security threats (86%), security policy formulation and application (75%), leadership skills (68%), business management skills (57%), project management skills (55%), and legal knowledge (42%) (Caldwell, 2013, p. 7).

The required skills are often cross-disciplinary:

The pivotal significance of cyber and computer networks to the security of critical infrastructure has contributed to raising awareness about how the comprehension of cyber and cyber security issues necessitates a complex skill-set. This skill-set includes competence within a variety of disciplines, ranging from engineering and computer technology, to law, diplomacy and management. (Røislien, 2015, p. 23)

Another critical capability is to think and innovate creatively, since so much of the field is ambiguous and undefined, and since cyberattacks are constantly being innovated by people.

The Job Market in Cybersecurity

The job opportunities in the cybersecurity field are wide ranging and dynamic. Cybersecurity personnel are needed to ensure that software created by developers is secure (through various forms of testing); once software is released, penetration testers need to assess software security for patching. Those administrators who operate datacenters and networks need to ensure that there is security and backups for business continuance. Administrators need to design and emplace policies and staff to ensure cybersecurity in the context of overall security. Forensic investigators explore technology systems to understand compromises. Cyber weapons developers create exploits to achieve particular aims. Engineers are needed to design and set up effective cryptographic systems for secure interchanges. Audit specialists are needed to assess for compliance (Caldwell, 2013, p. 6). Analytics have also come to the fore in cybersecurity, with surveillance depending in part on mass-scale data analytics and machine learning. For as many cybersecurity experts are on the “tip of the spear,” there are many support staff who provide clerical, documentary, and other forms of support.

The job market for workers in cybersecurity, based on multiple studies, converges on a shared number: an approximately 1.5 million worker shortfall or gap in 2019 or 2020 (Furnell, Fischer, & Finch, 2017, p. 5). In the United Kingdom, an official report suggests it may be some two decades before the cyber security skills gap may be addressed “at all levels of education” (Morse, 2013, p. 27). This shortfall is thought to be at both the entry level and at the higher levels of organizations:

The most significant issue, as I see it, will be on the high and low ends of the spectrum, in terms of applicable skills, as you will likely have people being put in place in entry level operational IT security jobs who simply do not have enough background to do the work to its fullest, and you will have people elevated into management positions sooner than they might merit based on sheer demand alone,” says Bernard Zelmans, general manager EMEA at FireMon. “As you can imagine, this will also make life harder on workers in mid-level positions as they will be the ones who have to pick up the slack. (Caldwell, 2013, p. 6)

The existence of cybersecurity talent gaps in global labor markets has implications on human endeavors both within and beyond cyber. Existing social, data, manufacturing, guidance, weapons, and other systems are at some level of constant (and sometimes heightened) risk, with the cybersecurity worker shortfall. The challenge goes beyond this: a cybersecurity worker shortfall may constrain not only the applicable uses of the Web and Internet, the Internet of Things, but also anything that depends on cybertechnology. An inability to provide secure services may be a huge hinderance. Conceptual and notional applications may be slowed by a lack of expertise in this area on design and development teams. Innovative talents that may be able to conceptualize and bring to reality new products and services may be relegated to the maintenance of cybersecurity for existing systems. An e-skills manifesto suggested the need is broad for ICT (Information and Communications Technology) skills, without which many emerging endeavors will be stunted:

Align Supply With Demand: Governments, industry and academia alike should work closely to ensure that Europe has the advanced ICT skills needed in emerging areas such as Cloud computing, Green IT, Cyber-security, Interoperability and eHealth. Skills for success in the ICT industry will have to evolve and align to new streams of growth. The impact of e-skills upon sectors such as health will have the capacity to change and improve the way we address some of society’s biggest challenges. (McCormack, 2010, p. 70, original author’s boldface subheading)

This work proposes a parsimonious and abstract model (inspired by general systems theory, social networks, game theory, and abductive logic and up-to-date data) of this challenge to better understand some possible implications of this cybersecurity talent shortfall and what may partially mitigate this situation. Through theorizing, this model formalizes the cybersecurity space and examines the risks of the shortfall in cybersecurity talent. Another objective is to provide a higher-level view of the challenge to benefit the work of recruiting cybersecurity talent occurring at the local levels. In this work, a “model” is only an abstraction of a real-world phenomenon, and it is used to better understand and engage that phenomenon. This model is multi-dimensional in nature, so that different aspects of this complex challenge may be captured and explored theoretically (and ultimately practically).

REVIEW OF THE LITERATURE

Cybersecurity as a Dynamic Space

On the legal front, the social environment is affected by the criminal prosecution of cybercrime by law enforcement officials, third-party lawsuits from customers, and other endeavors that affect cybersecurity (Yang & Hoffstadt, 2006). In the early days of cyber, before there was awareness among many that cybersecurity might be an issue, there were a number of reports of corporations and organizations not even being aware that their data had been compromised (Strand, 2014). Since then, with news of compromised systems and stolen data and stolen identities, awareness of cyber risks has grown:

Organisations may be uncertain about whether they have been attacked in the past, but they are surer of future dangers. Almost two thirds (64%) believe that they will be targeted within the next year, if not sooner, 27% expect it within the next 12 months, with another 23% anticipating an attack within the next six months. And 14% were particularly pessimistic, expecting a cyber-attack in the next few weeks. More than a third of companies, however, did not expect to be targeted at all in the near future, and 36% believed that they were not on attackers’ radar. (Strand, 2014, p. 14)

The cost to network compromises “typically entails more than the cost of repairing the compromised data or system, as news of the intrusion may adversely affect the company's “market capitalization or consumer confidence” (Yang & Hoffstadt, 2006, p. 202). The cost to reputation may be highly expensive, if it is recoverable. The cost of recovering from security breaches may be three times as much for “enterprises lacking security skills” (Furnell, Fischer, & Finch, 2017, p. 5).

Historically, talent gaps in the labor market have been addressed in a variety of ways. To address immediate needs, organizations and corporations often will train talent themselves to address particular issues. They may hire individuals who have not yet earned their formal degrees—through internships, through special programs, through temporary agencies, and other means. Or they may hire simply based on professional certifications. They will often reach out to local vocational schools and community colleges to develop programs (and curriculums) to train individuals for their needs; in other words, they will build the pipeline to bring employees to their organization. They will raise wages and create benefits packages that are appealing to the particular target skill sets. They will host booths and tables at professional conferences to head hunt and recruit. They will support skill-based contests to identify talent in the general population. Multinational companies have also created branches abroad to benefit from the local talent there. Experts and expert teams with particular niche skills may be brought in to address issues temporarily. \[To think of niche skills, who would have thought experts in SCADA-related technologies might be critical in cybersecurity prior to Stuxnet? The reality of the high costs for acquisition and expertise in complex technical systems means that mixed teams have to take on hard problems, in either collaborative or compartmented ways. (“SCADA” refers to “supervisor control and data acquisition” systems that are used in manufacturing contexts.)\]

Government may play a role. For example, there may be potential employees who were born and educated and trained abroad whose capabilities match standards in the USA. In that case, the government may pass laws and extend visas to bring such high-skilled individuals to work in the USA. Traditionally, a government has to work the policy levers to create an economy that lifts “both firms and citizens” (Porter & Rivkin, 2014, p. 31).

The general public also plays a critical role in the self-development and self-exploration to develop and maintain skills in a demanding workplace, with global competition, and known and unknown adversaries.

MODELING PROCESSES AND OUTCOMES FROM THE CYBER TALENT GAPS IN GLOBAL LABOR MARKETS

To understand the global cyber talent gap, it helps to begin with a system-based model. The main “model” is “A Simplified National Cybersecurity Ecosystem and the Global Cybersecurity Talent Gap,” which is mostly a descriptive model. This suggests there are three main entities: the general public, the public sector, and the private sector with regards to cybersecurity. Each broadscale “vertical” has its own power, its own interests, its own private concerns, and some space or capacity for collaboration with the other entities. The collaborations may result in “loose coupling” on some issues and “tight coupling” on others; these relationships may be short-term, mid-term, or long-term. These are developed over shared interests and usually through trust relationships.

In this system, each entity needs to be clear about its own interests and should not give away competitive advantage unnecessarily. Each entity also should not put too much reliance on others to protect their own interests—so as not to blunt their own initiative.

The section in the middle of Figure 1 shows potential for information sharing, co-design, collaboration, and other endeavors. In cybersecurity as in other issues, it is better to anticipate and plan for potentialities than to be caught up short and overtaken by events. A more specified systems model would observe the “‘wholes’ and ‘wholeness’” with modifying interdisciplinary insights (Von Bertalanffy, 1972, p. 416) and mathematical insights (“Systems theory”, 2017). This system, like all, may be conceptualized as tending towards equilibrium, and how effectively it maintains this “steady state” or “steadily oscillating state” will determine its continuance as a system (Kuhn, 1974, as cited in Walonick, 1993).

About Cybersecurity Worker Recruitment and Retention

The concept of systems and various states of systems may be captured in a Markov chain \[“a stochastic model describing a sequence of possible events in which the probability of each event depends only on the state attained in the previous event” (“Markov chain”, 2017)\]. In this case, a modified, informal, and unspecified Markov chain is used to depict cybersecurity workforces. The patterns at the macro level are conceptualized as a result of individual ego-level decisions made based on various cost-benefit calculations, expected utility, and incentives / disincentives.

At any one time, writ large, the cybersecurity workforce may resemble Figure 2. The transient state is one in which cybersecurity workers may move from position to position and stay in the cybersecurity field. The “recurrent” states are areas in which cybersecurity workers may move, but once they are in those spaces, they are unable to leave; they are “trapped.” Each circle represents a trapping set from which there is no escape velocity back to the main transient state area. As drawn, the figure would suggest that most entities will eventually cycle out and be absorbed in respective traps and end up elsewhere.

Structurally, if everything is dynamic and constantly moving, one-way connections will result in leaving a system. This system, as depicted, only works because there is constant new blood in the field. In this case, the conceptualization is memory-less, so it does not matter how individuals came to be part of the cybersecurity workforce, whether through formal or informal ways, for example, but only that they are there. What is of more interest is how long they can retain in the field.

From this conceptualization, expanding participation in the cybersecurity transient state may be achieved in several ways and on several dimensions. The “who” refers to bringing in young talent (some knowledge-based corporations will bring in high school students as interns and even as employees) and to maintain retirement-age experts, to stretch out the “time” of productivity. Another approach is to think of training “breadth” by broadening capabilities in current staff, so the cybersecurity coverage may be addressed. (All staff, to some degree, must have a level of expertise in cybersecurity, so that they do not end up being the “weak link” at the organization. Assigning cybersecurity work to those outside of the field is necessary, but it does not generally replace hardcore highly-trained expertise.)

Another dimension here relates to technologies (as amplifiers, as magnifiers) because these may be harnessed to expand human capabilities. Technological capabilities may bolster substitution effects. Also, policy can also expand the cybersecurity space by disallowing particular high-risk behaviors; enabling heightened levels of surveillance for restricted behaviors, and ultimately decreasing the exposure space, which theoretically might lessen the need for some cybersecurity mitigations.

Another implication of the conceptualization is the high-achievers in the cybersecurity field should be well-supported in their endeavors. Per the Pareto principle (the so-called “80/20 rule”), a vital few (a fifth) are the ones producing 80% of the effects in many fields. This pattern may be seen in cybersecurity as well (although it may be less than a fifth). The idea is that if the high producers can be well supported, they may stay productive longer than normal creativity lifespans and may contribute insights, technologies, and methods that may ultimately mean competitive advantage.

Understanding what these traps are in the cybersecurity workplace context would be beneficial to understanding what changes may be made. For example, what are the points-of-no-return? What are the other career paths that are one-way out of the cybersecurity realm? What percentage of people wash out from the field given its high-pressure, sense of risks, professional stress, and ambiguity? Are there early retirements from stress and burnout? \[With empirical data, it is possible to use a time-to-event analysis or “survival analysis” to see the data patterns in terms of employment. This approach could show time periods of risk when people leave the field, such as those who have just started their careers and dislike aspects of the work, or those who wash out early, and maybe mid-career leaving due to more lucrative opportunities, and so on. Such data can provide an insightful narrative about how employees behave in the field—within organizations and within the field.\]

| Figure 2. A conceptualization of the cybersecurity work(er) space |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-5225-5927-6.ch001.f02](i/ch001.f02.png) |
| --- |

Figure 2 is a conceptualization of this cybersecurity workforce space as a very early form abstract system, without any probabilities specified…and the spaces not even really defined except in a general sense. What is the “stable state” view once this is informed by actual in-field statistics? Does this look different if comparing across nations? Across developed and developing countries? Are there ways to build bridges back into the cybersecurity fold from terminal states (and do those turn out well)? The data that can be used to inform the specifications in Figure 2 are eminently available in human resources offices in both the public and private sectors. Early and “blurry” work may be inferred from publicly available labor statistics.

Those entities (organizations, corporations) that manage and supervise cybersecurity workers have an interest in creating a robust pipeline of talent for cybersecurity work. They have an interest in understanding what skill sets and personality types may be most effective in the field, albeit without locking themselves into spurious stereotypes and profiles. Once personnel have been onboarded, those entities have an interest in supporting the work of those individuals, particularly their analytical and creativity skills.

When properly managed, individuals and teams may be able to achieve their full potential; if improperly handled or mismanaged, their talent may be squelched under political or other interests (which results in a net loss for all involved). They have an interest in observing career arcs and trajectories. They must know what such workers want in a workplace and how to provide for their wants, within reason. They have an interest in keeping cybersecurity employees active and productive for as long as possible.

About Strategic Decision-Making

The implied suggestion in Figure 1 only works if the respective entities think such interactions may be beneficial and achievable, after rational consideration. An individual or group or organization is said to be acting rationally when “you are aware of your objectives or preferences and of any limitations or constraints on your actions and choose your actions in a calculated way to do the best according to your own criteria...” (Dixit, Skeath, & Reiley, 2009, 2004, 1999, p. 5). As the prior definition suggests, the various incentives and disincentives will vary for different actors. For example, if there is an open-source project to set design regulations in a field, this may draw a variety of actors with different interests and capabilities. Some commercial organizations may want a voice in this process, so that they can ensure quality and alignment with their products. Government entities may want input in order to ensure alignment with their regulatory mandates. Members of the general public may be interested because the topic aligns with their professional areas of interest. And beyond those basic interests, there may be other motives and expected utilities (“utils”): access to privy information, power, prestige, professional interrelationships, extended capabilities, and so forth.

A simple symmetrical payoff table, with two players, follows: If Player 1 and Player 2 both engage and follow through on the collaborative project, both stand to gain (+5, +5). If the first player engages, but the other withdraws, then Player 1 stands to lose (-12), but Player 2 has a gain of 3. Conversely, if Player 1 withdraws, then Player 2 stands to lose (-12) because Player 2 will have invested into the shared effort but lost IP, investments, and reputation. If both withdraw, both sides stand to lose their investments and potential of gain (-7, -7), and there may be reputational harms. A two-player sample payoff table is clearly limited, but it conveys the idea of expected payoffs and how these may be deployed to understand strategic interests.

Table 1. A symmetrical sample payoff table

|  || Engage || Withdraw |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Engage || +5, +5 || \-12, 3 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Withdraw || 3, - 12 || \-7, -7 |

If a bad actor wants to engage, he or she may engage in “cheap talk” about goals and projects and capabilities without actual costly signaling (evidentiary proofs). For some naïve players, they will be dazzled by the false promises and invest something real and receive nothing in return. Each actor has to engage in due diligence to understand possibilities as well as impossibilities, and when they go through a decision process, they need to prune impossibilities from their decision trees. Suffice it to say that going with pretend and not using facts is always a dominated strategy because the player is not dealing with reality but paying out in reality.

In basic game theory, the type of game also matters, and the strategies change with the game types. For example, if a collaboration is open-ended or infinite, that changes the calculus for cooperation (as in an extended Prisoner’s Dilemma game). If a collaboration is simultaneous vs. sequential, that also changes strategies. The “pregame” is important because this is where the enforceable rules of play are made (Dixit, Skeath, & Reiley, 2009, 2004, 1999, p. 25).

| Figure 3. A simple binary decision tree: Cooperate or not |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-5225-5927-6.ch001.f03](i/ch001.f03.png) |
| --- |

Based on the proposed scenario of cooperation among the general public, the public sector and the private sector around shared interests related to cybersecurity, the decision-making of a sequential game is depicted in Figure 3. This decision tree is simplified in numerous ways. First, this is from the perspective of one player, potentially with another player or multiple other players, and the decision-making is set up as a binary “do” or “don’t do.” The “player” may be an individual “ego,” or it may be an individual group or “entity” (like a corporation, organization, office, or some other informal or formal group).

In this game tree, each player cooperates (continue) or defect (stop, opt-out, or withdraw) at each phase. Each player is assumed to have incomplete information but is also assumed to be striving to collect as much solid and accurate information as possible at all times. Each player is also assumed to have different calculations for wins and losses…and motivations. Continuing has a cost but stopping does as well. Stopping involves potential harm to the relationships, the player reputation, and the potential of the collaborative project, among others. Of course, in the real world, information technology projects of some complexity are challenging and difficult to fulfill successfully. Leadership may be insufficient, or it may change.

Participants in collaborative projects have evolving authorizing environments—in terms of their time, supporting resources, and organizational permissions. When collaborative projects work well, synergies are achieved, and the achievements are much greater than the sum of the parts. Ideally, all members of shared projects achieve the game Nash equilibrium, with optimized outcomes. In the real, in dynamic in vivo spaces, perfect outcomes are much harder to achieve. Trust itself is fragile, with a potential long sequence of mutual trust and then a black swan event (Taleb, 2010, 2007). Rule enforcements may be too expensive and complex to take to legal counsel. And sunk costs may be just that. Unless fundamentals are established effectively, collaborative projects may be built on fragile alliances with high turnover.

Figure 3 is set up framed towards “yes.” After all, people have to be at the table to direct the course of a project or policy or framework. Nothing ventured, nothing gained… No outcomes are known ahead of time, and even if work is partial, it may contribute to a constructive endeavor that yields positive results in the long run. Often the more ambitious an objective the higher is the likelihood of initial failures. Collaborative work between the general public, the public sector, and the private sector often addresses issues enabled by technological advancements in a lagging way. Recent examples include efforts to address privacy in the age of social media. However, that same decision tree may be framed otherwise, with left nodes reading as follows:

*   • Pursue one’s main organization objectives (or not)
*   • Protect organizational resources: staff time, strategic capabilities, intellectual property, and others (or not)
*   • Propose external representatives to shared business or governmental endeavors (or not)
*   • Answer emails occasionally from such collaborative groups (or not)
*   • Offer some low-cost symbolic help (or not)
*   • Offer some cheap talk (or not)
*   • Free-ride others’ communal efforts (or not)
*   • … and so forth….

There should not be communal engagement without consideration for real costs. There are scenarios that are wholly “dominated” (losing) strategies. For example, in a hypothetical case: an organization puts out a call for proposals for a particular design problem. It promises a six-figure prize and potential development of the design. The organization does not have a clear provenance, but its prize package is compelling. A firm invests the time of multiple staff members to compete, and their cost in hours is higher than the prize, but if the plan wins and is put into production, the firm stands to gain.

However, if they do not win, their hard work and creative ideas are not protected, and these may be usurped by the host organization (which does not have a clear record of achievement in this area). Giving away intellectual property and other forms of competitive advantage is a dominated strategy. (A similar dominated strategy example involves going open-source with one’s intellectual property, unless there are other benefits such as reputational gains, positive public relations, and so on.) Whenever possible, it is important to leverage access and savvy to raise the odds of constructive and non-losing outcomes.

Some Current Efforts in Engaging Cybersecurity in a Time of Scarce Hands

Among the three main areas—the public sector, the private sector, and the general public—there are efforts to harness synergies in the cybersecurity field, where interests overlap. At the policy front, with the public sector in the lead, some of the following efforts include the following:

*   • Assigning “Good” and “Bad” Actor Labels: Practitioners in cybersecurity laud those with high skills and legacies of achievement (such as discovering zero days or expanding the field into new areas, such as “social engineering”). The management of reputation helps those in the field know which are the “good” and “bad” actors, who has actual earned reputations and who is fronting, and so on.
*   • Sharing Information: There have been efforts are creating standards for information-sharing that will not result in harm to the information sharers (particularly if they are corporations). Indeed, in the academic literature, there is a work about a proposed platform through which information may be shared and cybersecurity heightened (Al Sabbagh & Kowalski, 2012).

In terms of efforts by both the public and private sectors, some of their main shared endeavors include efforts for preparing and attracting individuals to the cybersecurity field. These efforts include the following:

*   • Defining a Talent Pipeline: For people to become fully productive individuals, there are developmental windows that have to be met for their care, nutrition, health, learning, and other supports. Research in education has shown that if developmental windows are not met, certain human capabilities may be lost forever. Because skills often build on other skills, the loss of basic skills can have far-reaching negative impacts on the individual. There are some pre-requisite skills that are needed for cybersecurity, and these may include basics such as literacy, numeracy, logic, and technical skills, as well as more complex capabilities. The Skills toward Employment and Productivity (STEP) conceptual framework lists five steps: “getting infants off to the right start, ensuring that all students learn, building job-relevant skills, encouraging entrepreneurship and innovation, (and) facilitating labor mobility and matching” (Arias, Apr. 2012, Slide 11). There are various skills frameworks for cybersecurity (Furnell, Fischer, & Finch, 2017). Clearly, all three entities in the model (the general public, the public sector, and the private sector) have a role in human development. The levers that may affect this preservation of talent through the pipeline in middle-school and high school, do not only involve courses but student clubs, publications, internships, and competitions. 
    *   o Reaching Beyond Traditional Populations for Recruitment and Support: Men fill 86% of cybersecurity roles “while women fill only 10% (there is no data for the remaining 4%) (Caldwell, 2013, p. 8). There are efforts to reach out to less traditional populations for cyber and Science, Mathematics, Engineering and Technology (SMET) (Sosnowski, Feb. 2014).
    *   o Providing Grants for Study: Acquiring graduate degrees in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Math (STEM) fields involves not only surviving a grueling pipeline of learning from birth through graduate-school age, but there is a cost of acquisition in tuition, time, energy, talent, and opportunity costs.
    *   o Raising the Profile of Cybersecurity Work: There are clear efforts at glamorizing the cybersecurity field. For example, cybersecurity conferences are often held in glittery and glamorous cities like Las Vegas, Nevada. There are contests with six and seven figure payouts. Job positions hint at some of the glamor, such as “virus hunter” (as in digital virus hunters). White and gray hat hackers may benefit from the dark and hooded images of black hats in stock images used for various cybersecurity events. In mass media, there are appealing stories of white hats saving the day and protecting the general population.
*   • Improving the Workplace Experience: Some efforts involve improving the workplace experience. One issue is the geographic location and how much employees of various industries may cluster and share ideas across verticals for the creativity-inducing cross-fertilization of ideas (Saxenian, 1996). A range of workplace factors affects job satisfaction: “pay, working hours and unions; insecurity and uncertainty; socializing, networking and isolation” (Hesmondhalgh & Baker, 2009, p. 4). Fatigue and overwork will detract from productivity as well as job satisfaction. 
    *   o Workplace Cultures Have Been Evolving: To accommodate various cyber skill sets and talent, even military cultures have had to change:

The attributes of the ideal cyber officer (i.e., the ideal skill-set this officer type requires), and how the military most beneficially and efficiently can acquire a professional “cyber officer workforce”, is understood very differently by different military institutions and nations. A cyber warrior in a “red team” in the Chinese “Information Security Base” or in the US Cyber Command, operate according to different standards, procedures and practices.5 This leads to both conceptual confusion and operational challenges. It is consequently a paradox that the cyber officer is a neglected object of study. Focusing on the cyber officers’ narratives, this article feeds into the gap in the literature. (Røislien, 2015, p. 24)

Certainly, other endeavors are ongoing but not touched on in the academic literature or mainstream media.

DISCUSSION

This work offers a “back of the napkin” model of the cybersecurity talent gap shortfall in global labor markets using a range of modeling techniques, including general systems theory, social network analysis, abductive logic, game theory, and available data. There are a number of assumptions made here—that the case of cybersecurity talent gaps is not atypical and should not be addressed as a special case and not addressed in isolation. The “predictions” are several-fold.

Strategic Alliances

One suggestion is that alliances between the general public, the private sector, and government may lead to benefits for all entities. Such work has been ongoing, with information sharing, for a ready cyberdefense.

Substitution Effects

One, the 1.5 million cybersecurity worker shortfall will not be filled to the number. Rather, there will be innovations (some technical) and adaptations that will help address some of the gap in needs. “Substitution effects” will occur, and technologies and other approaches may stand-in for this particular gap. In the traditional conceptualization of substitution effects, if individuals are priced out of a costlier good, they will bring in some other resource that is less costly. A healthy market also is sufficiently adaptable to provide substitute products. (For example, some companies offer cyber insurance. The pooling of funds around cybersecurity may be harnessed to harden the cyber space and to increase cybersecurity for those insurance holders.)

Constraints on Advancements

Two, the gap in cybersecurity talent will not only mean that anything that touches cyber will involve some increased risk, including hardened systems. It also will mean that potential products and services and capabilities will not necessarily come to fruition. The thinking work related to cybersecurity—for research and development, for theorizing—will also come up short. It may be easier to measure the cybersecurity system compromises and data losses and racked-up costs of recovery, but counting lost opportunity may be more difficult (but equally crucial).

Different Outcomes for Haves and Have-Nots

Three, certainly, the “haves” in this context will be able to attract the necessary talent globally and to support that talent to achieve innovations and outsized capabilities. They will be able to build and maintain in-house cybersecurity talents and pay for external talents where available. The “haves” may be able to build on the important thinking work in cybersecurity—for R&D (research and development), for policy, for strategy and tactics, and for advancing the field (and for advancing products and services in other areas but which depend on cybersecurity). The risks of insufficient thinking work applies to academia and its contributions to respective fields. One researcher highlights the lack of cyber considerations in political science:

The costs of scholarly neglect of the cyber issue to the advancement of theory are apparent: when the range of empirical topics that theory is able to elucidate narrows, the academic enterprise inevitably enters a process of internal corrosion, which reveals itself in one or both of two ways—a loss of conceptual fertility or a reduced capacity for explanatory analysis, each of which inhibits intellectual progress in the study of international relations (Kello, 2013, p. 12).

The development of human talent to engage in thought-work related to cyber is not inexpensive. In addition, the development of such talent generally does not occur in a social vacuum. Usually, design teams, development teams, and academicians work in social environments, and their respective work benefits each other.

Organizational “have-nots” in terms of cybersecurity talent will rely on software maker capabilities, open-source talent, and off-the-shelf tools for safety but may also be less of a target for those who would compromise cybersecurity systems. In general, organizations may face the cybersecurity labor gap in a few ways: mitigate it through stop-gap measures; collaborate with others to address this shortfall; fill the gap by training employees; ignore the labor gap; delay programs dependent on cybersecurity; and so forth.

There are cybersecurity best practices in professional settings that should be in play whether there are assigned cybersecurity roles and team members within an organization, such as building informational systems with security in mind, updating software consistently, staying atop news of cybersecurity breaches, training staff to be aware of phishing and other scams, having recovery systems in case of data compromise or loss, isolating infected machines from a network, maintaining surveillance of systems, training staff to use due caution in travel (such as using cleaned machines without any sensitive data), and so on. Cybersecurity is a basic business function whether or not an organization has assigned roles to that effect. Eventually, as the need lessens for such talent, the pay and rewards will plateau (and they may even normalize and drop). Those in the educational pipeline should have the proper level of adaptivity to move in a number of directions, even if it is not into cybersecurity work.

What are the purposes of the abstract and parsimonious model? The target audience includes those involved in cybersecurity policy, strategy, and work. One purpose is to highlight the important roles of the general public, the public sector, and the private sector, and the synergies that may be found there. Figure 1 aims to be both descriptive and somewhat analytical but not comprehensive by any means. Figure 2 focuses more closely to the cybersecurity job market. The aim is to show the importance of striving to identify strategic methods to tide organizations over the cybersecurity worker shortfall, which will require strategic decision-making (what security systems to roll out, what skills to hire for, what technologies to adopt, and so on). A third is to help cybersecurity workers better understand the 30,000-foot level of their employment space.

FUTURE RESEARCH DIRECTIONS

This work offers a model of the cyber talent gap in the labor markets based on general systems theory, social network analysis, game theory, and abductive logic and up-to-date data. This work stops short of integrating the data with the model, in part, because only general summary workforce data is available.

It may help to see what the employment market will bear in terms of cybersecurity talent. One example comes from the U.S. Department of Labor’s Bureau of Labor Statistics. As of May 2016, those working as Information Security Analysts earned a mean hourly wage of US$46.17 for a mean annual wage of US$96,040 (“15-1122 Information Security Analysts”, 2016). In terms of percentiles, the formal estimates may be seen in Figure 4.

| --- |

According to the U.S. Department of Labor, the industries with the highest levels of employment in this occupation include the following in descending order: Computer Systems Design and Related Services (27,300), Management of Companies and Enterprises (8,820), Depository Credit Intermediation (7,080), Management, Scientific, and Technical Consulting Services (4,650), and Insurance Carriers (3,900) (“15-1122 Information Security Analysts,” May 2016).

The top-paying industries for this occupation include the following (in descending order): Wholesale Electronic Markets and Agents and Brokers; Securities and Commodity Contracts Intermediation and Brokerage; Advertising, Public Relations, and Related Services; Newspaper, Periodical, Book, and Directory Publishers; and Commercial and Service Industry Machinery Manufacturing, with pay scales all in the six figures. Of course, in this area, there are many other professional roles, and many of them do not bring such high salaries. In addition, other positions in cybersecurity offer even higher wages and job perks. The specificities of such data may shed illuminate other insights, in combination with theory-informed modeling.

The two earlier conceptual "modeling" visualizations in this chapter embody the informal conceptual model, with pretentions of some applied practicality. Both would benefit from further empirical data-based specifications. For example, “A Simplified National Cybersecurity Ecosystem and the Global Cybersecurity Talent Gap” (Figure 1) would benefit from specifications across a number of nations to understand what efforts are being taken and where major gaps (unexploited potentials) exist. For “A Conceptualization of the Cybersecurity Work(er) Space” (Figure 2), empirical data may be used to estimate probabilities of cybersecurity workers being in any particular state…at a slice in time…at an organization level, at a state level, at a national level, at a regional level, and even at a global level. It would help to map cybersecurity worker work trajectories over a career lifespan to understand their experiences and decision-making (particularly at critical junctures, such as moments of their absorption into non-cybersecurity work). Combining models with data may inform awareness and decision-making in the real world.

CONCLUSION

This cybersecurity work demands high-level skills and expensive training—both initially and throughout their careers. The various shapes of threats in the cybersecurity space are continuously changing, and it is not clear whether people are up to the task at securing critical infrastructures that rely on cyber. If there were a current tally sheet, the situation looks quite dire with billions of value lost from corporations and governments. This early work suggests some possible mitigations for the cybersecurity worker shortfall.

KEY TERMS AND DEFINITIONS

Cybersecurity: A state of non-compromise of computerized systems.

Game Theory: A mathematical-based method to analyze strategies among competing entities.

Labor Market: A system within which workers with varying capabilities are recruited and find employment.

Markov Chain: A model of “possible events” based on prior steps and decisions.

Social Network Theory: A conceptualization of how people interact as individuals and groups.

Systems Theory: A multidisciplinary set of concepts about how a group of connected parts interact.

# Chapter 2

The Role of Cyber and Information Technology Security in Automated Business Environments

*   Antoine Trad  
    Institute of Business and Information Systems Transformation Management, France
*   Damir Kalpić  
    University of Zagreb, Croatia

ABSTRACT

The business transformation project (BTP) of a modern business environment needs a well-designed information and cyber technology security automation concept (ITSAC) that, in turn, depends on measurable success factors. These factors are used for the evolution of the transformation process. During the last decade, due to the global insecurity and financial crisis, the security strategies are not efficient. That is mainly due to the fact that businesses depend on security standards, cyber and information technology evolution, enterprise architecture, business engineering, and multilevel interoperability. They are restricted to blindfolded infrastructure security operations. Major BTPs are brutally wrecked by various security violations that may cause a no-go decision.

INTRODUCTION

The Business Transformation Project (BTP) of a modern business environment needs a well-designed Information and cyber Technology Security Automation Concept (ITSAC) that, in turn, depends on measurable success factors; these factors are used for the evolution of the transformation process. During the last decade, the security strategies and measure are insufficient due to the global insecurity and financial crisis. That is mainly due to the fact that businesses depend on security standards, cyber and information technology evolution, enterprise architecture, business engineering, and multilevel interoperability. They are restricted to blindfolded infrastructure security operations. Major BTPs are brutally wrecked by various security violations that may cause a no-go decision. Most of such security misfits are used for internal politics, while highly important issues and teams' problems are simply ignored.

The most damaging fact is that business environments lose their transformational momentum, what can negatively affect their business sustainability and leave it open to security breaches and financial loses. Financial Technology (FinTech) is the latest technology buzzword that aims to change the traditional financial environment in the delivery of interactive financial services. In this article, the authors propose a set of managerial recommendations on how to avoid such critical situations.

Today many security architectures exist, and even when very advanced, unfortunately they often follow a silo model. This chapter can support the Cyberbusiness transformation process of the traditional business environment through the automation of all its security operations and their related business processes. Transforming a traditional security subsystem and the related archaic legal constraints is an important challenge, because of the probability that the security and legal team(s) resist to change. An ITSAC subsystem may provide the base for flexible business services for the future business environment to avoid the security-human dependency.

The aim of this chapter is to support business transformation managers or enterprise architects in managing frequent changes to business environments and the integration of automated ITSAC procedures. To achieve this goal, the authors offer an ITSAC automation pattern that could support transformation processes. Security controls for a business entity, regional body, government, or geopolitical entity is a set of interrelated activities from various domains like security architecture, financial engineering, geopolitical influence, governance and legal conformance. All that can be used to avoid financial crimes, business disruptions and corruption.

Complex transformation initiatives must be coherent with the entity’s business and security strategic planning goals; where the main strategic goal is to minimize the various types of criminal acts. Security controls are the fuel of the entity’s sustainable business growth and its integration in global economies. Security control schemes can be supported by security and risk frameworks, standards, and legal controls that are necessary for the company’s business strategy that is based on a cybersecurity background (Trad & Kalpić, 2017a; Trad & Kalpić, 2017b)

BACKGROUND

In a holistic cybersecurity architecture, the Business Transformation Manager’s (BTM) role is important and his or her (for simplicity, in further text – his) decisions are aided by using factors within an implemented applied mathematical model. A large set of factors can influence such a mathematical model, including: a) the role of the cybersecurity enforcement control by using ITSAC; b) global geopolitical factors; c) political and cultural setup; d) level of skills; e) cyber and technological conditions; f) financial competition and financial greediness; and g) security, financial and legal control mechanisms. A systems approach is the optimal to model such controls (Daellenbach & McNickle, 2005; Trad & Kalpić, 2016a). As shown in Figure 1, the decision model interacts with the external world via an implemented framework to manage the security risks and that is this article’s focus.

FOCUS OF THE ARTICLE

The Research Processes

This research’s main topic is related to BTPs with the following research question: “Which business transformation manager characteristics and which type of support should be assured in the implementation phase of a business transformation project?” Decision making concepts based on critical success areas are their main research component.

Critical Success Areas, Factors, and Decision Making

The Critical Success Area (CSA) is a category of Critical Success Factors (CSF) where, in turn, a CSF is a set of Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) in which a KPI corresponds to a single requirement or feature. For a given problem, a framework analyst must identify the initial set of CSFs to be used for the decision-making system. Hence, the CSFs are the most important mapping/relation between the geopolitical construct, financial status, organisational predisposition and decision-making system; that defines the business ecosystem of global financial crime (Peterson, 2011). The proposed applied mathematical model or the AMM delivers a set of recommendations and solutions for the cybersecurity architecture that is a part of the Framework (Trad & Kalpić, 2017c; Trad, & Kalpić, 2017d).

The Framework

The BTM or enterprise architect’s security design decisions can be made in a just-in-time manner by using outputs from various credible technology logging sources. The defined cybersecurity strategy should asses and govern global system security risks and at the same time legally assert or control the BTP’s resources that are formalized with an enterprise architecture blueprint. A research framework can support such an undertaking, as shown in Figure 2. Unfortunately, an immense set of archaic factors can influence such a process, like: 1) the influence of cyber security on business transformation projects; 2) working with complex systems with a very strict legal framework; and 3) the holistic cyberlaw control mechanisms for such projects are non-existent or are too complex to implement.

A global concept and the management of related cybersecurity systems approach is optimal for such control mechanisms (Daellenbach & McNickle, 2005). In this research, the focus is on the ITSAC module that manages the BTP’s global security. The ITSAC can be applied to many BTPs and general fields in the Framework and it is a part of the Financial Management module (Fm) and the Architecture and Modelling module (Am). In this chapter, the authors propose a set of ITSAC managerial recommendations and a reusable real-world module (Trad 2017b; Trad 2017c).

| Figure 2. The neural network implementation environment that enables business engineering |

| ![Figure978-1-5225-5927-6.ch002.f02](i/ch002.f02.png) |

The ITSAC component is managed by The Open Group’s Architecture Framework (TOGAF) architecture development method’s phases in which each architecture microartefact circulates through its phases. The architecture microartefacts contain their private set of Critical Success Factors, as shown in Figure 2. These CSFs can be applied to (Peterson, 2011): a) select the important cybersecurity factors; b) detect the BTP’s security risks high points; c) estimate the actual risks status of the BTP using the decision support system’s interface; and to eventually take a decision on BTP’s continuation; d) control and monitor the needed ITSAC mechanisms; e) upgrade the BTP’s team cybersecurity skills; and f) support the architecture and project management activities.

The Framework or the Environment is composed of the following modules:

*   • “Sm”: for the selection management of the Framework.
*   • “Am”: for the architecture and modelling strategy that can be applied by the Framework.
*   • “Cm” for the control and monitoring strategy that can be applied by the Framework.
*   • “Dm” for the decision-making strategy that can be applied by the Framework.
*   • “Tm” for the training management of the Framework.
*   • “Pm” for the project management strategy that can be applied by the Framework.
*   • “Fm” for the financial management’s support to the Framework.
*   • “Gm” for the Geopolitical mind-mining to the Framework.
*   • “F” for Framework

This chapter is a part of the research cluster that has produced many articles, literature reviews, usable items and research artefacts. In this chapter, the minimum of sections from previous works are reused for a better understanding of this complex subject. Therefore, this work can be considered as a pioneering one in the field of global architecture concepts. For this phase of research, the authors attempted to deliver their findings and recommendations to clarify the risks patchwork, using the mathematical model of a decision-making system that is based on critical success factors. For that purpose, this phase’s research sub-question is the following: “What are the risks of Cybersecurity on transformation projects?”

The Decision-Making System

The Decision-Making System (DMS) is conceptually based on a mixed method, combining Action Research (AR), tree heuristics, and directed quantitative analysis. The authors believe that qualitative and quantitative methods can be united in a single method. AR is applied in education research and this fact supports the BTP’s capability to build business intelligence microartefacts in a continuous learning process. This process inspects and learns from configurable intelligent microartefacts that are found in the DMS. The decision system is generic and can be applied to any business domain and is easily adaptable (Trad & Kalpić, 2017c; Peterson, 2011) and a second step, if needed, applies a precise quantitative analysis.

A DMS must be managed by existing audit or governance frameworks where the BTM’s acceptance of various types of risks is required. These risks are estimated by the BTM, by using DMS actions to deliver solutions. The DMS actions’ map to the governance processes, found in TOGAF’s phase G, which is responsible for implementation governance that adjusts the business view. DMS artefacts are implemented in all the BTP components and the implementation of governance mechanisms should be able to identify critical risks. They are to be managed (as CSFs), what might need many iterations to limit the risks which can be modeled and managed by a mathematical model (The Open Group, 2011a).

The Applied Organizational and Mathematical Model

The proposed AMM is domain agnostic and is not related to any specific methodology and contains a configurable reasoning module that uses CSFs sets and actions (Peterson, 2011); here the enterprise refers to a considered organisation. As shown in Figure 3, the applied AMM supports a microartefact based architecture, which uses a business-driven approach and uses also the Open Group’s Architecture Development Method (ADM) (Trad & Kalpić, 2017b).

THE SECURITY CONCEPT

Cybersecurity is the state of a business system that can be prone to any type of danger or threat; where the BTP must deliver a system that is designed to provide maximum security (Oxford Dictionaries, 2017a). This section presents the factors that influence the ITSAC and this first CSA tries to argue the various aspects of cybersecurity requirements. Cybersecurity depends on the following fields: 1) Cyber technologies; 2) national security requirements; 3) international security requirements; and 4) organizational security requirements. Cybersecurity requirements are the most fundamental for an organization’s business survival and they enclose various subdomains.

The Modules Chained Link to the Technology Integration

THE INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY INTEGRATION

Global or holistic Cyberbusiness agility is achieved by combining various methodologies that promote business and technological agility to be used on various levels of the BTP to unbundle the existing business environment and glue its renovated parts using dynamic Internet microartefacts. Using a bottom-up approach, the BTP team can design the optimal Cyberbusiness technology integration concept that can handle various types of cybersecurity requirements to be used in the standard architecture development method.

Architecture Development Method’s Integration

The Architecture Development Method’s (ADM) integration in a BTP enables the automation of all its activities, throughout all the ADM iterations. The ADM encloses SecDevOps; as shown in Figure 7 where all their phases log information to a unified logging system.

A Unified Control and Logging Subsystem

Cyberbusiness platforms are not dedicated to any specific business environment and offer: 1) performance; 2) reliability; and 3) Cybersecurity. These platforms are controlled and monitored in real-time using Unified Logging Subsystem (ULS) and are integrated to support the ITSAC. ULSs exist and are powerful monitoring subsystems that support presentation, sorting, and tuning. ULSs can be designed to analyse, collect and store ITSAC data from various BTP microartefacts to support central decision-making logging system.

Decision-Making System’s Integration

The ITSAC’s DMS logs are inputs from various subsystems and the inputs depend on the warning level. If the BTP team signals a problem to be solved, then the DMS is activated to propose possible solution(s). ITSAC’s underlined model includes microartefact scenarios of interactive atomic service actions. Atomic services make the integration flexible (Trad & Kalpić, 2017a). DMS’s components support the BTP by offering security microartefacts that are instances of the building blocks.

ITSAC’s Microartefact

ITSAC’s microartefact is an instance of the building block that can interact with other BTPs microartefacts in a traced and synchronized manner and uses TOGAF’s ADM to assist it in the grouping of the needed services (The Open Group, 2011a).
