The Modules Chained Link to the Financial Reasoning

This section’s deduction is that the technology is the backbone of the ITSAC subsystem in which intentional breaches can promote illegal financial profit.

THE FINANCIAL BACKGROUND

Holistic business agility is achieved by combining various methodologies that promote cybersecurity and technological agility to be used on various levels of the BTP to unbundle the traditional business environment and glue its transformed components by using dynamic technology microartefacts. Using TOGAF’s ADM, the BTP team can design the optimal Cyberbusiness environment that can handle various types of financial and technology engineering risks.

Finance and Technology

As previously mentioned, FinTech is the technology that aims to change the traditional financial environment in the delivery of interactive financial services. The usage of intelligent financial endpoints provides some of the technologies intended to make financial services open to many external endpoints. Although FinTech can be used to tackle financial cybercriminality, it seems that the countries that support massive financial crimes are making the largest investment in these innovative technologies (Ravanetti, 2016). FinTech companies are transforming the usage of financial services using blockchains and Bitcoin-based technologies very probably for the mere goal of financial profit (Wikipedia, 2017a).

| Figure 8. Finance and technology leading countries |

| ![Figure978-1-5225-5927-6.ch002.f08](i/ch002.f08.png) |
| --- |
| *Ravanetti, 2016.* |

Blockchains and Bitcoin

Blockchain is the technology framework that supports cryptocurrency like the Bitcoin; Bitcoin supports exchange of currencies in a digital encryption form (PWC, 2017). FinTech automation causes the synchronization of various Cyberfinance services that need specific regulation and cybersecurity mechanisms, knowing that today the most important phenomena are cybercriminality as an emerging type of criminality and on the other hand, the apparent disappearance of traditional currencies.

Currencies

With the rapid emergence of FinTech, blockchain technologies will dominate the leading financial giants and will cause the domination of the Bitcoin. This new media would lead to disappearance of leading currencies like the Swiss Franc; such an event would be a major problem for tracing financial fraud. This scenario is not assured; a possibility that the bulb of cryptocurrencies might blow, should not be completely excluded.

FinTech Fraud

FinTech would make money more abstract and difficult to trace; individuals and institutions in countries that have the culture of financial secrecy and arbitral confiscation, would be tempted to use FinTech to obfuscate the origins of money. Paula Ramada estimated the amount of lost money due to the benchmark of interest rates debacle is estimated at US$300 trillion in financial instruments, ranging from mortgages to student loans in which a trillion represents 1 billion of billions (10⁹x10⁹) or 10^(18). Therefore, a change or manipulation of a mere 0.1% has a damage of 10^(15) of euros per year; this is the mechanism that banks used to cover the decrease of loans and save their investments at the cost of ruining middle and lower-class households; whereby some banks like the Swiss UBS got much richer (Ramada, 2013). FinTech would make such operations more embedded and abstract.

The Modules Chained Link to the Legal Aspects

This section’s deduction is that the legal aspects can be the major problem for the ITSAC subsystem in which intentional legal breaches can bring profit to a country’s economy.

THE LEGAL ASPECTS

ITSAC supports the business environment’s legal integration in the globalized environment; to achieve this legal support, CSFs are used to assert and monitor the BTP artefacts. The CSFs manage the differences in cyberbusiness local and international laws. Cyberbusiness environments must have the capacity to proactively recognize erroneous cybertransactions (Daellenbach & McNickle, 2005).

Cybertransactions’ Security Violations

The European Commission defines a legislation to govern Cyberbusiness and progress has been done in its assertion. European Commission member states have implemented and enforced business-engineering related national practices. Cybertransactions outcomes have to be continually legally asserted, traced, and their periodic summaries are reported to the executive management (Fu & Mittnight, 2015). Cyberbusinesses are orthogonal to cybersecurity requirements, where the business environment roles define the responsibility for enterprise’s resources. Management of the enterprise’s legal interests, resources, and accesses, should be managed by enterprise architect(s). Thus, the Cyberbusiness structure is an important consideration in the legal assertion and access management of Cybertransaction’s security. The regulation for the Cybertransaction’s security and law needs qualified time-stamps for robust (e)certification like those used in the European Union (European Union, 2014).

Cybertransaction Law

Cybertransaction is influenced by the Uniform Law Commissioners who promulgated the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act in 1999. It is the first adaptable effort to prepare a Cyberlaw for Cyberbusiness. Many countries have adopted Cyberbusiness regulations. The Uniform Electronic Transactions Act represents the first effort in providing some standardized rules to govern Cybertransactions. (The Uniform Law Commissioners, 2015).

Cyberbusiness Legislation Assertion

The integration of the business engineering module is done with the use of the standardized legal environment of The Open Group’s Architecture Framework. This legal environment supports data protection laws, contract law, procurement law, fraud law and many other legislation domains to counter organized financial crimes.

Financial Crime Model

Brutal dictators like neo-Nazi brigands have a special status in states where the ownership of substantial financial assets can remain anonymous. Some Third World dictators maintain strong financial relationship to banks in financial havens. Some of these banks have even been established by criminals emerged from former wars. An example can be the notorious Nazi banker Francois Genoud (Brown, 2016). A country where the money cannot be transparently audited can provide security to dubious investors, although otherwise the same country may serve as role model of law obeying common citizens.

Some of financial havens and their financial institutions have been the main leaders in worldwide financial scandals, misdeeds, and criminal acts including: a) the Libor manipulation; b) currency manipulations; c) credits manipulations; d) supporting arms dealing transactions; e) hijacking people’s wealth; f) financial fraud; g) the subprime crisis; h) war victim wealth confiscation; i) tax evasion; j) drug dealing financial support; k) war support against future financial competitors; l) forced confiscations; m) drastic fines; and l) arms dealing (Trad, 2017a); the major problem with combating such a system is that some countires have hermetically closed system characterised by the following attitudes:

*   • Police and information services, blocking any attempt to pursue financial criminal acts.
*   • The legal system, ignoring any attempt to investigate financial criminal acts.
*   • Legal support too expensive, to discourage any action of law enforcing.
*   • Psychological harassment,, to discredit investigators.
*   • Intolerance and discrimination, to block any foreign request.
*   • A powerful global network, to embed and hide various dubious operations.
*   • Financial guerrilla-like and hit and run tactics, to confiscate wealth.
*   • Occurrence of financial locked-in situations.

Some financial haven states target to become leaders in FinTech, which is not very assuring; because FinTech should combat state criminality and enforce cybersecurity international law.

*   • Avoid any form of financial collaboration with organizations in above described countries acting like financial havens.

Some states targets to be leaders in FinTech, which is definitely not very assuring because FinTech should combat state criminality and enforce cybersecurity international law.

Cybersecurity International Law

Facts show that international law on cybersecurity is inefficient and agonizing. Advanced states are hesitant to integrate international law that is based on the emergence of non-government norm-making initiatives. States insist on their traditional central legal system that marginalizes the inter-state governance of cyberspace (Mačák, 2016).

SOLUTION AND RECOMMENDATIONS

In this chapter the authors propose the following set of managerial recommendations:

*   • A BTP must build a holistic architectural concept to insure an efficient cybersecurity.
*   • Important efforts applied to integrate underlying technology to support a huge number of Cybertransactions.
*   • Cybertechnologies should replace traditional exchanges in order to improve productivity and to enforce in real-time ITSAC.
*   • Cybersecurity architecture should fit in the company's global enterprise architecture framework.
*   • The architecture development method’s integration in a BTP enables the automation of all its activities.
*   • Applications’ development and operations are coordinated by the SecDevOps.
*   • ISTAs are controlled and monitored by ULSs.
*   • FinTech would make financial operations more embedded and abstract.
*   • Cyberbusinesses are orthogonal to cybersecurity requirements.
*   • Cybertransaction is influenced by local and international Cyberlaw; where both are limited.
*   • Avoid any form of financial collaboration with doubtful financial organizations.

FUTURE RESEARCH DIRECTIONS

The Environment future research will focus on the evolution of the mathematical model.

CONCLUSION

This research phase is part of a series of publications related to BTPs and enterprise architectures. This research is based on mixed action research model; where critical success factors and areas are offered to help BTP architects to decrease the chances of failure. In this article, the focus is on cybersecurity. Cybersecurity architecture is business-driven and describes a structured inter-relationship between the technical and procedural security solutions to support the long-term needs of Cyberbusiness. The ITSAC component’s holistic integration is an important factor for the Cyberbusiness’ evolution. The most important managerial recommendation that was generated by the previous research phases was that the business transformation manager must be an architect of adaptive business systems. The PoC is based on the CSFs’ binding to a specific research resources and the reasoning model represents the relationships between this research’s requirements, microartefacts and the CSFs. The result is that security and financial and technology CSAs are very important for cybersecurity.

# Chapter 3

Cyber Risk Insurance

*   İsmail Yıldırım  
    Hittite University, Turkey

ABSTRACT

Security vulnerabilities available in cyber security systems lead to virtual and physical damages to financial systems which in turn cause national- and individual-level security issues. Today’s world is being shaped by digital technology, and cyber threats to information constitute a significant risk factor for businesses. This study explores the cyber security risks the banking system may encounter. The status of banking system, a system which includes a number of online services, in Turkey with respect to cyber security risks and the current risks are assessed and presented along with possible solutions. This study analyzes e-payment systems (online banking and e-trade/the use of debit/credit cards) and the supply chain, the backbone of the e-finance system, with respect to national cyber security risks. Nevertheless, cyber risk insurance, an emerging tool for cyber risk management, was analyzed in detail.

INTRODUCTION

Many nations introduce radical solutions against cyberattacks and make investments in such solutions. A number of nations such as the United States of America prefer to protect their critical infrastructure of cyber security on the market level, while nations such as Israel developed state-centric security strategies. Many cyber security specialists stated that it is not possible to adopt an effective defense and counteracting security regimen without cooperation with the stakeholders from the private sector, as the state services are backed by a number of private service providers and telecommunication companies (Grauman, 2012).

Cyber risk is a type of risk which includes any unexpected technical failure of the IT infrastructure of a business or any cyberattack targeting such infrastructure which leads to possible financial losses and damaged brand value. Today, any commercial establishment ranging from Small- and Middle-sized Enterprises (SMEs) to international businesses face the financial consequences of the risks arising from cyber threats. As a result, a new market has emerged with the increasing interest in cyber security products.

Cyberattacks brought with them a new opportunity for insurance companies which offer their services in a highly competitive market and that want to expand their product range. Many companies have already introduced their cyber insurance products. And many more are preparing to launch their products. According to the survey by ABI Research, it is expected the global cyber risk insurance market will reach up to US$10 billion in market value by 2020. The main factors behind this growth are reported to be the increased costs associated with cyber breaches and cyberattacks, and the adoption of risk management strategies which tend to transfer the risks associated with cyber threats to insurance companies. It was further reported that the cyber risk insurance market has been growing at an annual rate of 20-30% in the USA and Europe (www.usom.gov.tr).

Cyberattacks constitute a major risk factor for both privately-owned and state-owned enterprises. Insurance companies have developed insurance packages to minimize the possible effects of cyberattacks on enterprises under the names of data recovery insurance, data protection insurance, cyber insurance, and cyber liability insurance. Cyberattacks may have adverse effects on the automation infrastructure of enterprises. However, the reach of such attacks are not limited to these systems. These cyberattacks are associated with legal, managerial, public relations, and financial consequences (Assaf, 2008).

Cyber liability insurance companies offer assurance against such cyber risks having analyzed the relevant consequences. A cyberattack may have adverse effects on the reputation and market value of an enterprise, not to mention the damages such as confidential information theft or corruption of the information. Coverage of cyber liability insurance policy may include damages and protection costs associated with a breach of information, virus threats to the third party data, unauthorized access to third party information, access to system codes, software theft, employees’ disclosure of confidential information, and so forth.

Moreover, it is also possible to be insured, optionally, with policy coverage of any damages associated with an interruption in network functions, payments made to third parties in order to eliminate any security threats, corruption of electronic information due to negligence, and any costs arising from protective measures taken.

CYBER SECURITY RISKS

Aon, one of the global leaders in risk management, insurance, reassurance brokerage and human resources consultation, publishes a number of reports annually based on the opinions of specialists, their know-how and research data available. And one of the most important reports is the Global Risk Management Survey. According to the survey made in 2017, “Damage to Reputation/Brand” was listed on top of a list of 10 risks, which emphasizes the need to manage this risk properly in enterprises. Defective products, fraudulent business practices and corruption remained among the major risks threatening a company’s reputation. Cyber risk, on the other hand, was listed in the fifth position.

Top 10 Risks to be Managed Properly by Businesses

*   1\. Damage to reputation/brand2. Economic slowdown/slow recovery3. Increasing competition4. Regulatory/legislative changes5. Cybercrime/hacking/viruses/malicious codes6. Failure to innovate/meet customer needs7. Failure to attract or retain top talent8. Business interruption9. Political risk/uncertainties10. Third party liability

Cyber risk is a type of risk which includes any unexpected technical failure of the IT infrastructure of a business or any cyberattack targeting such infrastructure which leads to possible financial losses and damaged brand value. Cyber risks are often analyzed under two categories (Felici, 2012);

*   1\. 1st Party Risks
*   2\. 3rd Party Risks

In general, 1st Party Risks consist of damaged data or data theft due to a cyberattack targeting an enterprise, and any adverse impact on the revenue of an enterprise as a result of a cyberattack. Among the risks classified under 1st Party Risks which may arise due to data theft, data breaches or viruses are, as follows:

*   • Loss of Data
*   • Software Errors
*   • Ransom demands made in order to unlock the data encrypted by hackers
*   • Any damages associated with network failure
*   • Deleted or manipulated enterprise data
*   • Halt and/or slowing down of operations
*   • Risks involved in the disclosure of stolen data
*   • Damage to reputation

On the other hand, 3rd Party Risks are those involving the persons and enterprises affected by a cyberattack other than the insured itself. Such risks may include any court actions or claims which can be made to the insured by any 3rd parties affected by a data breach or other cybercrimes. A cyber liability insurance policy must include both 1st and 3rd Party risks in its coverage to be preferable. Among the risks classified under 3rd Party Risks are, as follows:

*   • Security and privacy breaches
*   • Investigation of privacy breach
*   • Customer notification/PR expenses
*   • Multi-media liability
*   • Loss of third-party data
*   • Third-party contractual indemnification

Unfortunately, we are not yet able to offer a solution to eliminate cyber risks permanently. Therefore, it is an important discussion for the businesses to decide on which cyber risks must be mitigated. Today, many companies base their decision making process on the analysis of the damages caused by a number of vulnerabilities. It is often impossible to suggest clearly if the measures taken are able to protect against cyber threats, not to mention the degree of protection they provide (INSA, 2009).

How to invest in this field when it is so difficult to interpret and analyze the benefits of investments made in order to mitigate the ever changing cyber risks? It is quite hard to calculate the material damages associated with a data breach before it happens. Enterprises often use the methods they apply to other risks - focusing on actions to minimize the loss of revenue- in order to deal with cyber risks. However, it would be possible to take necessary actions against cyber threats and cyber risks when effective analyses are performed.

Reputation is one of the most important assets a business holds and it is one that is more difficult to protect. Any damage to the brand value is much more important for a firm when compared to immediate damages. The reason is that any damage to the brand value would mean long-term loss of revenue. Thus, cyber risk analysis and taking measures against such risks are of utmost importance for managers. Any measures taken to mitigate the cyber risks may prevent the loss of hundreds of millions of dollars annually.

The first step of cyber risk analysis involves the identification of important assets a company holds and the vulnerabilities associated with these assets. Any possible damages of cyberattacks may manifest themselves in the form of loss of revenue or in the form of expenses made in order to recover the system after an attack or costs arising from forensic information analyses and consultation costs. Customer’s loss of trust may prove to be significant when the cyber criminals are able to get their hands on critical data (Grauman, 2012).

Managers are expected to decide on what measures to invest in and how much to invest in it in order to mitigate the risks, having properly analyzed the cyber risks or having taken measures based on their past experience. Therefore, what are the parameters managers need to use in order to analyze the cyber risks? And how to derive such risk parameters? The answer to these questions will vary depending on the sector. Moreover, a commonly accepted fact is that reliable data is needed to conduct risk analysis and that such data is used to create risk models. Continuous Surveillance is the most effective method used in cyber risk analysis.

CYBER DEFENSE MECHANISMS

Personal data theft and their malicious use, blocking or disruption of critical processes, organizing cyberattacks which will produce a burden on the economy, theft of national secrets or the disclosure of stolen data are just some of the cyberattack types and their numbers are increasing every other day. Individuals, business world and state-owned enterprises store or transfer their intellectual properties, economic, or personal data using technological devices. It is known that such data transfer may lead to significant economic loss or damage to reputation, if the data is corrupted or it was not transferred at all in this process (BTK, 2014).

A closer look into the nationwide applications showed there are many different financial security mechanisms in place and corporate software vary widely; some nations have taken their practices very seriously and covered a lot of ground in this respect while others failed to build even the most basic corporate structures. Briefly, we cannot talk about a consensus between nations in terms of the standardization of practice. For example, in the South African Republic, the rules behind deposit protection, a very basic financial security element, are not clearly defined by the authorities.

Some other countries, on the other hand, preferred to build a separate authority for each important element and some countries brought a number of missions together under the umbrella of a single authority. Nevertheless, the most common practice has been the formation of an authority responsible for money laundering investigations, systemic and cyber security risk investigations.

While some countries do not feel the need for a liquidity window as defined by their central bank, nations such as Spain, Greece, and others preferred to take out loans from international organizations (e.g., International Monetary Fund, European Commission, AMB-SSM) which, in return, led to be closely supervised and controlled by those organizations. Excluding nations such as Singapore as extremes, these countries were never welcoming to foreign banks above a certain threshold in terms of both the number and size of assets. The same also applies to shadow banking systems (Yeşilyurt, 2015).

While some nations performed stress tests and scenario analyses on a quarterly, biannual or annual basis, the others choose not to perform such analyses at all, or performed them randomly. Financing of projects, especially in important sectors such as infrastructure, power, information, telecommunication, defense, finance is managed under specific regulations in many countries. It can be seen that local authorities are able to impose business models on businesses in countries other than those which strictly follow liberalization practices such as the USA.

Furthermore, another practice which calls for standardization is “credit recall” which is being discussed for functioning whether as a safety bump or as a trigger for crises in economy. Some nations give enough flexibility to banks to recall their credits, while others strictly ban such a practice (Kendrick, 2010). There are three main features of an effective and balanced cyber defense practice: To be safe, to be aware, and to be resistant (www.usom.gov.tr).

*   • To be Safe: It implies a focus on providing protection against the risk. Here, risk involves the most valued assets of a business from the perspectives of both the company and its rivals.
*   • To be Aware: It implies raising awareness in every level of the organization and development of the capacity of detecting any risky behavior associated with important assets before such behavior occurs.
*   • To be Resistant: It implies the ability to respond quickly to the damage, to ensure it does not affect other operations, and the ability to use necessary and several tools in order to minimize damages which involve direct costs, loss of workload, damages to reputation and loss of brand value.

In conclusion, it can be said that any nation which did not establish necessary financial security mechanisms, which did not place the priority on financial security, and which did not put into motion reforms and restorations based on the insights derived from past crises (e.g., Russia, Argentina, Greece) is vulnerable to serious economic and financial crises.

ELECTRONIC AND CYBER RISK IN THE TURKISH BANKING SECTOR

The regulation imposed on banks operating in Turkey to have their automation systems and their backups in Turkey is a security measure in place both in terms of financial security and electronic and cyber security as its subsegment. According to the amendment to the Regulation on the Internal Systems of Banks dated June 1, 2010, banks operating in Turkey are obliged to have their primary and secondary IT systems located in Turkey. Regulation on Internal Systems of Banks and Measurement and Evaluation of the Capital Adequacy of Banks, which superseded the aforementioned regulation maintained the same provision in the paragraph 4 of the article 11. Thus, banks are required to have their primary systems and also their secondary (backup) systems located in Turkey (http://www.usom.gov.tr/).

Members of the banking systems in Turkey most commonly purchase necessary e-commerce and other online finance cyber security software from foreign countries. The important point here is that cyber security software are purchased from the Internet without being subject to any controls as opposed to the procedures in place for products purchased in sectors such as automobile, pharmaceutical, and so forth. The fact that the procedures used in other fields are disregarded for the cyber security software supply chain brings with it important risks for cyber security.

A National Cyber Security Coordination Foundation was founded in accordance with the Decree on Execution and Coordination of National Cyber Security Affairs published in the Official Gazette on October 20, 2012. The 4th item available in the decree reads, “Members of this foundation will be assigned to define the measures to be taken in association with cyber security, to approve plans and programs, reporting principles and standards, and to coordinate the application of such function”. The foundation consists of executives from departments and state-owned enterprises as assigned by the Minister of Transport, Maritime Affairs and Communications in addition to authorities assigned by specific ministries, state-owned enterprises under the presidency of the Minister of Transport, Maritime Affairs and Communications (BTK, 2014).

With the decision encouraging the cooperation of state-owned enterprises, it has become essential for all state-owned enterprises to comply with the plans, programs, principles and standards published by the Ministry with the purpose of National Cyber Security. It is another important component of the decree that it encourages locally developed solutions to national cyber security. On the other hand, the fact that National Cyber Security took precedence in the monetary resource planning and resource allocation stands out as a principle paving the way for research in this field.

Turkish Government released a Cyber Security Strategy and an Action Plan. The following are the principles to be considered in order to ensure national cyber security (http://www.udhb.gov.tr/doc/siberg/2016-2019guvenlik.pdf):

*   1\. Cyber security is only possible through efficiently and continuously improved methods based on risk management.
*   2\. An integrative approach is taken in order to define strengths and weaknesses, threats and opportunities in technical, legal, administrative, economic, politic and social aspects.
*   3\. Risk management is based on the principle that possible damages are minimized through the elimination of technical vulnerabilities and the prevention of attacks and threats.
*   4\. It is widely expected from the individuals, enterprises, society and the state to comply with all their legal and social responsibilities in order to ensure cyber security.
*   5\. Full cooperation of private sector and their participation in decision-making mechanism is necessary in order to ensure the protection of critical infrastructure.
*   6\. In addition to the cooperation of state, private sector, academia and NGOs, international cooperation and information sharing is the key for the cyber security and its sustainability.
*   7\. Uninterrupted and efficient use of diplomatic, technical and law enforcement channels is the basis of international cooperation and information sharing.
*   8\. International deals and regulations are considered when the necessary legislation is discussed.
*   9\. The rule of law, basic human rights and protection of privacy are among the principles to be adopted.
*   10\. Transparency, accountability, ethic values and freedom of speech are supported in cyber environment.
*   11\. There is a fine balance between security and usability.
*   12\. Regulatory and monitoring organs ensure that the cyber security is provided in the fields they are responsible for.
*   13\. The use of local products and services is promoted in order to satisfy cyber security needs; R&D projects are supported to develop such local products and a sense of innovation is established.

There are various penalties for banks regarding cyber-attacks conducted in Turkey. A person who seizes or holds a bank or credit card of someone else in any way under penalty of imprisonment for a period of three years up to six years and forensic money if he or she benefits him or her by using or using it without the request of the cardholder or the person he shall be punished by his penalty. A person who makes a fraudulent or fraudulent use of a bank or credit card to punish him or another for up to seven years in prison for a period of four years if he does not commit another crime requiring more severe punishment.

CYBER RISK MANAGEMENT IN BANKS

The success of Cyber Risk Management depends on the CEO. The role of each senior executive is also very important. However, the most important point is that all top managers and their affiliated units need to carry out their risk management activities in perfect communication and cooperation. Although the risks of the cybercrime that the banks face are very diverse, it is possible to reduce the risks of the cybercrime by few steps. For banks to manage cyber risks, it is necessary to do the following (http://www.sigortacigazetesi.com.tr):

*   1\. Raise awareness of cyber risk
*   2\. Restrict data backup and access
*   3\. Utilize systems that prevent data breaches
*   4\. Identify cyber risk management strategies
*   5\. Obtain Cyber insurance.

In order to protect against cyber-attacks, banks must first raise awareness of cyber threats and security within the organization. Effective risk management extends from the manager to the consultant. All employees should be aware of the responsibility for the privacy and protection of data. In order to calculate the size of the threat that the bank is facing, you must first determine the amount of sensitive data. Backing up files can prevent data loss in the event of an attack. Again, the risk is reduced that as few people as possible have access to sensitive data (Randazzo et al., 2005).

Use systems that prevent data breaches, especially intrusion detection systems. Make sure these systems are constantly monitored and updated. It is also important for the employees of the company to be aware of the situation immediately and to act when such an incident occurs, as well as to prevent the breach of data. Banks must be an effective cyber risk management strategy. The strategy should include in detail what kind of cyber threats the bank faces, the potential damage, the precautions to be taken to prevent attacks, the steps to be taken in case of an attack, and to whom the tasks are falling.

Preparing and protecting is very important, but no precaution provides 100 percent protection against cyber-attacks. It is not possible to protect your data with only technological and organizational practices. Obtain cyber loss insurance solutions that minimize cyber-attacks. The needs of each company, the sector it operates in, the size, varies according to the risks. For this reason, the cyber insurance solutions have to be customizable.

CYBER RISK INSURANCE

Many insurance companies have been investing in security tools and processes for many years; however, such investment may lead to a false sense of security. As cyber criminals are specialized in decryption and other cyberattack techniques, firewall, antivirus software, unauthorized access detection systems and cyberattack prevention systems are gradually being rendered useless. As a result, it can be observed that many insurance companies are investing their limited resources into easily identified threats which are defined by the regulations without regards to the hidden and long-term risks which may be associated with bigger threats.

Insurance solutions and their application play an important role in the cyber risk management strategy. Insurance, in its simplest definition, is the transfer of risks. Insurance policies shall never replace efficient management strategies. However, after taking every reasonable step to mitigate a specific risk, insurance policies must be purchased in order to ensure full protection of the organization. Risk management of an organization is a process which must involve the transfer of cyber risks to insurance company. Many brokers and underwriters operating worldwide, especially in the West, are specialized in collateralizing cyber risks.

Cyber insurance may cover the damages arising from direct effects of cybercrimes and it may also cover any damages caused to the 3rd parties (customers). The following table shows a comparison of the cyber risk insurance versus other types of insurance.

Cyber responsibility policies cover a number of risks arising from the use of electronic data and the Internet:

1st Party Risks

*   • Theft and fraud
*   • Forensic inquiry
*   • Halt of operations
*   • Computerized data loss and its recovery

3rd Party Risks

*   • Lawsuit compensation
*   • Notification costs
*   • Crisis management
*   • Credit tracking
*   • Media responsibility
*   • Confidentiality responsibility
*   • Insurance coverage offered for cyber risks

From the Perspective of Internet Risks

*   • Any damages arising from the violation of intellectual rights and copyrights,
*   • Responsibilities arising from actions such as defamation and insult,
*   • Any expenses associated with the public relations and promotion activities necessary for the restoration of the reputation which was injured due to the cybercrime, any liabilities arising from false online ads and those which are in violation of personal rights,
*   • As it was noted with regards to the accountants before, any ransom payments made in order to recover the access to the system or to recover the data which is locked,
*   • Any compensation liabilities which may arise due to the negligence of the employees or those arising from intentional violations of privacy (i.e. disclosure of employee, customer and consumer data),
*   • Disclosure of 3rd parties due to a cybercrime and any expenses made to escalate the situation to the relevant authorities.

From the Perspective of Technological Risks

*   • Any damages made to systems, networks, and IT hardware (i.e., systems and hardware which need to be renewed as they were rendered unstable as a result of hacker or virus activity)
*   • Problems in IT systems, Halt of Operations and Loss of Profit due to hacker or virus activity, any damages arising from the violation of regulations and standards (e.g., fines)
*   • Legal protection insurance for specific conditions

As the quantity and types of the aforementioned warranties would suggest, there is no standard policy in the cyber risk insurance field and insurance companies issue package policies which may cover a number of warranties depending on the quality and needs of the insured. It is a need to perform necessary risk analyses and to define the right extra warranties and limits.

The level of operational and technological cyber security measures taken by the insured as mentioned elsewhere in this study is an important factor in defining the content and cost of a policy, and it will be safe to say that it is preferable that the insurance professionals to have at least the know-how about cyber security technologies as there is insufficient data about the documented damages for this field.

The “Cyber Risks” product and its coverage are designed in a way to include any damages caused by the lawsuits filed by 3rd parties and the direct damages caused to the business (Russell, 1996).

Lawsuits Filed by 3rd Parties

*   • Disclosure of sensitive customer information (e.g., ID info, health records, credit cards)
*   • Any virus infecting the other parties through the network, hacking, and so forth
*   • Media responsibility (lawsuits filed due to violation of copyrights on social media and other platforms, or insults shared about others)

Direct Damages Caused to the Business

*   • Cyber blackmail (Turkey is listed in the Top Five in cyber blackmail. It is highly possible that hackers infiltrate a system and threaten to crash it.)
*   • Data corruption (hacking, unauthorized access, human error, software error)
*   • Loss of profit (due to the halt of operations as a result of data corruption)

Exceptions to the Cyber Risk Insurance

*   • Physical injury and damage to physical assets
*   • Contractual obligations
*   • Employers’ liability
*   • Intellectual property
*   • Intentional act
*   • Criminal act
*   • Previous demands and events
*   • Competition
*   • Infrastructure or security failure

Cases of Damage

*   • Security Vulnerability: The firewall of a hotel chain was breached by hackers and a total amount of US$10 million in damages was caused due to stolen card info of 600,000 guests.
*   • Hacking: The stock value of the largest processor of Mastercard and Visa had dropped by 12% in four days due to the hacking and stolen card info of 1.5 million users.
*   • Theft: An international bank has lost the credit card data of 46,000 customers after a cyberattack and faced a fine of GBP 27.5 million.
*   • System Breakdown Attack: An airliner was not able to process any request for six hours, the fights were delayed and the airliner faced losses due to failed ticketing as a result of an attack targeting its security network.

CONCLUSION

Uploading and storing sensitive reports and documents which require confidentiality in electronic information management systems pose serious security risks. While offering convenience, practicality, and accessibility, such techniques may compromise the system as a whole. The loss or seizure of printed documents may cause partial damage, while the access to the system as a whole may lead to the confidential and critical documents being available for malicious and unauthorized people. It is necessary to develop measures to store the critical documents and reports without being incorporated into the electronic information management system.

Banks are starting to focus more on building customer loyalty, offering new products to their clients, and to take a bigger share in their customer’s financial portfolio. Such an expansion brings with it the increased number of cyberattacks. Although such digital investments allow for new strategic possibilities, it may also bear new cyber risks for those corporations with relatively poor experience in dealing with the difficulties of a multichannel environment. Nevertheless, it is possible that these difficulties will shift as the bankers adopt big data and advanced analytics applications.

As bankers develop new and innovative methods for data analysis, they will also need to find the new ways to meet the security needs in the face of cyberattacks. Cyber criminals are aware of the fact that banks hold significant amounts of information about their customers. There is no doubt that such personal information attracts thieves and con artists. The fact that cyber criminals who target banks have substantial financial resources allows them to organize cyberattacks using software combining social engineering with malicious intents.

Any attack to banks may lead to substantial material damages including but not limited to fines, legal fees, lawsuit and fraud monitoring costs. Moreover, a less visible but important consequence of cyberattacks is the damaged customer trust and the customer’s concern about the safety of his/her personal information. As the banking system is built on trust, an extensive violation would lead to adverse effects on the brand and market value of the bank. It may be important here to state that the violations announced by banks so far involved the hackers gaining access to the bank’s system, stolen information in a short period of time and moving on.

It is necessary to analyze the transparency of the shareholder structure before the issuance of certificate of incorporation and official authorization, along with the presence of speculators, unknown hedge funds, shadow banking enterprises, SWFs, conduit and SIVs or if the application constitutes a hostile takeover, the provisions of information and document sharing based on international deals and memorandum of understanding between companies must be investigated with the help of intelligence agencies, if necessary.

KEY TERMS AND DEFINITIONS

Critical Infrastructure System: Any system which may lead to disruption in the public order, loss of lives, economical damages, etc. if it is compromised.

Cyber Media: The media that is connected to include the IT systems and networks available in the world and the orbit.

Cyber Security Case: Violation of access and confidentiality of information processed on information systems.

Hacker: A person who gains unauthorized access to personal computers or computers and networks of corporations. Simply put, a hacker tries to gain economic benefits using the security weaknesses of the digital world.

Hacking: Gaining unauthorized access to confidential data in a system. It is an act of infiltrating into a system bypassing the system admins.

Information Systems of Legal and Natural Entities: Any information system operated by legal or natural entities based on the laws of the Republic of Turkey.

IT Systems: Also known as Information and communication technologies. This is the system where all process and services are provided.

National Cyber Media: Any information system operated by legal or natural entities with a national public information system.

State-Owned Information Systems: Any information systems owned by the Turkish state and its enterprises.
