# Chapter 11

Mass-Scale Human Cognitive Limits to Explain the “Weakest Link” in Cybersecurity

*   Shalin Hai-Jew  
    Kansas State University, USA

ABSTRACT

If people are the “weakest link” in cybersecurity because of their psychological make-up and hardwiring—their socialized desire to trust and cooperate with others, their cognitive biases and misperceptions, their preferences for convenience, their general going with System 1 inattention instead of System 2 attention and thinking—this begs the question of whether the same micro-scale cognitive limits found in individual users are also present on a mass scale. After all, there have been discovered problematic unthinking leanings in group decision making: obedience to authority, bystander effects, groupthink, and the Abilene paradox, among others. Using a range of often mass-scale data sources and data analytics tools, research questions were asked around three areas: (1) the level of sophistication of the cybersecurity electronic hive mind towards cybersecurity issues, (2) the gap between the non-expert members and the expert members in the hive mind, and (3) whether the extant hive mind was more reflective of mob unthinkingness or deliberation and wisdom.

INTRODUCTION

In every chain of reasoning, the evidence of the last conclusion can be no greater than that of the weakest link of the chain, whatever may be the strength of the rest. – Thomas Reid in Essays on the Intellectual Powers of Man – (1786)

A chain is only as strong as its weakest link. – a common saying

Intelligence is highly improbable, and collective intelligence is even more so. It runs into misinformation, misjudgment, and misunderstanding. This is unavoidable because thinking is a site for conflict, tactics, and strategies. Insight jumps out of the clash of argument as well as linear discovery of truths. – Geoff Mulgan (2018), in Big Mind: How Collective Intelligence Can Change Our World (p. 126)

Online is where a large portion of the world’s population live and breathe and have their being. As the cyber footprint is broadened—through mobile devices, locational apps, games, smart cars, medical devices, and the Internet of Things (IoT)—there are that many more potential attack surfaces through which people may be affected negatively through hacks and cyberattacks. Adam Segal (2016) writes: “An estimated 75 percent of the world’s population now has access to a mobile phone, and the Internet connects 40 percent of the planet’s population, roughly 2.7 billion people. Information and communications networks are embedded in our political, economic, and social lives.” (p. 1). He predicts an intensification of the battle over cyberspace, with Year Zero of this battle starting June, 2012 or June, 2013, given a number of high profile uses of cyberattacks by nation states. In 2016, there were four billion cyberattacks, a major jump from the 600 million in 2015 (IBM, as cited in Balaish, Aug. 21, 2017). By 2021, cyber crime is estimated to cost US$2 trillion (Cybersecurity Ventures, as cited in Balaish, 2017). Cybersecurity efforts focus on preventing the illegal exploitation of technology systems and the protection of data integrity, among other things.

In cybersecurity studies and practices, humans are known as “the weakest link” (Belbey, 2015); their decisions and actions put their information at risk and also those of others. Humans will use and re-use weak passwords or leave passwords unchanged from factory defaults; they over-share with friends, family, and strangers; they click unthinkingly on risky links and download files (with malware) from others; they will receive emails from strangers or apparent colleagues and click on links or download files without thinking; they’ll receive USB drives at conferences and use these in their laptops and desktops; they’ll download apps from unknown websites; they will visit the Web’s dark spaces to buy illicit goods; they’re prone to being social engineered; and they do not begin to understand the “cyber” threats arrayed against them.

One way to begin to understand why people are so vulnerable to cyber-exploitation is to not only explore people and their individual cognitive limits and biases but also to explore the “electronic hive mind” around cybersecurity to understand mass-scale human cognitive limits and biases. A “mind” refers to consciousness, thinking, intellect, and will. A “hive mind” refers “group intelligence” (Jones, 2011, p. 2). A hive mind refers to the consciousness, thinking, intellect, and will of a collective of people. Such collectives occur organically, with people coming together around shared interests. A core purpose of a hive mind is to learn from the environment, from others outside the hive, and from each other. Bloom’s taxonomy of learning domains types (1956) can apply to group intelligence: the steps include remembering, understanding, applying, analyzing, evaluating, and creating. (Conceptualize teams collaborating around shared research and design and development work.) As in learning communities, consensus and dissensus are both important. Certainly, if hive minds can function like individual ones, they can also be misled, misinformed, irrational, and deluded.

A hive mind does not have centralized control; rather, control is distributed and devolved, with each member and small groups within the collective making decisions, sharing ideas, and taking actions. How these hive minds coalesce and evolve is determined in part by the group impetuses and interests, and evolved social norms. Hive minds can be informed by co-created culture. In the same that that the cultural features of a society may head off some possible futures and make others more likely (Dieffenbach, 1992), how “hive” populations evolve may also change.

From localized and small acts of individual members, it is possible for emergent patterns of intelligence and self-organizing behavior to emerge at the macro level. The purpose of a hive mind is conceptualized as promotion of the hive’s (population’s) survival. A hive mind has been referred to as “swarm intelligence” and “collective consciousness.” The macro consciousness can create new insights and can act as a macro-entity en masse towards shared aims (such as advocating particular government policies, for example).

In such contexts, in which information is shared openly and broadly, individual expertise no longer holds the command it once did. One researcher explains:

If we can easily exchange large chunks of knowledge and are connected by high-bandwidth communication paths, the function and purpose served by individuals becomes unclear. Individuals have served to keep the gene pool stirred up and healthy via sexual reproduction, but this data handling process would no longer necessarily be linked to individuals. With knowledge no longer encapsulated in individuals, the distinction between individuals and the entirety of humanity would blur. Think Vulcan mind-meld. We would perhaps become more of a hive mind — an enormous, single, intelligent entity. (Burger, 2002, p. 150)

And yet, the contributions of experts to a hive mind are critical for understandings and guidance. Without expertise, it is difficult to place current events into context. It is difficult to vet complex information. The germane cognitive load of cybersecurity is demanding, and expertise itself is difficult to find. One author has pointed to the pendulum in the U.S. swinging too far to the side of non-expertise and even self-ignorance. He writes:

In the end, expertise is difficult to define, and experts are sometimes hard to tell from dilettantes. Still, we should be able to distinguish between people who have a passing acquaintance with a subject and people whose knowledge is definitive. No one’s knowledge is complete, and experts realize this better than anyone. But education, training, practice, experience, and acknowledgment by others in the same field should provide us with at least a rough guide to dividing experts from the rest of society. (Nichols, 2017, p. 39)

Worse yet, experts may have high WTGA tendencies (“willing to give advice”) even outside of their areas of expertise or with carelessness which renders their suggestions not particularly valuable (Dillon & Carlson, 2017). While online communities are open spaces with people coming and going as they choose, the relevance of expertise might suggest that newbies should be constantly striving towards expertise and not fronting knowledge or skills that they do not possess. One example of hive mind collaboration is from “folk” or non-expert tagging of contents on the Web.

Today, users are adding metadata and using tags to organize their own digital collections, categorize the content of others and build bottom-up classification systems. The wisdom of crowds, the hive mind, and the collective intelligence are doing what heretofore only expert catalogers, information architects and website authors have done. They are categorizing and organizing the Internet and determining the user experience, and it’s (sic) working. No longer do the experts have the monopoly on this domain; in this new age users have been empowered to determine their own cataloging needs. Metadata is now in the realm of the Everyman. (Kroski, 2005, p. 1)

Another example in the research literature refers to the hive mind’s usage in enhancing collaborative design (Zhu, Mussio, & Barricelli, 2010).

Hive minds are not purposively created per se, but they emerge based on how individual actors make choices and how they behave. (This “emergent” phenomenon is observed in a variety of natural contexts. It is often modeled using agent-based modeling…to show how simple rules based on simple choices of the respective agents can form over-arching patterns.)

Each member of the community interacts locally with a limited set of other members of the community and with the environment according to local rules of behavior and communication. Each member follows the local rules of interaction and communication according to her/his experience, skill and knowledge. Even in absence of any centralized control, a global behavior emerges from local interactions, which is unknown to individual members of the community and not predictable by external observers. In the virtual world, online communities harness the Web technology to build collective intelligence which only experts, information architects and website developers could achieve before…In all these domains, communities of users find a virtual place were to congregate and collaborate, supporting one another, creating and sharing their own data and metadata on the Internet. (Zhu, Mussio, & Barricelli, 2010, p. 124)

Even without a centralized executive control, hive minds enable people to cooperate, collaborate, and co-create; it enables them to take part in shared endeavors larger than the individual. The “hive mind” is conceptualized as “a collective attribute of humanity” that makes possible large-scale endeavors, based on information, intercommunications, and “simultaneous action” (Dalley, 2014, pp. 82 – 83). The hive mind is enhanced and empowered by technologies:

All of these characteristics of the Hive Mind are demonstrable without technology. However, when they are supported by technology their effects increase exponentially. It is technology that is revealing our Hive Mind characteristics. The printing press, the telescope, the computer, the Internet, and mobile devices all give us visibility into how our Hive Mind operates. The technology gives us visibility into Hive Mind operations via psychological projections. (Dalley, 2014, pp. 82 – 83)

These technologies enable collaboration across global-scale distances and time. In a culture of participation, they enable the existence of “electronic hive minds,” the distributed consciousness of people with shared interests. As entities, electronic hive minds are built on the substructures of the Internet (aka the “Fifth Estate”), the World Wide Web (particularly Web 2.0 or the Social Web), social media platforms, and communications technologies. Socio-technical spaces have been created to enable people to collaborate, to share endeavors, and to keep and maintain personal profiles over time (and even into perpetuity).

The membership in an electronic “hive” is transient, and this is built on interested parties from the world’s electronically connected populations. There are some natural feeder communities in terms of cybersecurity—such as professionals in the field. In terms of non-professionals, there may be hobbyists, amateurs (those who dabble and are fairly well informed but who do not aspire to professional expertise), and novices (those who may aspire to be experts in the field one day). In the electronic hive mind, issues arise and disappear, given the limits of human attention and the speed of information flow.

As with all communities, there are bandwidth limits to attention. The memory behind the hive mind may vary depending on what is archived online and what is taken offline…and also depending on the membership (and the existence of old-timers and mavens). The popularity of a topic may ensure that the topic is top-of-hive-mind for a time but does not ensure long-term focus or interest (or even long-term memory). Participants may share expertise, pose questions (and begin article stubs in crowd-sourced dictionary sites), and engage in other ways.

The capture and archival of electronic desiderata central to the hive mind communicates externalized expressions of the hive mind’s thoughts. The digital contents online created by individuals and groups in the electronic hive mind may extend individual and collective memory for a “shared extended mind”. Not only are these an aide de memoire but enable an exploration of the “electronic hive mind” based on particular shared issues of interest. One authoring team describes this phenomenon this way:

Some types of species exploit the external environment to support their cognitive processes, in the sense of patterns created in the environment that function as external mental states and serve as an extension to their mind. In the case of social species the creation and exploitation of such patterns can be shared, thus obtaining a form of shared mind or collective intelligence. (Bosse, Jonker, Schut, & Treur, 2006, p. 151)

The “hive mind” is more than the sum of its human parts. In a broad sense, the electronic hive mind may be conceptualized as a sentient and potent mass entity with potential for various types of concentrated mass action as well as dispersed smaller-unit actions, among others. From social psychology, analogical “cognitive biases” in group dynamics may be found in research on group decision-making. They include:

*   • a tendency to follow authority figures, with a concomitant unwillingness to challenge them even in ethically challenging situations (“obedience to authority”) (Milgram, 1963);
*   • a tendency to experience a dissipation of individual responsibility and apathy in the presence of a group (“bystander effect” or “diffusion of responsibility (Darley & Latané, 1968);
*   • a tendency towards consensus and “groupthink” (Janis, 1972), and
*   • the occurrence of the “Abilene paradox” based on unthinking acceptance of an initial suggestion (based in part on social conformity) and not considering actual interests (Harvey, 1996)

In work places, healthy group dynamics have to be trained and inculcated. Members are encouraged to share leadership in a distributed way, to be empowered for speaking up and decision-making, to fight “groupthink” (group decision-making without individual responsibility) by having assigned contrarians (based on the 10^(th) man principle) and having diverse members at the table, and to test proposals on a range of metrics to ensure that the decision-making is as optimal as possible. Taleb (2007 / 2010) has suggested that the old model of assessing probabilities with the assumption of an underlying normal frequency distribution is limited and does not prepare people for rare and potentially catastrophic “black swan” and rare and anticipate-able “gray swan” events. The unthinkable has to be thinkable to enable anticipation, psychological readiness, planning, and defense.

Defining a Cybersecurity Electronic Hive Mind

Generally, a hive mind is inclusive of all potential members, no matter what their level of expertise is regarding the target topic. A “cybersecurity” hive mind is comprised of people who interact and engage around this topic, optimally with some regularity. For the interests of this research though, the direct expert expressions and points-of-view are not of direct interest per se. What is more engaging is studying the messages received and understood and engaged and regurgitated by the public non-expert hive mind (in order to compare against expert insights). How does the general public “swarm” the cybersecurity issue, and then how do they reflect or not reflect expert and opinions and insights?

Three general research areas were explored (phrased as related questions):

*   1\. What is the level of sophistication of the electronic hive mind in regards to cybersecurity? Are there blind spots (lacunae) regarding cybersecurity? If so, what are these, are they from critical areas of cybersecurity, and why might these exist?
*   2\. How does the folk electronic hive mind differ from the expressions of cybersecurity experts on the Social Web / Web 2.0? If these exist, what are the main differences, and why might these exist?
*   3\. Is the “hive mind” (related to cybersecurity) more reflective of (a) a mob mentality or herd mind, or is it more reflective of (b) collective intelligence and “wisdom of crowds”? Is the hive mind functioning effectively and prosocially regarding cybersecurity (or not)? How so? How not?

Various elements of the mass electronic hive mind relating to cybersecurity were explored to understand mass thinking about cybersecurity. There was information taken from the World Wide Web (WWW), the Internet, and social media platforms, from multimodal digital data sources. The analytical approaches include the following:

*   • Correlated search terms over extended time and at mass scale in Google Search using Google Correlate;
*   • Text analysis of cybersecurity subreddits;
*   • Correlated terms appearing over time in scanned books through the Google Books Ngram Viewer;
*   • #hashtag networks from Twitter;
*   • Social imagery from Google Images and Flickr;
*   • Related tags networks from Flickr;
*   • Audio files in iTunes;
*   • Social videos on YouTube, and
*   • Slideshows on SlideShare.

The focus is on non-expert parts of the hive mind, so contents in academia and the news media were not directly included. Nor were contents from government sources.

The Potential Relevance of Understanding an Electronic Hive Mind Around Cybersecurity

In a cybersecurity context, an electronic hive mind is potentially analytically relevant in several ways: (1) as an indicator of social knowledge regarding cybersecurity, (2) as a problem-solving community, and (3) as a social influence on others.

*   • First, it indicates at a mass scale what the public is thinking about cybersecurity and may be one indicator of how well prepared they are in the face of fairly unrelenting cyberattacks. The messages shared in the hive mind may be generalized out to some degree. It can be informative. The questions being asked by the hive mind, how they go about answering those questions, and what they do with the answers are also relevant. How well the hive mind responds to new information and surprises may be another indicator of health of the hive mind\*.
*   • Second, problem-solving may emerge from the electronic hive mind. If parts or the whole of the hive mind decide to take on particular challenges, they can have a powerful influence.
*   • Third, the electronic hive mind also may work as social influence on others. The hive mind can set a standard for “social proof” and in so doing set a standard for larger population readiness, capabilities, and actions. It can play an agenda-setting role in the way that traditional mass media did and how social media do today. In the best case scenarios, the electronic hive mind can serve as early warning of risks and can model proper responses to cyber hazards and threats.

\*The first bullet in this section can benefit from elaboration. This hive mind information can be used by cybersecurity experts and communications professionals to target messaging more effectively to strengthen individuals and groups against cybersecurity compromises. This information may inform gaps analyses, with intervention plans built around addressing such gaps. How expert-provided information and media-provided information are echoed back by members of the hive mind may also indicate how well that information has been received and understood and used. Those tasked with cybersecurity policies have a large task building societal capacities by appealing to citizens and their power as voters and taxpayers and users of technologies. There are challenges in terms of attracting public attention and interest, when there may be a low level of interest in the topic. There are challenges with building trust given the public fears of government interference in their lives. There is the difficult message of letting people know that some attitudes, thoughts, and behaviors make people the “weakest link,” but to do so without creating in them a sense of learned helplessness and passivity. It is important to convey the proper sense of threat, again, to change awareness and behavior but without shutting people down.

REVIEW OF THE LITERATURE

When Tim Berners-Lee originated the concept of the World Wide Web and created HyperText Markup Language (HTML), Uniform Resource Identifiers (URI), and Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) (in 1990), and the first web editor/browser and first web server, the initial idea was that the Web would be for people to build web communities (“History of the Web,” 2008 – 2017). Shortly after this spate of creativity, by 1991 people outside of CERN were invited to join the Web. In the intervening years, people started to realize that online security was an issue. There were various endeavors to steal people’s credentials and identities, steal funds, extort individuals, access sensitive intellectual property (IP), lock protected files and demand payment (through ransomware), infringe on privacy, troll and harass individuals, and others. Why there is this state of affairs can be attributed to many reasons.

One common reason that is pointed-to has been the idea that security had not been “baked in” at the beginning. Others have been that software makers have focused a lot of attention on software features, not on security. Nation-states have gotten into the game by setting up units of their respective militaries to exploit the cyber realm. Many also do not enforce cybersecurity regimes among their citizens who exploit other countries’ systems, so such individuals are protected against extradition in these spaces (beyond the reach of Interpol).

There are many cybersecurity responsibilities and efforts that occur outside of mainstream public awareness by governments and corporations. In terms of national security, governments deal with cyber as its own domain and work hard to secure it. There is work in figuring out how best to conceptualize cybersecurity to align the research to best deal with evolving security challenges (Langø, 2013). For governments, there is major interest in protecting critical infrastructure (like power grids); their focus is complex and multi-faceted, focused on “vulnerability, access, and motive” (Koppel, 2015). The private sector has a critical role to play in terms of providing cybersecurity (Etzioni, 2011). The thinking has changed on how to defend technology systems, with multiple defense lines for defense-in-depth (He, Chan, Zhang, Wu, & Wang, 2014, p. 19). For organizations, there are more formalized and structured ways to assess cyber vulnerabilities and enhancing preparedness (Johnson 2004).

There are studies on how people respond in disasters and some of their actions or non-actions may compound the risk. In mass-scale challenges, there is the need to make “new instincts” (Ripley, 2008, p. 203) and to build capacity and resilience.

Dealing With Cybersecurity Threats

The general public may choose to engage with cybersecurity threats in a number of ways. One general approach may be to simply not engage. This Luddite approach, though, comes with a fairly high cost given the importance of staying up with technological capabilities in most fields. Another may be to engage minimally so as to minimize a sense of threats. This approach does not require sophisticated cybersecurity defense skills, but this is about a kind of “security through obscurity” (in which the user himself or herself is obscured or hidden…in this case through non-engagement). Along this continuum are increasing levels of engagement (Figure 1). This continuum does not address the potential deployment of cybersecurity measures or countermeasures.

| Figure 1. Engagement levels in cyberspace (a continuum) |

| ![Figure978-1-5225-5927-6.ch011.f01](i/ch011.f01.png) |
| --- |

Even non-engagement does not mean there is no effect of cybersecurity lapses. After all, people in modern societies are still reliant on public works, electric grids, modern banking, online news, weather modeling, law enforcement, national defense, and pretty much various systems dependent on cyber. Post Stuxnet and its follow-on technologies, there have been more public awareness of the vulnerabilities of SCADA (supervisory control and data acquisition) systems. Cyberattacks on physical systems may have devastating effects (Bhalodia, Zala, & Nandy, 2017).

Hard-Wired Cognitive Limits

Whatever knowledge individuals may bring to the cybersecurity challenge, they do come at the challenge with challenges. For example, people tend to have a “confirmation bias,” which means that when they observe new information, they tend to try to fit that into a pre-existing conceptualization. If they observe something that goes against an earlier conceptualization, they will actually attempt to test their hypothesis with a “positive test strategy” instead of looking for ways to refute their hypothesis (Kahneman, 2011, pp. 80 - 81). Confirmation bias can close off accurate engagement with the world because each person is only seeking to reinforce what they already think they know.

Another cognitive bias is termed “WYSIATI” or “what you see is all there is” (Kahneman, 2011, pp. 85 – 88). This theory suggests that people do not consider “known unknowns” or “unknown unknowns” when making decisions but only consider what they have seen, which is also cognitively limiting. Based on the “law of small numbers,” people tend to over-weight observations even when they are limited and statistically insignificant (Kahneman, 2011, pp. 112 – 118). With necessary skepticism, the work would benefit from larger samples to increase the power of the research and to raise the confidence level of the findings. Another common cognitive bias is “availability bias.”

Here people tend to imagine that certain events are more likely than others because examples of that type of event come to mind more readily (Kahneman, 2011, pp. 138 – 145). Here, salience of memory is conflated with higher probabilities of occurrence. In terms of rationality in decision-making, people may be thrown off rational decision-making by a host of factors. They can subconsciously anchor to a certain number mentioned first. They are sensitive to how a context is framed or contextualized (Kahneman, 2011, pp. 371 – 374). They tend to be loss averse and will make irrational choices to prevent against loss (Kahneman, 2011, pp. 283 – 288). Beyond cognitive biases, there are challenges with executive control and attentional focus. Many lack the self-regulation skills to control their own behaviors.

These cognitive limits are not necessarily mitigated when people are engaging in a group context. In groups, people tend to follow authority figures in “obedience to authority” dynamics (Milgram, 1963). They have a tendency to experience a dissipation of individual responsibility and apathy in the presence of a group (“bystander effect,” “diffusion of responsibility”) (Darley & Latané, 1968). In group decision-making, people tend towards “groupthink” (Janis, 1972). A version of groupthink is the “Abilene paradox,” based on unthinking acceptance of an initial suggestion (based in part on social conformity) and not considering actual interests (Harvey, 1996) and impacts of the decision. Cultural factors may affect the group members’ “habits of thought” and so limit potentially creative approaches to problem-solving.

And yet, people do by necessity have to collaborate to achieve any number of tasks. There are some problems for which the “wisdom of crowds” may be harnessed:

…under the right circumstances, groups are remarkably intelligent, and are often smarter than the smartest people in them. Groups do not need to be dominated by exceptionally intelligent people in order to be smart. Even if most of the people within a group are not especially well-informed or rational, it can still reach a collectively wise decision (Surowiecki, 2004, pp. xiii – xiv)

James Surowiecki (2004) suggests that groups of common folk with individual imperfect judgments can be aggregated “under the right circumstances” in a way that makes for effective decision-making. The right circumstances include the following three types of problems:

*   1\. Cognition problems “that have or will have definite solutions” (p. xvii),
*   2\. Coordination problems that require members of a group to coordinate with each other (pp. xvii – xviii), and
*   3\. Cooperation problems that “involve the challenge of getting self-interested, distrustful people to work together, even when narrow self-interest would seem to dictate that no individual should take part.” (p. xviii).

It does not seem to be a wide stretch to see any of the above three problem types as applicable in a cybersecurity context and ripe for solving with a mass mind, even an electronic hive mind. How individual and human cognition manifest in a hive mind context is generally unexplored at present. In cyber psychology, online behavior has been studied through an evolutionary frame in terms of four domains: “(1) mating and sexual competition, (2) parenting and kinship, (3) trust and social exchange, and (4) personal information management” (Piazza & Bering, 2009, p. 1258). This work takes a different tact by looking at a specific type of “hive mind” (as a framework) surrounding cybersecurity, a form of defense.

EXPLORING THE ELECTRONIC HIVE MIND RE: CYBERSECURITY

One of the core challenges in this chapter is to define the electronic hive mind regarding cybersecurity. As noted earlier, the focus is on the non-cybersecurity expert parts of the hive mind in order to understand what is understood among the more general population. The three general research areas explored are as follows:

*   1\. What is the level of sophistication of the electronic hive mind in regards to cybersecurity? Are there blind spots (lacunae) regarding cybersecurity? If so, what are these, are they from critical areas of cybersecurity, and why might these exist?
*   2\. How does the folk electronic hive mind differ from the expressions of cybersecurity experts on the Social Web / Web 2.0? If these exist, what are the main differences, and why might these exist?
*   3\. Is the “hive mind” (related to cybersecurity) more reflective of (a) a mob mentality or herd mind, or is it more reflective of (b) collective intelligence and “wisdom of crowds”? Is the hive mind functioning effectively and prosocially regarding cybersecurity (or not)? How so? How not?

To capture a sense of this hive mind, the following online data sources were used:

*   • Text-based Data 
    *   o Web Search (Google Search, Google Correlate)
    *   o Social News Sharing (Reddit)
    *   o Word Uses in Scans of Masses of Books (Google Books Ngram Viewer)
    *   o #networks and Messages (Twitter) (using NodeXL and NVivo 11 Plus)
*   • Social Imagery (Google Images, Flickr) 
    *   o Related Tags Nsetworks (abstraction, meta) (Flickr)
*   • Audio Files (iTunes)
*   • Social Videos (YouTube)
*   • Slideshows (SlideShare)

Micro, Meso, and Macro Levels of the Hive Mind

The sources range from the micro to the meso to the macro levels. At the micro level, researchers have a zoomed-in proximal view of a single node in the hive and the perspectives of that individual and his / her consciousness regarding the topic. The details at the micro-level are specific to the code. Much of this level exists in private groups and denied spaces. At the meso level, there are smaller groups of shared consciousness. These are groups of experts who specialize in particular professional niches. Membership is determined by talent and capabilities and trustworthiness.

At the macro level, this is the proverbial 30,000-foot distal level with more summary and abstract data (which tells more coarse-grained and vague narratives). This is conceptualized as the broad public parts of the electronic hive mind. Said another way, the ability to receive information depends on how prepared the individual or group or population is to that information. At worst, people may misapprehend (misunderstand). Second worse would be if they do not comprehend at all and at least realize that.

TEXT-BASED DATA

The Electronic Hive Mind in Web-Based Search

When conducting Web searches, at least in initial years, people may have thought that their searches were private and maybe anonymized. After all, they were in the privacy of their own comfortable home and other spaces. It turns out that such data have been logged from the beginning by most service providers. In exploring such data, data scientists found the information could be reverse-engineered back to a specific individual with fairly high accuracy. In the interests of protecting user privacy, large search companies have decided against releasing individual search data for research but have enabled access at macro population-scale level. These data enable a glimpse at the changing macro patterns of people’s interests and information exploration over extended time. One inference from these time-based associations is that in-world incidences are informing the searches, given how people often search “just in time” for information that they need.

Google Correlate is an online tool that enables access to Google Search terms whose time-based search patterns correlate with that of the target term over time (from 2004 to the present in 2017, for a 13-year span) (FAQ – Google Correlate, 2007). One query that would be potentially useful in this context is to run “cyber” as the target search term and to see if any of the top 20 correlated search terms reflect cybersecurity or a similar term. In other words, when cyber is being explored, is security also top-of-mind? These queries are available for over 50 countries. The results are shown in a line graph, with time on the x-axis and the normalized search activity (standard deviations above the mean for the search term at that particular time) on the y-axis. (See Figure 2.)

The Electronic Hive Mind in Social News Sharing

Interestingly, the news-sharing bulletin board Reddit has been referred to as a social technology that enables the collective “hive mind” albeit in a slightly pejorative sense. Reddit (as in “read it”) enables members to vote up or vote down a reference to an online published news source. (Search engines offer an “upvote” and “downvote” function, too, based on the search algorithms and the results that they return to particular text-based queries. The algorithms are designed to not only particularize findings based on understood searcher intent but also on the popularity and quality of the returned sites.) Popular works attain more attention because of their placement on the website’s front page, and less popular works have even less opportunity to attract an audience from the site’s users / readers. \[This aligns with the Matthew effect, found in online social sharing sites, where the few attain most of the attention, and the majority of contributors are in the “long tail” of a power law curve with little to no attention.

This concept is drawn from Matthew 25:14-25:30, in the parable of the talents. In the Bible, Matthew 25:29 reads: “For unto every one that hath shall be given, and he shall have abundance: but from him that hath not shall be taken away even that which he hath,” in reference to money invested appropriately.\] Here, the editor role is fulfilled by group members. Their ability to vote is an expression of democracy-in-action and egalitarianism (one person, one vote—per posting). One researcher writes:

When such a post appears on reddit’s front page it has effectively been endorsed by the community (through the voting system) and broadcast to all of the community’s members who visit reddit while the post is visible on the front page. Do these successful ‘meta’ posts influence the collective behaviour of the website’s users? If they do, then this would constitute evidence that the voting system allows the community to self-regulate at a high level. If they do not, this suggests that the hive mind suffers from cognitive dissonance or poor discipline/memory. (Mills, 2011, p. 11)

This researcher found that on Reddit that “minority opinions are found to be slightly marginalised (sic) but not excluded from high visibility locations (Mills, 2011, p. 1). The concern is that collaborative systems may lead to unthinking or unexamined consensus instead of offering valuable human filtering of news to control for information overload. Other researchers express concern that online communities like Reddit may potentially lead to heightened tensions and discrimination between groups and even less democracy based on the depersonalization of other (Workman, 2014, p. 13).

To better understand the electronic hive mind, the main message headings were scraped from three subreddits, two for general users, and one specifically identified for cybersecurity professionals. A screenshot of the “cybersecurity” subreddit (https://www.reddit.com/r/cybersecurity/) is available in Figure 5. At the time of the data capture, the subreddit had 10.974 readers, and 48 users were online at that time. This is a moderated subreddit, with the moderators listed by their handles: Chumstick, CDSEChris, Jess\_V, Spncrgmn.

THE ELECTRONIC HIVE MIND IN MASS-SCALE SCANNED BOOKS

The Google Books Ngram Viewer, aptly named a “language time machine” (Weingarten, Sept. 9, 2013), enables users to explore word, phrase, name, and number histories in terms of their usages in published books, from the 1500s to 2000 or so, based on various text corpora in different languages. As a non-consumptive tool, it does not allow access to the underlying data, but it does offer word frequency counts above a word count threshold to show the commonality of term usages over time. “Cyber” and “cybersecurity” were both run together in the Google Books Ngram Viewer from 1950 to 2000, and based on the English corpus. The results may be seen in Figure 10, and it is clear that the popularity of “cyber” has far outpaced the reference to “cybersecurity.” The lines on the linegraph are not dispositive, but they do suggest greater awareness and usage of “cyber” as compared to “cybersecurity.”

The Electronic Hive Mind in #Hashtag Networks

Another way to get at a part of the electronic hive mind on cybersecurity involves exploring the hashtag network from the network of communicators discussing #cybersecurity on the Twitter microblogging site. This extraction from the Twitter API, using the Network Overview, Discovery and Exploration for Excel (NodeXL) add-on to Excel resulted in a network graph with 527 vertices (nodes) and 629 unique edges (links). There were 155 self-loops in the relationships (user accounts that self-retweeted or which self-replied). Over all, there were 896 relationships in this network. The network graph diameter was nine (9), and the average geodesic distance was 4.19.

In this hashtag network, there were 133 groups or clusters (as extracted using the Clauset-Newman-Moore algorithm), and some smaller motifs. \[The parameter settings on NodeXL was for the capture of a basic #hashtag network without the inclusion of the communicators’ friends, with a limit of 18,000 Tweets limited by NodeXL, beyond the rate-limits of the Twitter API). Socially shared images may shed light on various instantiations of cyber security. Of the 778 images, they were divided into the following categories (in a bottom-up coding method): A majority were decorative (531), used to illustrate cybersecurity with padlocks, circuit boards, fiber optics, hooded “hackers,” maps showing various affected countries, flags representing nation-states, humans in silhouettes, robots, and Guy Fawkes masks used as symbols of the Anonymous hacker collective. The decorative images had the sheen of stock image photos, and many of the people depicted looked like they were out of central casting.

For example, hackers are shown as males wearing hoodies with Caucasian hands. (By comparison, those news stories that address cybersecurity that merit images tend to show people much more from the real world instead of an imaginary one.) The decorative images are contrasted with informational images (97), such as screenshots of slideshow slides. It is generally assumed that more informative data visualizations are preferable to decorative ones because these actually contain information and so have informational value.

The next most common type of images seems to be from commercial companies and often are from events (108). Many of the images in the commercial category also serve advertising functions, to sell products and services. The last two categories are of equal size: government (21) and glyphs (21). Government imagery is publicly created images showcasing government reports or studies or data (statistics). Glyphs are small images usually with decorative or labeling icons (Figure 15).

The Electronic Hive Mind in Folk Tagging (of Social Imagery and Multimedia)

On Flickr, there were no related tags for “cyber security” or “cybersecurity”. This may mean that there were insufficient images tagged with “cyber security / cybersecurity” to meet a threshold to draw a related tags network.

A related tags network captures co-occurring tags that appear with a target tag above a particular threshold. In a one-degree network, the other tags captured are those that directly appear with the target tag. This may be seen in Figure 16, with “cyber” as the target tag on the Flickr social image- and video-sharing site. (“Cybersecurity” did not have any related tags in a query run on the Flickr API through Network Overview, Discovery and Exploration for Excel (NodeXL). A separate search for images based on “cybersecurity” as a tag found 24,223 photos on Flickr.) In terms of the related tags at one degree, the words seem to be culturally based. There is a reference to the immersive virtual world, Second Life. A perusal of some of the images pulled up include graffiti art in RL (real life), people dressed as Second Life avatars (in what appears to be cosplay or “costume play”), screenshots from Second Life, photos of pet dogs, musicians, and others.

SOCIAL AUDIO

The Electronic Hive Mind in Social Audio

A perusal of cybersecurity podcast listings on iTunes found several types to select from, targeted to different parts of the population. Some were directed to professionals specializing in particular aspects of cybersecurity. Others had more of a policy focus for politicos. One podcast was dedicated to social engineering, the manipulation of people based on cultural understandings and social mores to malicious ends. There was one that offered daily digest information about cybersecurity issues in the world. Most seemed to be created for information technology (IT) professionals.

SOCIAL VIDEOS

The Electronic Hive Mind in Social Videos

On Google’s YouTube, there are over half a million videos related to “cybersecurity” (based on video titles and folk tagging) (Figure 20). A perusal of the titles show a mish-mash of approaches: professional conference talks, invited talks at corporations, online trainings, news programs, late night comedy shows, workforce recruitment videos, and others. Some are by professed hackers, white hat, black hat, and gray hat ones. There are some for-pay movies as well.

| Figure 20. 506,000 “cybersecurity” videos on YouTube |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-5225-5927-6.ch011.f20](i/ch011.f20.png) |
| --- |

In terms of Hollywood films, a number of them over the years have addressed cybersecurity. They include, in part, the following: Wargames (1983), Sneakers (1992), The Net (1995), Hackers (1995), Johnny Mnemonic (1995), Takedown (2000), Antitrust (2001), Girl with the Dragon Tattoo (2001), Blackhat (2015), Ghost in the Shell (2016, remake), and others. Some of the Hollywood films even affected national security decision-making at the Pentagon and White House (Kaplan, 2016).

Using the YouTube auto-captioning feature and the availability of timed-text transcripts in a public way (through the ellipses underneath the YouTube video player), it is possible to extract verbatim transcripts. The transcripts of some 16 of the top “cybersecurity” videos were identified, and their transcripts were captured. Most of these transcripts are verbatim ones and not enriched with additional descriptive details.

The video transcript text set is comprised of 73,000 words and some 411 pages. This was run through a software program that enabled machine learning for both topic modeling and sentiment analysis. The top-level themes, in alphabetical order, were as follows: access, address, attack, code, computer, files, operating systems, people, programs, random, security, and systems. The focus, at least at a high level, deals with technological concerns, in general, and the mechanics of cyberattacks (including through people, such as through “social engineering”). The sentiment analysis showed that the transcripts were generally trending moderately negative (202), moderately positive (151), very negative (92), and then very positive (53). In other words, the text that reflects sentiment tends towards sentiment moderation, but with leanings towards negativity.

SOCIAL SLIDESHOWS

The Electronic Hive Mind in Social Slideshows

In terms of “cybersecurity” social slideshows on SlideShare, there were 14,463 results in SlideShare. These included directions on how to conduct cybersecurity trainings, how to conduct computer forensics, the employment market for cybersecurity employees, how to protect an organization’s critical infrastructure, cybersecurity trends and predictions, and others. Clicking through several pages of slideshows, though, suddenly, the number of found items related to “cybersecurity” jumps to 17,231,837 results for “cybersecurity.” However, the slideshows that are shown suddenly show wide disparities in terms of contents: e-commerce, personal hygiene, and “plastic waste in road construction.” It is unclear what led to this change.

DISCUSSION

Based on some summary data points, some light assertions may be made. It seems that when people think “cyber,” they are generally considering sales and online shopping, and some events, but not really security or threat or crime. In social news sharing, a wide range of topics are on the table, and based on titles of messages, there is sophistication in the lists for the general public as there is for the cybersecurity professionals; this broad result could be a factor of cybersecurity professionals engaging on multiple subreddits. Or it could be that the common person interested in cybersecurity (and who opts-in to a public message board) does come at the issue with some sophistication. The linegraph trajectory for a scan of mass book corpora for “cyber” and “cybersecurity” did find a discrepancy with the popularity of the first much outweighing the second.

In terms of #hashtag discussions of #cybersecurity, there are a healthy number of groups of various sizes engaged in 140-character-length discussions and referencing online resources. Social imagery related to cybersecurity showed that a majority of the images were decorative and not particularly informational (although there were some informational graphics). In terms of related tags networks (which are somewhat abstract and meta), the references are not to security but rather the visual aspects related to “cyber” (and there were no related tags available for “cybersecurity”).

About Data Sources

Which data sources are most revelatory? This would be hard to answer because each of the informational sources shed light on a facet of the electronic hive mind around cybersecurity. That said, this approach only leveraged some of the available data sources. These respective digital data sources may be understood as ranging from the micro to the meso to the macro levels of the hive mind. At the micro level, researchers have a zoomed-in proximal view of a single node in the hive and the perspectives of that individual and his / her consciousness regarding the topic. At the meso level, there are groups of shared consciousness. At the macro level, this is the proverbial 30,000-foot distal level with more summary data (which tells more abstract narratives).

Table 4. Micro, meso, and macro-level sources to understand the electronic hive mind

|  || Micro Level || Meso Level || Macro Level |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Source Examples || news articles, academic articles, books, blog posts, podcasts, websites, social media accounts, crowd-sourced encyclopedia articles, and others || delimited news collections, edited books (with multiple contributors), data collections, datasets, data bases, blog series, podcast series, and others || search term data (to scale), text corpora, social image imagesets, social video collections, social audio collections, social slideshow collections, crowd-sourced encyclopedias, and others |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

Those interested in follow-on research may want to explore a much broader range of source information, and Table 4 may offer some ideas. Finally, in terms of audio files, social videos, and slideshows, there seemed to be a sufficient store of resources for a general public curious about aspects of cybersecurity—at least for the basic user level. A perusal of books and Hollywood films also showed further resources.

Some Recurrent Messages in the Electronic Hive Mind Around Cybersecurity

What are some of the recurrent messages that are being shared in the cybersecurity electronic hive mind? Some common extracted observations follow:

*   • Cyber is engaging, but cybersecurity itself is not that interesting—in the main population.
*   • Cybersecurity is informed by narratives of war and conflict. The thinking is not “Hello, World!” but is more adversarial in posture and untrusting in approach; the sense is that there are malicious actors in the world that will try to catch you out. At the macro level, the stories go like this: Nation-states are in competition among themselves, and technology corporations and peoples are caught in the crosshairs. International criminals are exploiting cracks in the system to benefit themselves financially, at the expense of the larger public. At the micro level, the stories go like this: anyone who talks to you wants something; deception is a common tool in social relations; anything that looks promising is a honeypot; any service which is free…is selling you and your information; trust is for dummies.
*   • The heroes and heroines of the cybersecurity hive mind are “white hats” who defend systems against the “black hats.” The point is to be so skilled and are that it is hard to be pwned (or “p0wned”). Heroes and heroines are also those who are on a path of treasure-hunting, with zero days as the most rare and elusive objective. In this meritocracy, having skills is most critical; certifications are not necessary per se. The field of cybersecurity itself is maturing, with degree track opportunities, but there is still room too for the talented renegades. Gray hats exist, and they are not generally trusted by either side. (At the bottom of this hierarchy are the “script kiddies” who may cobble code or deploy others’ cyberweapons—and then take the fall for it—but they are not respected because they do not offer fresh tools and insights. They praise themselves in leetspeak but do not have the admiration of the real professionals in the field.)
*   • The space is informed by a culture of secrecy. This is not about “trust but verify” but much more about “never actually trust and always verify”. Also, there are so many pseudonyms available in the world, and there is no reason why a person has to share his / her actual name and personally identifiable (PII) data in RL (real life).
*   • Reputations are based on capabilities as expressed on designed “exploits.” It is poor form to brag at all or to claim credit. If an exploit is sufficiently daring and indicative of skill, others will come to the fore to praise the individual. Big claims require big evidence, as the saying goes. It is not enough to assert, but it is important to back up assertions with proofs. Things may seem unsolvable, but they may just be very hard problems. With enough know-how, a person can avoid being out-classed.
*   • There is a rebel vibe in the cybersecurity hive mind. For example, there is no trust of The Man, even if The Man (the government) can occasionally do something right. (For example, one of the members who hosts a newsgroup has a handle of “not\_not\_government.”) In cybersecurity conferences, there is an inherent understanding that The Man is in their midst scouting talent; the point is to spot the government agents where possible. \[The role of government in cybersecurity is deeply contested, with recent wranglings over citizens’ civil liberties and privacy from surveillance (Hart, Jin, & Feenberg, 2014). If a public health analogy was applied to cybersecurity and network hygiene, the implication may be that government has to step in more coercively, with effects on public privacy and other aspects of modern life. Currently, how much of a role government should have in the provision of cybersecurity as a “public good” and how intrusive and coercive is can be is highly contested (Weber, 2017, p. 1).\]
*   • For all the background and posing, the important thing is to be able to secure machines and information and people.
*   • There is hand-to-hand combat going on at a high level between nation-states and those who are on the side of advanced persistent threats (APTs). Everyone else outside this elite tier are out-classed, out-gunned, out-(hu)manned, and in the dark. Nothing will be purposefully let into the sunlight, except strategic threats as cyber-deterrence.
*   • A common truism is that user errors are often an underlying cause to a cybersecurity compromise. Users are often the “weakest link.” Too often, common folk do not even know that they are at-risk (they are “ground zero”), and they often do not even know that they have been compromised and are being exploited.

The Electronic Hive Mind and “Weakest Link” Issue

This work provides an initial mapping of the electronic hive mind around cybersecurity. As such, it can offer some basic observations about the “weakest link.”

In terms of mistaken ideas, these seemed to exist more in the subtext. One common one is that losses incurred by careless engagement in cyberspace will just be covered by someone else. People assume that the loss will be borne elsewhere and that they will not take a direct hit to the pocket book. Financial institutions will make the individual “whole”. Workplaces will just absorb the harm without cost to the employee. Commercial companies will stand in the gap because they do not want to lose customers or deal with the negative publicity. These may have been true for a time but have become somewhat less true over time. Being co-opted comes with a direct cost to the person, borne by the person.

Another mistaken idea is that if the crowd is on an app that the app must necessarily be safe. Remember hackers and those who would exploit systems like crowded places because these are target-rich environments. Where people are is where the con artists also go, and they are on a constant prowl for vulnerabilities. In a cyber age, a person cannot “hide” in a crowd. Each person is identifiable to a person, and their computational fingerprint is unique to them.

The electronic hive mind focuses a lot of fleeting attention on information that makes it into the mainstream media, but it is less sensitive to publications in academia and in some of the more technologically-based news outlets. The depth of coverage tends to be light, and respective individuals in the hive have to purposefully pursue the information of interest to find it. Then, too, there are strategic silences, so the quality of information in the live mind is necessarily limited. In other aspects, the allure of using particular software or apps or devices involves so much dazzle that taking the safe route is unappealing.

For example, a social media user may be faced with a new follower…who is complimentary of something the user has said or pointed-to…and a common social response is to return the favor in kind…with followback. The followback may be to a fully automated social bot or a semi-automated social bot, and this exposes the person’s network to a potentially malicious agent, and creates a trackable relationship with an unknown entity (essentially). The glamor of the hyper-sociality online eclipses the sense of possible risk.

Questions Still to Be Answered

What was not examined here directly was how far the electronic hive mind for cybersecurity issues extends beyond the expert community and those aspiring to expertise. After all, a hive mind would be weak as only an echo chamber. Its power should be in its bridging connections through which messages may be amplified, and interactivity may occur for information moving in both directions of the relationship (questions and answers, co-commentary, disagreements, and others). Certainly, the digital leave-behinds of the electronic hive mind are reference-able by people because of archival of contents on the Web and Internet. These provide richer points-of-entry to the subject, which might be overwhelming and too complex otherwise. People do filter information through personality frames and stories and conflict, and the hive mind provides some access in these ways. There is some value added in terms of commentary because comments draw attention and interest.

Additionally, it would help to know if the electronic hive mind originated its own ideas. If the hive mind only echoes what others have said, while that does have value, that does not add to the underlying advancements of the field. Most works that are shared are somewhat derivative and never starting from true scratch. In the cybersecurity arena, what is novel and original are new programs and new applications of these programs, for offense and defense. There may be new thinking in cyber policy. There may be newcomers to the scene. To create works from true scratch then, a person must have access, trust, and expertise – none of which is easy to cultivate.

Initial Responses to the Three Research Areas

The collected data offer a beginning approach to the three research areas but nothing absolutely definitive. To review, the areas were:

*   1\. What is the level of sophistication of the electronic hive mind in regards to cybersecurity? Are there blind spots (lacunae) regarding cybersecurity? If so, what are these, are they from critical areas of cybersecurity, and why might these exist?
*   2\. How does the folk electronic hive mind differ from the expressions of cybersecurity experts on the Social Web / Web 2.0? If these exist, what are the main differences, and why might these exist?
*   3\. Is the “hive mind” (related to cybersecurity) more reflective of (a) a mob mentality or herd mind, or is it more reflective of (b) collective intelligence and “wisdom of crowds”? Is the hive mind functioning effectively and prosocially regarding cybersecurity (or not)? How so? How not?

Regarding the level of sophistication of the electronic hive mind, because of the presence of cybersecurity experts, the hive mind itself comes across as quite advanced and informed. No obvious blind spots were clear except the assumed ones where the cybersecurity experts are not sharing sensitive information. In terms of differences in social expressions between non-cybersecurity experts and cybersecurity experts, technical / policy prowess and depth of knowledge are probably the main indicators. In the third part, is the cybersecurity electronic hive mind more representative of mob mentalities or wisdom of crowds, it does seem like this particular hive mind tends toward the latter and sophistication. There have not been over-zealous calls-to-actions or behaviors that might indicate the herd mind. (This is so even with a diverse global population of participants and likely quite a few trolls.)

If survival is the goal of a “hive,” and the collective mind’s role is to promote the overall survival of the hive, it is fair to ask if the “electronic hive mind” is commensurate to the challenge of protecting the population against cybersecurity threats and attacks. Are there efficiencies made possible by the hive mind?

A “Healthy” or “Limber” Electronic Hive Mind Re: Cybersecurity

Theoretically, a healthy electronic hive mind should have an accurate long-term memory for relevant issues in the past (in electronically findable and retrievable ways). It should be attentive to the right and relevant things—and not to distractions (which cost in attention but give little back except entertainment). It should have some ability to anticipate the future in a somewhat accurate way. It should be resilient in the face of surprises. A healthy electronic hive mind should be informed by ethical and beneficent practice.

In terms of membership, there should be an inclusive mix of member types, varying in terms of levels of expertise (from novice to expert) and breadth of interests. In many ways, the hive mind seems to be informed by democratic ideals and egalitarianism. Ideally, the public faces of cybersecurity should be far-thinking and provide insights into the future and future potentials. (With the niche aspects of expertise in cybersecurity, only a few likely understand the particulars of new threats and can process the implications and the defenses, and of that sub-population, only a few will actually be able to speak coherently and publicly about that. The electronic hive mind should be sufficiently safe and welcoming to encourage participation and communicative sharing.)

The electronic hive mind should be informed and accurate, with information flows that enable the putting forward of the best ideas. It should be up-to-date on known threats. The hive mind should be able to conceptualize complexity in an accurate way, not be deceived by misperceptions; this hive mind should have discernment to separate the wheat (relevant data) from the chaff (inaccuracies, falsehoods). While any number of trial balloons may be floated as solutions for issues, an electronic hive mind should be able to vet through the options and come to some consensus on optimal solutions before any stance hardens into collective resolve.

While the mind should be influence-able and open to ideas, it should not be manipulated for malicious purposes. It should be deliberative in considering choices, and enable proper actions as-needed. A healthy electronic hive mind should be able to function well in both a “cool state” (calm) and a “hot state” (emotional, under pressure). The hive mind should be able to maintain privacy for information that should remain private. It should keep its population (and others) safe from being “pwned” (“player owned” or “utterly defeated,” through social engineering, hacking, and / or other exploits).

In the same way that corporations may be treated as “persons,” the electronic hive mind may have personality and a sense of personhood. The group can have personality; it can have directed attention and directed energies. It can have outputs based on the efforts of the group and its group members. The membership of hive minds evolve, and some move on as their needs are no longer met in a satisfactory way, and new membership comes in with new energy and often new goals. New members bring new perceptions as well as new capabilities. They change the consciousness of the hive mind.

FUTURE RESEARCH DIRECTIONS

The electronic hive mind is important in the sense of illuminating what the public may know about critical issues for population health in terms of cybersecurity. This is also important in terms of public permissions—how far along a public will go with a government or with industry in particular directions. The electronic hive mind around cybersecurity has responded around issues of mass (meta)data collection, private industry roles in breaking encryption for law enforcement, funding for the National Security Agency and the intelligence community (IC) in general, and other issues. Where the public is too unwieldy to bring along, government agencies seem to just keep information quiet. When the public is let in on complex issues, too often, the major responses are heated and reactionary. Sometimes, various stakeholders who should be on the same side may seem like they are working at cross purposes. This work has left some extant questions:

*   • Cognitive Limits to the Electronic Hive Mind?: At the individual levels, were there signs of confirmation bias? WYSIATI? The law of small numbers? Availability bias? Framing sensitivity? What about at group decision-making level: obedience to authority? Bystander effect/ diffusion of responsibility? Groupthink? Abilene paradoxes? These would be easier to explore given case studies in real-world contexts. (At the macro level of analysis, only summary data are engaged.)
*   • Mental Models vs. Conceptual Models?: As to the question of how the non-experts think vs. the experts, targeted surveys would be stronger instruments to ferret this out.

Besides shoring up this initial research, with additional data sources and analytical methods, there are other possibilities to extend this work. Some questions about generic electronic hive minds may be asked.

*   • How does an electronic hive mind coalesce and evolve?
*   • What are seminal moments of change for electronic hive minds?
*   • What are some ways to add capabilities to the hive mind?
*   • How can critical membership in hive minds be maintained, particularly the high-value experts who can provide information and insight?

Researchers have debated the morality of decisions arrived at by human swarms, and these questions have become even more complex with the harnessing of artificial intelligence (AI) swarm processing (Rosenberg & Baltaxe, 2016, p. 1).

About Building Up the Electronic Hive Mind

Mulgan (2018) defines the elements of collective intelligence as inclusive of the following elements: “a live model of the world, observation, focus, memory, empathy, motor coordination, creativity, judgment (and) wisdom” (p. 41). He asserts that smarter “assemblies” of combined human and machine intelligence may be cultivated with proper approaches, processes, and selectivity, to arrive at mutually advantageous and even optimized solutions. This work requires that the electronic hive mind not just evolve organically and in a feral way but adopt methods that enhance its development and selectivity.

CONCLUSION: A WORD ABOUT CYBERSECURITY AND “WEAK LINKS”

What are the managerial implications? So the electronic hive mind related to “cybersecurity” could be strengthened to fill in more gaps. There can be more focus on cybersecurity habits instead of just the technological prowess of some cyberattackers and some cyberdefenders. The limits of the hive mind come from the hive (and the hardwired cognitive biases in people) and from group limits in decision-making. However, these are not issues that cannot be somewhat addressed by awareness of these challenges and various mitigations. Using the Web as an extension of the mind can be positive, to extend collective and individual memory. Having members play roles of the 10^(th) man can broaden cognition and engagement with information; it can open up the thinking space. This ability to think broadly and outside conventional lanes is critical given the expressive range of code and how code may be harnessed for attacks in combination with other approaches.

Having cybersecurity experts engage more with the electronic hive mind can be positive, if they bring new actionable insights to the hive and do not overreach their expertise. They can offer more in-depth understandings and skills. They can communicate strategically to people at differing levels of sophistication and understanding. They should be able to finesse an approach that does not shut down people but keeps them engaged and curious and seeking. Ideally, experts can share a malign imagination for the multiple possible uses of a thing. They can extend vision to show the myriad possibilities of betrayals, new alignments, and the breaking of trusts; certainly, history is replete with such stories. They can convey the proper measure of worry about where actual risks lie and what to care about in terms of cybersecurity. They can suggest effective steps to take to address cybersecurity risks and suggest mitigations when harms are unavoidable. They need to reach the public where they are at—from those with simple understandings to those with more complex ones. Poor targeting of the audience can turn off people from dealing with cybersecurity or valuating it as a part of their devices and social media platforms and IOT services.

Warnings can raise awareness and break through complacency and the illusions of safety. Warnings can create sufficient skepticism; they can help enliven a healthier survival sensibility; they can enable people to better withstand manipulations like social engineering and to be comfortable with other-created social tensions and pressures, in order not to be manipulated and compromised. Ideally, this awareness can mitigate some risks. After all, cyberattacks are comprised of several steps: first an email elicitation and then a sharing of messages and then the capture of private information… or first a click on a corrupted link and the capture of credentials and then access to private financial accounts… In all of these, there is combinatorial complexity, and people may wise-up to issues during the “cyber compromise cycle” and simply not participate and simply notify relevant authorities.

Strategic considerations should be applied in terms of how much and what information should be conveyed to the non-expert parts of the hive. An expert cannot “mirror image” users and assume that their thinking processes, awarenesses, skills, and concerns are necessarily similar. Offering more information is not necessarily positive, since “TMI” can turn off the general public from the necessary engagements. Excessive complexity may raise the cost-of-entry for participants to the electronic hive. Does more information help people to better understand the cyber challenges at hand, or not? Does more information spark a healthy survival sensibility and encourage more appropriate defensive awareness and behaviors? Would it increase adherence to advised cybersecurity-promoting behaviors? Improve buy-in? Increase trust?

“What” information to share is also challenging. After all, there are no real hard-and-fast rules, which always apply. For example, anti-virus programs themselves have been compromised and served as attack vectors per “doubleagent” (sic) attacks (Newman, Mar. 23, 2017). The right decision is only right given certain contextual details and assumptions. Cybersecurity experts are always working in environments of incomplete information. If cyber health can be analogized with public health, there will be varying states of cyberhealth in the population, and while general health is desirable and worked towards, the resources are invested into preventing mass epidemics (or mass cyber compromises).

So to recap: To provide some insights on the electronic hive mind surrounding cybersecurity, various online indicators of data were explored, including mass-scale Web search correlations over extended time, news sharing threads, word uses in mass book corpora, hashtag networks’ message sharing, social imagery, image tagging, social audio, social videos, and social slideshows.

The software used in this study include NodeXL, NVivo 11 Plus, MS Visio, and Adobe Photoshop. The online sites and services used include Google Search, Google Correlate, Google Translate, Reddit (as in “read it”), Google Books Ngram Viewer, iTunes, YouTube, and SlideShare. The author does not have any formal ties with any of the applications or the software programs.

As to the issue of cybersecurity at the common user level, a few smart choices can head off some of the simpler exploits that can lead to major system compromises. For common users, it does not seem reasonable to expect hyper-vigilance at every turn and personal discipline against online enticements. There are known say-do gaps, know-do gaps. It is even more far-fetched to expect people to invest in learning about cybersecurity in depth and updating their knowledge constantly. It is hard to imagine that they will develop the skills for pre-emption in all cases of potential cyber compromise. Certainly, the piecemeal information in the electronic hive mind cannot really be said to have coalesced into coherent understandings of computing machines and their uses through online means.

Fortunately, cybersecurity does not only depend on user actions and tradecraft. Systems are somewhat more resilient. There are memory backups, logging, increased electronic surveillance, and recovery plans. Technologists and developers, meantime, have been working to bypass human error as much as possible, with clearer designs and encapsulated functions (hidden and hard-to-change). User-proofing of technologies and equipment has long been de rigueur to take user-based vulnerabilities out of the equation as much as possible. The machine speeds of potential (and even likely) cyberattacks far outpace human speeds in terms of responses, which is another reason why such defenses have become automated.

This is not to say that it is possible to ignore humans in the cybersecurity equation. However, in many cases, organizations have pushed down levels of system compromise as far as possible, and it is not at zero. At any one time, there are varying levels of machine compromises and low-burning infections. NASA scientist and research psychologist Steve Casner has written of the need for people to internalize safety understandings in all contexts:

The next safety revolution is going to have to happen in our own minds. In the everyday situations of life, we’re going to have to learn to tilt our head pensively to one side and think, ‘You know…I really should be more careful.’ This kind of being careful is different from being told what to do and handed a list of reasons why. When the idea to be more careful comes from within our own heads, we don’t need to be reminded or convinced. The hard question is, of course, how do we get there? How do we make it our idea to be more careful? (2017, p. 7)

If cyberspace consists of the four conceptualized layers—“the physical or hardware layer…the logic layer…the data layer…and the social layer” at the top—the most important is the human one because the entire structure is created for people as “the ultimate layer” (Klimburg, 2017, pp. 28 – 29). Hacking or the compromise of cybersecurity is essentially about “human beings and human decision making” (p. 51) and working through the social layer to access the target (p. 53).

Essentially, whatever users’ mental models of cyber, where users count is in their decision-making and actions. A series of decision trees related to cybersecurity are listed in Appendix A. These decision trees provide a sense of the choices that cautious users of cyber may follow to lower their risks of compromise. They also convey the sense that every single person is compromise-able, and recognizing that first is important. If people feel immune to cyber-compromise, that already heightens the risk that they are in, because they will not be necessarily vigilant or mindful. Consumers are not alone in their defenses; they are supported by some serious efforts by corporations and government to shore up system security and to encourage resilience in the face of well-funded and tough adversaries (including those supported by nation-states).

Finally, there is need for those in cybersecurity to have probes and sensors in the electronic hive mind, to listen for risks. Two practitioners in national security recently published a book about the need to heed those in-the-know who have identified risks into the future. They refer to these individuals as “cassandras,” truth-tellers who are often disbelieved. In their “Casssandra Coefficient,” the authors describe cassandras with the following characteristics: “proven technical expert, off-putting personality, data driven, orthogonal thinker, questioners, sense of person(al) responsibility, (and) high anxiety” (Clarke & Eddy, 2017, p. 170). They conceptualize cassandras or those with “sentinel intelligence” (an ability to perceive threat and warn about these threats) as engaging in electronic spaces, which may be swept for insights.

They write:

Buried in billions of pages of blog posts and tweets, academic research, and government reports. Cassandra figuratively calls to us, warning of calamity. Often she is unheeded, sometimes unheard. Frequently she is given only a token response or dismissed as a fool or a fraud. Her stories are so improbable, so unprecedented, that we cannot process them or believe them, much less act upon them.

The problem is, of course, that Cassandra was right, and those who ignored her may have done so at the cost of their own lives and that of their state. (Clarke & Eddy, 2017, p. 2)

Even if humans are the “weak link,” they are most certainly the most “critical link”: after all, information technologies are built to serve people in their many endeavors. Their engagement in the electronic hive mind is important for cybersecurity into the future.
