Zhu, L., Mussio, P., & Barricelli, B. R. (2010). Hive-mind space model for creative, collaborative design. Desire ’10, 121 – 130.

KEY TERMS AND DEFINITIONS

Black Hat: A term used to describe a malicious (and/or criminal) hacker.

Cassandra: A figure from Greek mythology who was cursed to see the future accurately but fated to be disbelieved, a figure harnessed as a figure of “sentinel intelligence” and “sentinel” (warning) behavior.

Cyber Psychology: Internet or web psychology, psychological phenomena related to cyber technology.

Cybersecurity: Acts taken, technologies created and deployed, policies written and enacted, to protect computer systems and networks against misuse, intrusion, and exploitation.

Defense in Depth: The creation of multiple lines of defense against attackers.

Groupthink: A phenomenon of group decision-making that tends towards uncreative and pro forma choices, without individual responsibility.

Hacker: A person or team that illegally accesses others’ computer systems and data.

Hive Mind: A large population of people who co-share information, resulting in unthinking conformity (to the negative) or to collective intelligence or a “wisdom of the crowds” (to the positive).

Insider Threat: The risk from a malicious agent who works within the organization and has the advantage of insider knowledge and insider access and internal trust-based social networks.

Internet of Things (IoT): A term used to indicate the interconnection of various home-based devices through the internet.

Keylogger: A software program (that may be used as malware) that captures the keystrokes on a keyboard.

Leetspeak: “Elite” speak as an informal language used on the Internet by those in-the-know and with serious technological skill sets.

Malware: Malicious software.

Socialbot: A robot created to manifest as a person in a social networking platform or other social media application; may be an avatar.

Unthinkingness: Making decisions or acting without mental consideration or awareness or questioning.

USB: Universal serial bus.

White Hat: A term used to describe a benevolent, ethical, and pro-social hacker.

WYSIATI: “What you see is all there is” (a term coined by psychologist Daniel Kahneman to describe this type of cognitive bias).

Zero Day: A software or hardware vulnerability that is as-yet unpatched (and maybe unknown) by the creator.

APPENDIX

It can be mind-boggling to consider all the different possible attack surfaces related to cyber, even for fairly common users. They have identities and reputations to protect, data to keep safe from theft and misuse, messaging to keep with integrity, funds to guard, and services to maintain. The Appendix contains a selection of decision trees related to “proper” choices to maintain cybersecurity from a general user point-of-view. These were created to give a sense of some of the simpler approaches to cybersecurity at the general user level. Given the fast-changing aspects of the field, these decision trees are not conceptualized as lasting forever. The three colors in the nodes are red, yellow, and green, and these may be understood with red indicating a risky approach, yellow indicating the necessity of caution, and green indicating a less-risky and even preferable approach. These decision trees are by no means a full taxonomy of steps and concerns, but they are a start. The trees are read from top to bottom. At each split, there are only binary choices; in the real world, though, there would likely be much more complexity at different decision junctures.

In addition, these actions are by no means foolproof. Rather, these protect against some basic risks but do nothing against larger-scale advanced persistent threats (APTs) and other cybersecurity challenges. Still, the common user is at the line level and may well be the first steps of cyber compromises unless they are trained not to engage in high-risk behaviors.

Figure 22 points to a common risk from not patching nor updating computer systems and leaving them vulnerable to newfound exploitations. This problem is even worse when people use computers with inauthentic operating systems and software, which are not updated by the actual manufacturers.

| Figure 22. Protecting against an outdated system |

| --- |

Figure 23 points to the need for maintaining hygienic computer systems, without viruses and malware. This is a function of protecting against exposures but also cleaning the system of exposures that occur. Users who are not focused on cybersecurity may not have formed a mental baseline of their system functions and what to expect. They may not have explored their built-in tools for system functions to understand the metrics of system functions. Gradual changes may occur to their computer systems without their noticing. Where cybersecurity professionals may be attentive to nuanced details and are savvy to complex interactions within technological systems, common users may not be so aware nor sophisticated.

Figure 24 points to common challenges with poor password creation and management. Once credentials and passwords are stolen, users can access systems as if they were the users, and they can wreak all sorts of havoc. The thinking on the optimal passwords is contested, though, and some are suggesting that biometrics may be a somewhat safer option (although there are hacks for biological biometric access systems). Two-factor authentication makes people’s privacy more robust: this refers to the need not only for a password but a dynamically generated code that is then passed to the user through a text message or telephone message…to authenticate the individual. (An update on this is that short message service or “SMS” messages can be more easily compromise-able since fraudsters may easily call telephone companies and have a phone number changed to another phone…which may then be used to capture the second-factor authentication. If a person’s password has already been compromised, the loss of this second authentication may mean that people’s accounts and other data may be at high risk for tampering and misuse. Having a secure two-factor authentication application on a phone may be a safer approach if the phone itself is locked and if those who own the phone pay close attention to ensure their own awareness if it is lost or stolen (Landau, Apr. 23, 2018).

Another protection, in the financial realm, is to not only go with a pin (a password for use of a debit card, for example), but also a “chip” to verify that the account is in good standing (and has not been reported stolen). The typical argument against additional measures for identity and security is that additional measures are inconvenient and lower utility.

While people may be aghast at how gullible some may be, the cons that are deployed range from the simple to the complex. Sometimes, the line between belief and unbelief can be quite thin. For many, the glitter of the Web and Internet is mesmerizing and addictive. Audio-visual elements, visuals, and sounds may create a sense of the “immersive parasocial” (Hai-Jew, 2009) with people pursuing illusory relationships through cyber means. When attention is drawn in particular directions, people experience “attention hangovers” that require almost half a minute to return to normal (Casner, 2017, pp. 19 – 20); in states of “hot cognition,” described as when people are under the “influence of emotions such as impatience, anger, stress, anxiety, disgust, contempt, boredom, fear, and depression,” risk judgment and decision-making suffer (pp. 58 – 60).

Personal information shared online may be used for lifestyle mapping…and have led to robberies, personal attacks, and worse. Oversharing can lead to false intimacies and stalking, fraud, and other types of harm. \[A study of some users on Twitter found that a majority would friend social robots and not even realize that they were just scripts—not people. (Boshmaf et al., 2011; Wagner et al., 2012). The social risks are compounded by a common human default setting of at least initially trusting others (Levine, 2014).

There are many “phishers of men” out there to try to gain advantage through trickery. A major mental hurdle for common users of cyber is to conceptualize adversaries arrayed against them personally (or impersonally). A “con” or “confidence trick” involves manipulating people into giving up something of value. These tricks “exploit characteristics of the human psyche such as dishonesty, vanity, compassion, credulity, irresponsibility, naïveté and greed” (“Confidence trick,” Aug. 17, 2017). There are a number of cons known to be deployed online, from “give to get” and romance-based cons. Too often, people are duped because of their own sense of being special (they will be the exceptions to the rule), their wishful thinking, and their over-trust in others. (Sometimes, just turning the situation around and asking relevant questions can be illuminating: “Why would someone be out there giving away free money?” “Or why would an attractive lonely hearts be out there looking for love with a stranger?”)

The ease of false rumors going viral and people acting on rumors by re-sharing and thus amplifying the messages have led cybersecurity researchers to look for ways to head off such attacks. (This can be headed off by thinking about the sourcing of information and the motivation of the sharer…and likely desired behavioral responses to that information sharing. It helps to think of the informational environment as a place of many interests and motivations, many self-interested and malign. The phenomenon of the “filter bubble,” people selectively consulting favored news sources only, is a further challenge since these can result in tunnel vision vs. breadth of understandings (Klimburg, 2017, pp. 12 – 13).

Depending on how they are provisioned, they may have “privilege over-entitlement” or excessive access for the work that they are doing. If their interests are not aligned with those of the organization, they can be positioned to cause some serious harm. For those who are more socially motivated, it helps them to know that some cybersecurity compromises come through trust networks. An individual who falls for a cybersecurity scam endangers his or her social networks. Cybersecurity, as in other types of security, is not an individual game. Defense occurs at a number of levels and spaces simultaneously. Individually, and in groups, people do play an important role.

These “cybersecurity” decision trees provide a simple start to a complex topic. Knowing the safer paths and the seriousness of cybersecurity compromise is important. Corner cutting and not following-through on the proper actions is risky, even “just this once.” People’s mental games of “unique invulnerabilities” (denial of potential negative outcomes for oneself) (Casner, 2017, p. 54) and senses of taking only “small risks” (which accrue over time) (p. 55) can mean serious cybersecurity exposures. It may be hard to see cyberspace as a hostile and dynamic environment with a number of different players, with different intentions and skills.

# Chapter 12

Exploring Social Networks, Geographies, and Strategic Messaging

*   Shalin Hai-Jew  
    Kansas State University, USA

ABSTRACT

Malicious political socialbots used to sway public opinion regarding the U.S. government and its functions have been identified as part of a larger information warfare effort by the Russian government. This work asks what is knowable from a web-based sleuthing approach regarding the following four factors: 1) the ability to identify malicious political socialbot accounts based on their ego neighborhoods at 1, 1.5, and 2 degrees; 2) the ability to identify malicious political socialbot accounts based on the claimed and linked geographical locations of their accounts, their ego neighborhoods, and their #hashtag networks; 3) the ability to identify malicious political socialbot accounts based on their strategic messaging (content, sentiment, and language structures) on respective social media platforms; and 4) the ability to identify and describe “maliciousness” in malicious political socialbot accounts based on observable behaviors on that account on three social media platform types: (a) microblogging, (b) social networking, and (c) crowd-sourced encyclopedia content sharing.

INTRODUCTION

A U.S. presidential election, which occurs every four years, is a high-stakes, high-impact endeavor with a large number of stakeholders, not least of which are the 326 million U.S. citizens (“U.S. Population (live),” 2018). This is not to say there have not been high levels of apathy regarding voting in presidential elections and low levels of civic engagement. Even though presidential powers in a democracy are limited by law, by practice (checks and balances), by mass media, and by the public will, it is still a position with inordinate influence. In most such elections, the choice is practically between two surviving candidates, each one backed by either the Republican or Democratic Party, and each representing different platforms. In the American democracy, the reduction to a two-way race means this offers a political chokepoint and, therefore, a system-based “weaknesses” which may be prone to manipulation.

In the current political moment, the U.S. is engaged in coming to terms with what “Russian meddling” during the 2016 U.S. presidential election and setting up a defense against further anticipated meddling in the 2018 midterm elections and into the future. The core question being addressed is whether the U.S. emplaced a “Manchurian candidate” in 2016 who might have been focused on trading power and influence for monetary and other gains from the Russian and other foreign governments. The story arc has evolved as investigators from various intelligence agencies have explored this Kremlin influence operation, with its agents creating social media platform accounts and using robots (‘bots or automated agents) to promote particular storylines, to discredit democracy and to promote one presidential candidate (Donald J. Trump) over the other (Hillary Clinton). An initial perusal of the first facts may have led an individual to downplay the importance of the effort. As more details emerge, the seriousness becomes somewhat clearer.

The actual investments into the effort were not minimal, with early efforts starting in 2014. There was a test run with #fakenews by disseminating false information claiming a family became ill from consuming a Walmart turkey (Earle, 2018). The Russian government apparently spent up to US$1.25 million a month and paid hundreds for this endeavor (Tamkin, 2018). According to a U.S. government indictment, Russian agents were sent to collect intelligence and research in multiple states prior to the presidential election to better target the messaging. In the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, based on an indictment filed on Feb. 16, 2018, the U.S. Special Counsel’s Office identified 13 Russian individuals involved in this endeavor. The identification of these 13 individuals, across borders, cultures, technologies, and languages, demonstrated the reach of American intelligence and law enforcement. The indictment deftly cited witting and unwitting individuals manipulated by this information operation. In the following section, the indictment describes some of the Russian agents’ travel to the U.S.:

Only KRYLOVA and BOGACHEVA received visas, and from approximately June 4, 2014 through June 26, 2014, KRYLOVA and BOGACHEVA traveled in and around the United States, including stops in Nevada, California, New Mexico, Colorado, Illinois, Michigan, Louisiana, Texas, and New York to gather intelligence. After the trip, KRYLOVA and BURCHIK exchanged an intelligence report regarding the trip.

Another co-conspirator who worked for the ORGANIZATION traveled to Atlanta, Georgia from approximately November 26, 2014 through November 30, 2014. Following the trip, the co-conspirator provided POLOZOV a summary of his trip's itinerary and expenses. (“United States of America v. Internet Research Agency LLC…,” Feb. 16, 2018, p. 13)

The indictment documents the setup of virtual private networks (VPNs) inside the U.S. (“United States of America v. Internet Research Agency LLC…,” 2018, pp. 15 – 16). Such technologies create a false sense that the computers used to access social media platforms seem to be U.S.-based. The effort itself was made possible by a Russian government military doctrine known as the Gerasimov Doctrine, according to cybersecurity expert Jim Lewis, Senior VP at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (Garrett, 2018).

The Gerasimov Doctrine suggests that modern war may engage an enemy nation’s society instead of a head-on attack and to create “permanent unrest and conflict within an enemy state” (McKew, 2017). McKew writes that it may be difficult to defend against this type of warfare:

Herein lies the real power of the Gerasimov-style shadow war: It’s hard to muster resistance to an enemy you can’t see, or aren’t even sure is there. But it’s not an all-powerful approach; the shadowy puppeteering at the heart of the Gerasimov Doctrine also makes it inherently fragile. Its tactics begin to fail when light is thrown onto how they work and what they aim to achieve. This requires leadership and clarity about the threat—which we saw briefly in France, when the government rallied to warn voters about Russian info ops in advance of the presidential election. For now, though, America is still in the dark—not even on defense, let alone offense. (McKew, 2017)

In the same way that traditional mass media used to set agendas and filter news for a broad audience, that role has now fallen to social media platforms. While the tampering with American elections was already highly problematic, along with the efforts to hack into the voter systems of a number of states, the attempts at undue influence have continued. A #releasethememo kerfuffle in January-February 2018, related to the House Intelligence Committee’s work on Russian meddling in the 2016 presidential election, was also found to have attracted the attention of the Russian government, which employed “computational propaganda techniques” focused on changing “public perceptions and the behavior of American lawmakers” (McKew, 2018, p. 1). There are widespread concerns that Russians will continue with their propagandistic approaches to interfere with the 2018 midterm elections and other political skirmishes in the U.S.

Information assurance or the accuracy of the information being shared over networks (without manipulation) is a core value in information science. Using fraudulent accounts to spread misinformation for political aims could be seen as the harnessing of cyber as a weapon. Latiff (2017) writes in a broad sense: “Cyber weapons thus provide an important means of destroying, degrading, disrupting, and denying adversary systems” (p. 51). If automated political bots are deployed as cyber weapons to degrade democracy and the sanctity of the vote, certainly the analogy may apply. Political bots have been used to “threaten activists, swing elections, and even engage in conversation with the President” (DiResta, Little, Morgan, Neudert, & Nimmo, 2017).

Additionally, in the same manner it is difficult to predict how cyberweapons deploy and manifest once they are released in the wild (Latiff, 2017, pp. 50 - 53), these methods of state-based manipulation of an adversary’s publics are predicted to expand to other nation-states and their cyber and information warfare arsenals. For all the national security implications and the seriousness of these issues, this chapter is not a political work, but it springboards from the current political issues to that of malicious socialbots.

While the issue is being addressed along the legal track, there are also political and social tracks, among others. Some are arguing the political discord was homegrown and based on “partisan polarization.” (Taub & Fisher, 2018) Another suggests that “the Kremlin had no grand plan to elect Trump” and that the Russian use of social media was not as threatening as portrayed (Gessen, 2018).

Regardless of how the complexities of this situation resolve, one basic generally accepted fact is that automated agents or “robots” (‘bots) were instruments used to create particular messaging and impressions on various social media accounts (including Facebook and Instagram, and Twitter). The social ‘botness of a scripted agent may encourage people to anthropomorphize them, but these are not human personages, just short coded programs that are designed to achieve particular designed aims. Many ‘bots have become more sophisticated and imbued with “personality” based on human psychology research models. Americans themselves are some of the most studied humans on the planet because of their access to resources and power, and that information may be used for any number of purposes, both benevolent and malign, and this information is used to influence them to various (usually commercial) ends.

Socialbot accounts, fully or partially automated accounts representing humans on social media platforms, may be fully automated or part human / part automated (“cyborgs” or “cybernetic organisms”). ‘Bots used for social ills are considered malicious bots or “malbots.” Different platforms handle robots in different ways. Some social media platforms are unable to effectively differentiate between human and robot accounts, as part of their business model. Some require robot accounts to be registered, to pass human review, and to be flagged (identified) as such.

Using social media platforms for influence operations makes a lot of sense. Many Americans are acculturated to socializing on social media, so there is a built user base. \[Statista has identified 81% of the U.S. population who use social media as of 2017 (“Percentage of U.S. population who currently use any social media from 2008 to 2017,” 2017)\]. In many cases, and on many platforms, Americans have shown themselves as socially acquisitive and socially “promiscuous” in their friending and inter-relating. This may be especially so if they believe they are interacting with other Americans. In heightened emotional states, such as around politics, people may be more easily sparked to actions—such as faux events—based on the catalyst of a message or an image or a story.

Influence operations are not about subtlety but about sparking people to actions (confronting others, holding marches, voting a particular way for a candidate or issue, “voting” by microblogging or texting, and others) and to non-actions (not voting). In addition, the deployment of ‘bots requires continuous efforts to ensure they are actionable, and it is likely the human agents behind this endeavor had to monitor near-constantly to engage timely issues and to have an effect on-ground. As to how to measure the effects of their efforts, though, that may be harder to assess.

Even after the revelations of the Russian meddling by U.S. intelligence agencies, many whose agendas were promoted by robots have made public statements in the press decrying the assertion they were involved in any #falseflag (misleading claim of a false identity) influence operations, but also not backing away one step from their relatively extreme (non-mainline) views. In light of the sense of threat to American democracy (and the consent of the governed) and the mis-use of social technologies, it is in the interests of individuals and entities to be able to identify ill-seeking socialbots.

In an earlier work, the author considered some indicators that may indicate botness: membership patterns, relationship patterns, interactional patterns, messaging and contents (particularly advocacy), geographical patterns, time patterns, and cross-type differences (bots, sensors, cyborgs, humans) (Hai-Jew, 2017, pp. 394 - 395). Arrayed against detection are a range of tools, with ‘bots programmed to act “as if” they were people—with slowed responsiveness, with geographically localized time patterns and “waking” hours, with alignments to various types of personalities, with tapping the local electronic environment for resources (information, links, images, and others), and other tools.

Artificial intelligence (AI) agents have improved signficantly since the days of the chatbots (automated agents designed to interact with people through interactive textual communications) in the 1990s. Then, it was sufficiently easy to detect botness by asking a question or two and getting the chatbots to repeat earlier lines (usually written in long sentences). Today, socialbots engage in online grammars and syntaxes, so how difficult would it be to identify an automated agent in social media platforms today? An initial sense was there would need to be multiple and combined ways of arriving at a sense of identifier of the generic bots. For example, a bot might be identifiable because its ego neighborhood (the “alters” within one degree of relationship) contained many other bots, and it does not have many geographical ties to physical space, and its messaging is strident and thematic and derivative of human messaging.

A “political” (or propaganda) socialbot is a “political actor,” one that is used to engage political messaging and to achieve political aims (to change elections, to modify policies, and to ultimately change on-ground realities). Built for such ends, such socialbots tend to be generally unsubtle. On microblogging sites, they share pithy messages to excite people to desired actions. In the same way that egos of a social network may be seen to have preferences (or “biases,” without any derogatory implication), political socialbots may be seen in a similar manner. \[In the same way that human-embodied social media accounts may be described and profiled based on “likes,” so too can bot accounts. Political bots may be especially informative in terms of their behaviors: who they socialize with, what messages they take up, their stances on various issues, their tactics and strategies, and ultimately, their “politics” and “policy stances.”\]. A political or propaganda socialbot is a subtype of socialbot.

Expressed as a decision tree, the decision sequence may go something like the following as in Figure 1. First, there is the encounter with the social media account (whether human-embodied, cyborg, or fully automated…and whether benevolent or neutral or malicious). Using the available information, a person may explore the profile, its ego neighborhood and social network, the (claimed) geographical features of the account and linked network members, the strategic and shared messaging…and determine (potentially) whether the account is fully human, a cyborg, or a fully automated ‘bot. Of course, more complex explorations may be done to test for identity, although those paths are not fully explored here.

This is a theorized decision tree, and whether this approach works or not, whether there are evocative identity tells, is the basis of this research. The three general steps in this work are to: (1) identify potential social media identity indicators; (2) settle on an apparent identity type (fully human, cyborg, or ‘bot); (3) determine whether the social media account is benevolent or malicious, and (4) potentially validate or invalidate the two prior impressions (identity and benevolent/malicious). The fourth step, if not connected to the other steps, is an added step. The “More Complex Explorations” steps may be steps taken for validation or invalidation.

At the end, the state of the social account being benign or malicious is explored. This may be done as a binary categorization (benevolent/malicious) or as a continuum or a matter of degree (direction and intensity) (Figure 2).

Hypotheses 1 – 3 are about using various public information (robot ego neighborhoods, geographical locations, and strategic messaging) from the social media platforms to identify botness, and Hypothesis 4 is about identifying something more complex: intention and effect of the underlying account (ranging from benevolent to malicious) in identified Russian bots to see how they compare with human-embodied social media accounts.

*   Hypothesis 1: Malicious political socialbot accounts may be somewhat identifiable from human social media accounts by their ego neighborhoods (at 1, 1.5, and 2 degrees) on respective social media platforms.
*   Hypothesis 2: Malicious political socialbot accounts may be somewhat identifiable from human social media accounts by the geographical locations of their accounts (from the claimed location in the profile) and their ego neighborhoods (from claimed locales and messaging locales based on mobile and other apps) on respective social media platforms and from artificial #hashtag networks promoted by ‘bots.
*   Hypothesis 3: Malicious political socialbot accounts may be somewhat identifiable from human social media accounts by their strategic and shared messaging (content, sentiment, and language structures) on respective social media platforms.
*   Hypothesis 4: It is possible to describe the “maliciousness” in malicious political socialbot accounts based on observable behaviors as differentiated from human maliciousness expressed on social media platforms.

From this research, insights about the efficacy of using public information to identify botness and bot malice are discussed.

Delimitations

This work only engages a few social media accounts on three main platforms: microblogging, social networking, and crowd-sourced encyclopedia content-sharing (specifically, Twitter, Facebook, and Wikipedia). Based on current numbers from Statista, Twitter is said to have some 330 million monthly active users, and Facebook is said to have 2.129 billion users. Wikipedia, according to Wikimedia Foundation, has some 33 million users. All three named platforms are implicated in the Russian meddling—the first two with faux socialbot accounts, and the third one with manipulated edits. By contrast to Twitter and Facebook, Wikipedia is a counter-example of a site which has controlled and flagged robots that are required to serve pro-social aims. Each of the respective socio-technical platforms has some similarity and some different technological enablements, policies, enforcement of those policies, and user bases.

This work examines the uses of human, cyborg, and robot accounts in the political space. This begs the question: How much do people actually “trust” and “befriend” others on social media (and by extension, trust and befriend malicious social media accounts)? Certainly, some people do go online to engage trustfully and in actual friendly ways and will even meet others in “meatspace” and create relationships of all kinds and depths there. Botsman (2017) suggests that “trust” refers to “a confident relationship with the unknown” (n.p.) and that humans have moved from trusting first locally, then institutionally, and now in “distributed” ways through networks (pp. 6 – 7). For others, they may go to a microblogging site to hear others’ opinions, but they may view relating in a more shallow and fleeting way. They may see the space as one of a-trust (where trust is not relevant) and non-trust (where they are skeptical, cynical, and untrusting).

The same cannot really be said for a social networking site like Facebook in which users start, build, and maintain relationships, and this usage of the platform may make the vulnerability larger. With regards to Wikipedia, the data design is to include “objective” and referenced information, not subjectivities…so the sense of trust may be something else. While it would be inappropriate to over-generalize about the uses of accounts, with hundreds of millions of people engaged, it is important to consider how people build mental models around social media and act based on those models.

Finding authenticated samples of the Russian ‘bots is difficult. With the high amount of attention on malicious automated political agents on social media platforms, the companies behind the respective sites have removed the identified accounts listed in legal documents and news articles. Some of the political social accounts analyzed here are those mentioned in journalistic articles as suspected robots, and some are peripherally related accounts, and a few have no direct relationship to the Russian meddling issue but are used as a comparative “control.” Capturing data from social media platforms is seldom an N=all because of data rate-limiting on the social media platforms, and limits to the software used to extract the research data.

REVIEW OF THE LITERATURE

The debut of socialbots did not begin with the present age. Rather, socialbots as “chat bots” have been around since the early 1990s and the dawn of the Web and a decade into the Internet. Chatbots, as precursors to present-day ‘bots, used to be highly programmed and rigid, without the adaptivity, personality, smarts, humor, and sophistication of high-end artificial intelligence (AI) agents like personal assistants (like Siri, Google Assistant, and others). The socialbots created for presence on social media platforms are a volume business. The more followers a business can provide to an individual, the more they can charge. The socialbots that appear on social media platforms are generally more sophisticated than chatbots, but only by a little.

Socialbot-makers face some basic challenges. They need to create ‘bots with somewhat believable profiles but also which are attractive and appealing (many ‘bots are portrayed as attractive young females). The ‘bots must be friended by people to achieve cover and to access their social networks. They must converse in a somewhat believable way through text, link-sharing, image-sharing, and video-sharing. They have to ensure that the ‘bots are able to collect information from the online environment and behave on that information to keep the Tweetstreams and post content streams fresh.

To survive, the ‘bots have to avoid “tells” (indicators) that algorithmically identify them as automated agents because then these accounts will be blocked. Deploying low-cost automated agents to create a “viral” message is an effort that does not age well. After all, people tend to be fairly skeptical and open to calling out others on the Social Web. There are algorithmic back-end tells to identify some of the robots in the online social ecosystem. What is on social media platforms—as it is for much of the content on the Internet—is captured and saved into practical perpetuity, which enables retroactive analyses. Having access to permanent information means that any future-created methodologies may be used to analyze the data and to learn from that.

In addition, for issues of interest to not only U.S. researchers but also to others, there will be many eyes analyzing the available data today, with many insights available. Making a fake persona for a limited objective is no easy feat, and many of the more generic ‘bots will not pass the tests of “personhood”. Remember the so-called “reverse Turing test” or CAPTCHA (Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart) uses a few simple images and text boxes to validate human identity, and that is enough to prevent some types of simple ‘bots.).

With increasing awareness, the lifespans of automated agents have decreased significantly. For example, one researcher observed that Twitter bots “have a very short shelf life” (Tynan, 2012, p. 5). At present, the survival curve of automated agents on respective social media platforms have not been publicized; however, in light of the focus on this issue, the likely survival rates are dropping, and most faked accounts are under actuarial risks. Those who sell socialbots as a service have to identify clients, set a market price that attracts buyers, handle customer requests, and not fall afoul of law enforcement. Essentially, this is a fly-by-night volume business, and those who succeed have to provide some value for their customers.

This is to say that socialbots have been around for years before the identification of their role in the Russian meddling in the 2016 U.S. presidential elections. Some early bots had “nonsensical” handles, photos of attractive young females, links to porn websites, a low number of Tweets, and relatively new accounts (with the explanation: “Bot herders have to continually generate new accounts as their old ones get nuked” (Tynan, 2012, p. 3).

The New York Times studied a company that sells automated “followers” to plump up the sense of online popularity of individuals. It would seem that individuals with a public-facing side and media interests may buy adoring robot followers online.

The Times reviewed business and court records showing that Devumi has more than 200,000 customers, including reality television stars, professional athletes, comedians, TED speakers, pastors and models. In most cases, the records show, they purchased their own followers. In others, their employees, agents, public relations companies, family members or friends did the buying. For just pennies each — sometimes even less — Devumi offers Twitter followers, views on YouTube, plays on SoundCloud, the music-hosting site, and endorsements on LinkedIn, the professional-networking site. (Confessore, Dance, Harris, & Hansen, 2018)

The ’bots that were created were variations on people’s names but with extra letters or underscores; in other cases, there were letter substitutions like the lower-case “l” to stand in for an upper-case “I” (Confessore, Dance, Harris, & Hansen, 2018). One real person could be versioned “into hundreds of different bots, each a minute variation of the original” (Confessore, Dance, Harris, & Hansen, 2018).

The various socialbots may be understood as having been created for varying reasons. Some ‘bot accounts are merely created to communicate information from sensors, such as those that link to sensors that measure air quality in mega cities…or earthquake reports in certain regions…or warnings of incoming missiles. Some socialbots are professional “followers” who meld adoringly with an individual’s social network and interact by passing along laudatory messages and being companionable to people engaged in that social network. Those socialbots used for political aims have been dubbed “political” and “propaganda” bots.

In information operations, fraudulent accounts are used to manipulate target audiences’ senses of reality—to motivate actions that benefit the manipulating entities. For example, a foreign power may be interested in having particular policy stances for another nation, so they may work towards putting sympathetic politicians into positions of influence, or they may create a false sense of popularity or unpopularity for policy positions, in order to achieve their own aims. One truism in the deception literature is that the deceived—at some level—choose to be deceived.

An American Cultural Preference for the Fake?

People turn to social media to meet a variety of human needs. Depending on what social media platforms are used and to what purposes, people may experience very different senses of others and of themselves, with differing levels of veridicality. Many people go online for a sense of fantasy—the artificiality of digital avatars in immersive virtual worlds, the amorous attentions of dating ‘bots, the thrill of gaming interactions, and even the hyper-sociality of social media platforms. In online spaces—in immersive virtual worlds, in online persistent world gaming—nonplayer characters (NPCs) play important roles to enhance the sociality of the respective spaces and the gameplay.

Automated robots may do the same on social media platforms. This enhancement of online services may partially explain why corporate owners of such systems have been slow about red-flagging socialbots and disabling their accounts until the U.S. government put pressure on them. Another interpretation for this corporate behavior enabling bot proliferation is that the business model has to avoid building barriers for people to use the platforms. To this end, there are low barriers to entry, with few verifications of humanness; simple interfaces; simple language; supportive help documentation; and hands-off management.

When people made multiple accounts and sought other methods of advantage, many times, they were left alone. The End User License Agreements (EULAs) describe how the platforms should be used for the social good, but users are generally known not to read these closely (if at all), and the enforcement of EULAs have varied between social media platforms. Social norms exist for how social media platforms should be used, and there may be some sousveillance and user enforcement, but these are limited. Even though there is widespread concern about how ‘bots may be harnessed for political manipulations, the purging of “spammy accounts” by Twitter in light of the 2016 election manipulations resulted in user outcry by some users and political groups (Scola, 2018).

Umberto Eco suggests that the American post-modern sensibility is especially primed for what he called the “hyper-real,” the imaginary, the artificial, the pretend, to create a sense of the real (informed by mass media).

This is the reason for this journey into hyperreality, in search of instances where the American imagination demands the real thing and, to attain it, must fabricate the absolute fake' where the boundaries between game and illusion are blurred, the art museum is contaminated by the freak show, and falsehood is enjoyed in a situation of “fullness,” of horror vacui. (Eco, 1973, 1976, 1983, p. 8)

Americana is about the play of the human imagination but engaging in the world through facile setups that mimic reality. While Eco was writing in a time prior to the Internet and Web, this same preference for the over-heated imagination may explain some of the tendencies on social media platforms, with automation harnessed to evoke particular experiential realities. Other words have come to the fore about similar and analogical proclivities. Stephen Colbert introduced the idea of “truthiness” or “the quality of stating concepts one wishes or believes to be true, rather than the facts” (Colbert, 2005, as cited in “truthiness,” 2006). There is the concept of “filter bubbles” based on technologies that incrementally allow people to select data sources and data types and which affect that person’s sense of the world in a limiting way.

The consumer preference for a sense of their own social impact may explain the protectionism around socialbots for many years. Some 48 million Twitter or 15% of accounts may be robots (Newberg, 2017). Additionally, approximately 5-6% of Facebook accounts are considered bogus (40 – 50 million)…or as high as 27% (200 million) (Tynan, 2012, p. 1). One researcher describes the two types of “Facebook fakes”:

One is a ‘bot account that is created and operated remotely via software. The other is a sock puppet – a false account that is operated by a human being pretending to be someone or something they’re not. (Full disclosure: I operate a couple of sock puppet accounts, mostly for testing purposes.) (Tynan, 2012, p. 1)

‘Bots are automated and back-stopped by human creators, and sock puppets are faked accounts back-stopped by human actors who play a role. Tynan suggests there is a “subtle difference” between bots and sock puppets (Tynan, 2012, p. 1).

“Political” and “Propaganda” ‘Bots

While there is no “hierarchy” of ‘bots, except maybe by technical sophistication, “political’ and “propaganda”, ‘bots are harnessed for people’s political aims. Amplification ‘bots (hordes of digital “yes” automated agents that distribute messages broadly to support a certain line of thought) are developed to raise the decibel of particular political messaging (Confessore, Dance, Harris, & Hansen, 2018). In social network theory, the agents or entities (expressed graphically as nodes or vertices) that are most powerful for information dissemination are those with high followership, high in-degree and high out-degree, and those with high centrality in a network (and thus high social influence). Automated agents take part in foreign influence operations on Facebook to advance the agenda of a foreign government (Thompson & Vogelstein, 2018). Some “watcher” bots monitor accounts and retweet when something changes.

Such actions are not simple pranking, but these actions of creating fake accounts in order to sway elections through propaganda are not legal. These acts of usurping real people’s identities and falsely attributing information to them may be defamatory. They may involve “wire fraud” (Akerman, Feb. 12, 2018). The scope of the information operation is only now partially known, and it may be years before the full extent of this effort is finally revealed in the public domain.

In terms of the government investigations, the findings have been revealed piecemeal. For example, when the use of socialbots were first suspected, the numbers have been changing. Initially, 200 “Russia-linked bots” were found and identified on Twitter (Schultz, 2017). Over time, those numbers have arisen, resulting in some 65 pages of bot names (with all of them suspended by the social media platform service provider). Current analyses suggest that 150 million Americans were reached on Twitter with the Russian messaging (Russell, 2018).

On the Facebook social networking platform, “470 inauthentic accounts were likely operated out of Russia” (Schultz, 2017, p. 1). These accounts engaged issues like the Black Lives Matter (BLM) campaigns and anti-Clinton campaigns during the 2016 lead-up to the election, among others (Schultz, 2017, p. 2). One faux account on Twitter--@crystal1johnson--has been linked to the BLM movement. Later, Facebook identified 3,000 ads from Russian sources on their platform (Wagner, 2017). One ad reads: “Hillary Clinton has a 69 percent disapproval rate among all veterans” (in all caps) (Wagner, 2017, p. 2). Many of the ads by Russians piggy-backed on themes of “patriotism” and “supporting veterans” (Wagner, 2017, p. 3).

Faux events, such as a “Miners for Trump” event in Pennsylvania, were created by a fake group called Heart of Texas. The ad read: “’\[Donald Trump\] said he would put miners back to work,’ the ad reads. Trump ended up winning Pennsylvania’s 20 electoral votes by less than 45,000 votes” (Wagner, 2017, p. 4). Another tranche of messages advised readers to “submit their vote for president via Twitter” in a message that usurps TV actor and comedian Aziz Ansari’s picture (Wagner, 2017, p. 6), and this misdirection could have led some to misunderstand how to vote legally and validly. Other messages encouraged people to vote via texting for yet other potentially wasted votes (Wagner, 2017, p. 7). Facebook released a tool to enable its users to see which of them were duped by Russian trolls (Webster, 2017).

The created bots were linked across multiple social media platforms. Twenty-two (22) of the Facebook accounts had parallel accounts on Twitter, and 179 Twitter accounts had links to “false Facebook Russian accounts” (Schultz, 2017, p. 2). Researchers identified particular warning signs of account fakeness on “inanimate Facebook accounts” as compared to “real virtual people” (Tynan, 2012, p. 1). Warning signs include the following: old layouts, the so-called “babe factor,” “few photo uploads,” “oddball biographies,” “zero saved messages” (these accounts tend to be unresponsive to messages or overtures on Facebook), “a mostly blank Wall,” and “a whole lotta Likes” (Tynan, 2012, pp. 1 - 3).

If there are three or more of the indicators, the account is seen to be artificial. The pile-up of likes is explained through the uses of automation. Most ‘bots are coded just below the technological limits of liking before warnings are triggered by the social media platform provider. The automation, though, if left unchecked, results in enormous (unhuman) numbers over time because humans “like” somewhat preferentially and somewhat idiosyncratically.

This particular ‘bot is part of a network that’s been set to like no more than 20 pages a day, to avoid tripping Facebook’s bot filters. Over time, though, the likes can total in the thousands, often completely schizoid and spanning several continents. In one day, for example, Alice liked a Beverly Hills chiropractor, an Egyptian actor/director, a martial arts school in mainland China, the movie “Tattoo Nation,” and 16 other pages. She’s nothing if not eclectic. (Tynan, 2012, p. 3)

Finessed management of such accounts and skilled coding of such ‘bots may result in more realistic-seeming socialbots. One interpretation for why such faked accounts were not addressed systematically and with more rigor sooner may be explained by a business model that benefits from the sense of high and energetic sociality with strong followership, message virality, and influence—all of which require the sense of others’ social presences. There are patterns also in bots on microblogging sites linked to the Russian interference. One author writes:

*   • Many are spammy-looking Western names, such as @\_TraceyJohnson\_ or @CarolineReeeed or @justin\_mc\_call, or Russian-seeming names, including @BogdanKravcov and @VladEvlanin.
*   • Others are designed to look like local U.S. news agencies, including @DailyNewsDenver and @DallasTopNews. Nineteen include “news” in their handle.
*   • Nine have “Russia” in their name, including @RussiaIsBeauty.
*   • Some 27 contain “novosti,” the Russian word for “news.”
*   • Others seem designed to play up racial tensions, or are tied to hashtags for police shootings (@Justice4Jamar\_).
*   • Seven contain “Trump,” including @March\_for\_Trump. Zero contain “Clinton.” Five include “GOP.” One is @NewYorkDem. (Frommer, 2017)

Another source observes that many of the bot names include “not only handles that could pass for activist groups such as @NotMyHeritage, @LgbtRally and @BlacktivistsUS, but ones with specific partisan references to U.S. politics” (Sharkov, 2017) Furthermore, there is a name preference observed:

Seven contain President Donald Trump’s last name such as @March\_for\_Trump, while five mention the “GOP,” such as @10\_gop, @TEN\_GOP, @realTEN\_GOP and @ELEVEN\_GOP. Hillary Clinton’s surname features in none of the handles, while her first name features only in two: @hillaryssTr and @PeeOnHillary. The DNC is not mentioned but one accounts, @NewYorkDem, possibly refers to the Democratic Party (Sharkov, 2017).

A glance at a 65-page published list of identified Russian-linked bots shows a use of the full span of the alphabet, including names like ViolaPus, Trevitova, 1D\_Nicole\_, Ben\_Sar\_Gent, KirdaLove, marrissatrr, Ragland\_land, and zubovnik (Frommer, 2017). Some of these “bot” and “sock puppet” (fraudulent accounts with a different person represented running the account) accounts established by the Russians garnered a large number of followers (those who declared their interest in the contents created and shared by those accounts).

For example, @TEN\_GOP on Twitter, which asserted it was the Tennessee Republican Party’s official Twitter account, garnered over 100,000 followers, according to a U.S. formal indictment. A new account listed 140,000 followers (Warzel, 2017). \[One news account claimed @TEN\_GOP had 130 million followers and that its backup account @10\_GOP had 40 million followers (Popken, 2017), but it is difficult to verify which numbers are accurate now with the user accounts taken down.\]

To date in the public space, researchers have taken several different approaches to identify the Russian ‘bots. Some have noticed “poor grammar, spelling, and general weirdness” (Zielinski, 2017). One journalist asserts the sparsity of information on Twitter accounts make Twitter ‘bots “actually easier to identify than Facebook bots” because there is “less information to verify” (Tynan, 2012, p. 1). Others have found indicators of botness by usurped imagery, such as imagery belonging to others’ social media accounts or those from stock imagery stores.

Stock imagery may be fairly commonly used in marketing endeavors that are used to create “social consensus” around particular issues (DiResta, Little, Morgan, Neudert, & Nimmo, 2017) or consumer behaviors. Another suggests that microblogging accounts that are automated may be easier to identify based on their relationships than on their own individual merits (Confessore, Dance, Harris, & Hansen, 2018). Another tell or indicator of botness may be the ratio of following to followers:

The ratio of Following to Followers is about 10 to 1, which is pretty high. High ratios are true of massively popular Twitter accounts like @charliesheen or @ladygaga. But with accounts like this one, it’s a sure sign that the bot owner is following people at random in the hopes they will follow back. (When the number of people followed exceeds 2000, Twitter starts monitoring this ratio to suss out bots, so spammers respond by creating lots of little bots that fall under that threshold – another reason why many appear to be new accounts.) (Tynan, 2012, p. 3)

Many mainline human social media accounts tend to have fewer following to followers as a matter of personal ego (which ‘bots lack). Unusual ratios and anomalies may be an indicator of an automated agent. Another potential tell is if the image used in the social media account does not belong to the stated individual…or is a stock image…or is taken from another social media account. In one case, a profile image was “colorshifted and recompressed, possibly to evade automated detection” (McKew, 2017). The assembly line nature of ‘bot coding sometimes show in the unanticipated behaviors:

The tweets lack actual content. There are two kids of bots: The ones that tweet out spammy links, usually obscured by some link-shortening service; and the ones that tweet out things that could be mistaken for real tweets but are simply brain-dead aphorisms like “It’s the hardest thing to let someone go when you have no other choice but to let go.” This bot exists for one reason only: To get horny guys to click on the photo and visit that porn site. (Tynan, 2012, p. 3)

Another approach has been to create a play-by-play of a #hashtag evolution and the various social media accounts that were involved, including both human and ‘bot participation. Reporter Molly K. McKew tracked how both Twitter bots and Trump fans “made #releasethememo” go viral for Politico Magazine. In her work, she described how @KARYN19138585, “an account that has the 8-digit fingerprint with some Russian bot accounts” gets in on promoting the #releasethememo effort (McKew, 2018, p. 4). McKew writes:

The KARYN account is an interesting example of how bots lay a groundwork of information architecture within social media. It was registered in 2012, tweeting only a handful of times between July 2012 and November 2013 (mostly against President Barack Obama and in favor of the GOP). Then the account goes dormant until June 2016—the period that was identified by former FBI Director James Comey as the beginning of the most intense phase of Russian operations to interfere in the U.S. elections. The frequency of tweets builds from a few a week to a few a day. By October 11, there are dozens of posts a day, including YouTube videos, tweets to political officials and influencers and media personalities, and lots of replies to posts by the Trump team and related journalists. The content is almost entirely political, occasionally mentioning Florida, another battleground state, and sometimes posting what appear to be personal photos (which, if checked, come from many different phones and sources and appear “borrowed”). In October 2016, KARYN is tweeting a lot about Muslims/radical Islam attacking democracy and America; how Bill Clinton had lots of affairs; alleged financial wrongdoing on Clinton’s part; and, of course, WikiLeaks. (McKew, 2018, pp. 4 - 5)

The topics of focus are those “promoted by Russian disinformation campaigns,” McKew asserts. She suggests the entire early network of the #hashtag promotion has some sketchy features:

Use any basic analytical software to scroll through the early promoters of #releasethememo, and you’ll see most of the accounts meet basic criteria for bot/troll/cyborg suspicion—what the Atlantic Council’s open-source intelligence research group DFRLab describes as “activity, amplification, and anonymity.” There is also a consistent theme in the list of identities—the repetition of certain words (deplorable, Texas, mom, veteran) and certain first names; use of an American flag emoji at the end of the name; specific numbers or patterns of numerical sequences associated with bots; names changed to hashtags, or frequently shifted between trending right-media topics (Benghazi, NFL boycott, the memo, the emails); photos that aren’t faces, or not unobscured faces, or certainly not of them if they are. (McKew, 2018, p. 7)

Virality, based on empirical research, requires that it quickly expand beyond local networks and jump across bridging nodes and links to other social networks. That fast-share momentum is necessary to help the message break out from the gravitational pull of the original online community. If a botherder (or bot master) is interested in pushing information out quickly, he or she or they may well use known socialbot resources to do so.

Another strategy: the Russian ‘bots also focus on key influencers such as “media personalities, far-right brand names, and elected officials” (McKew, 2018, p. 7), to magnify the impact and potentially to legitimate the messaging. Some verified accounts are seen to take part as well (McKew, 2018, p. 8).

MAPPING “MALICIOUS” POLITICAL SOCIALBOT ACCOUNTS, NETWORKS, GEOGRAPHIES, AND STRATEGIC MESSAGING ON MULTIPLE SOCIAL MEDIA PLATFORMS

To study malicious political socialbots, a few social media accounts from three social media platforms types were explored: microblogging (Twitter), social networking (Facebook), and crowd-sourced encyclopedia (Wikipedia). Specifically, their ego neighborhoods (at 1, 1.5, and 2 degrees) and friend linkages; geographical locations (of the profile and the network); strategic messaging (content, sentiment, and language structures), and levels of maliciousness, were explored. The research methods involve social network analysis, geographical data analysis; autocoded topic-modeling, autocoded sentiment analysis, and other computation-based analyses, using NVivo 11 Plus, NodeXL (Network Overview, Discovery and Exploration for Excel), and LIWC2015 (Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count).

First, it may help to begin with a general public and macro sense of “bot.” Google Correlate enables the study of correlated search terms related to “bot” over extended time (2004 – 2017) in terms of web searches through Google Search. With “bot” as the seeding term, the top 20 correlated terms include some references to a tagline for security software, and words like “spyware,” “destroy,” and “spybots.” (Figure 3).

#Hashtag Networks Around an Incident in Politics

A #hashtag network is comprised of the social media accounts of those who use a shared #hashtag to label particular microblogging messages. The relationship or “tie” is based on the sense of a shared conversation. Additional ties may come from replying as well as retweeting. Another way to start exploring this political issue is to extract two “feuding” #hashtag networks. The #releasethememo and the #demsmemo involves partisan tensions that erupted in the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence examining Russian interference in the 2016 presidential elections.

Using NodeXL (Network Overview, Discovery and Exploration for Excel), both hashtag networks were extracted. For the #releasethememo topic, though, the extraction was several days into this media issue, and for the #demsmemo, it was near the beginning. Broadly speaking, the first hashtag is considered in the interests of Republican members of this committee, and the second follow-on hashtag considered in the interests of Democratic members of this committee. The timing matters because if a topic has been around for a while, it is likely that the network that is extractable may be bigger given the functions of the Twitter API and the data capture in NodeXL. (There is no capture of the full set of the data from either hashtag network because of the limits to the available data extraction.

A full set of N is possible but would require going with a commercial vendor that provides access to this information, which is likely in the realm of remote-hosted big data.) The graph metrics of the #releasethememo (Table 1) and its available group clusters and group membership (Figure 5) and those for #demsmemo (Table 2) and its related groups (Figure 6) do not look all that different. \[The Clauset-Newman-Moore clustering algorithm was used for both group graphs.\] The average geodesic distances are 3.335 and 2.915, which suggests close potential relations between nodes, with only three hops between any two nodes in a network.

The #releasethememo resulted in fewer nodes (373) than for the #demsmemo (512) hashtag network, but that may be because of the timing of the data extractions and the fact that the first memo kerfuffle primed interest in the second. The maximum geodesic distance (graph diameter) for the #releasethememo hashtag was 8, and for #demsmemo was 5—which suggests a more interconnected and denser network graph for the latter #hashtag network.

Note the grouping patterns in both group graphs show a large set of disconnected individuals who used the #releasethememo or #demsmemo hashtags, and there were smaller groups who actually interacted with each other around the hashtagged messaging. While there were six extracted clusters in #releasethememo, there were seven for #demsmemo. These social media graphs do show the ability of common users to access public data from social network platforms and to create data visualizations specific to individuals. This software enables the extraction of the actual Tweets, profile data, the time patterns in the networks, and others.

In theory and possibly in practice, capturing #hashtag networks and observing their virality…and their sequence of activities…and their messaging, it would be possible to possibly identify and infer some hidden hand advocating for macro-level interest and potential behaviors by the readers.

Dedicated Technologies for ‘Bot Hunting

Then, there are various online tools that purport to help identify and “out” ‘bots. One that identifies ‘bots on Twitter use machine learning (pattern identification) to study the behaviors of various accounts (Hughes, 2017). These are dedicated sites programmed for the particular purpose. For example, Robhat Labs creates Botcheck.me (https://botcheck.me) with a web-facing side and elicitations for funding with Bitcoins. Botometer (https://botometer.iuni.iu.edu/#!/), formerly BotOrNot) is created by the Indiana University Network Science Institute (IUNI) and the Center for Complex Networks and Systems Research (CNetS). Botometer looks “at over 1,000 factors, ranging from the tweets themselves (including metadata on how and where they were posted) to the composition of followers” (Brandom, 2017, p. 1).

Generally, a score of under 40 is a finding for a “human,” and over 40 is a finding for a “robot.” In the FAQs, the creators of Botometer write:

Bot detection is a hard task. Many criteria are used in determining whether an account is controlled by a human or a bot, and even a trained eye gets it wrong sometimes. If this task were easy to do with software, there wouldn't be any bots — Twitter would have already caught and banned them!

Another point to keep in mind is that humans and machines have different strengths when it comes to pattern recognition. Some “obviously” bot/human accounts according to a human observer will fool a machine learning algorithm. Likewise an algorithm may confidently classify some accounts that humans have a hard time with. The best approach is to use this tool to complement, not to replace, your own judgement. (Botometer FAQ, n.d.)

Botometer has a presence on Twitter as @botometer, based out of Bloomington, Indiana, USA. This account was established in April, 2014. Its profile reads: “Online tool to classify Twitter accounts as human or bot. Formerly known as BotOrNot, part of the OSoMe project at Indiana University” (@botometer landing page). Its sociogram (Figure 7), its sub-group discussants (Figure 8), its geographical locations (Figure 9), and its strategic messaging contents (Figure 10) are observable. @botometer has a score of 42% on its own platform (Botometer), and it does not come across as a propaganda bot on Botcheck.me. This suggests that the account is run by people with automated supports.

In social network analysis, the concept of “homophily” suggests people socialize with others who are like themselves, and based on “the company you keep,” you can be somewhat more knowable. This assertion of homophily may / may not apply to socialbots, which seem to prefer connecting with real people more than with other bots. (It is unclear if socialbots can identify or discern other socialbots. In general, this is not an easy task. However, socialbots may be deployed together en masse around a particular topic and so may interconnect. On some platforms, bots do seem to interconnect and interrelate—but these are not on microblogging or social networking sites per se.)

Online social network communities tend to evolve in patterned ways over time. People coalesce into large network graphs based around temporal shared interests; in the online communities, those who are part of center mass tend to connect and participate longer. Those who are of the periphery, in smaller groups, in motifs, and isolates, tend to disappear over time (Morgan, Neal, & Carder, 1997). The online community may evolve and stay relevant to its members, or it may dissipate when the shared interests no longer exist and member needs are no longer met. #hashtag communities are transient groupings of people with particular shared interests around issues, which spark, bring people together, and then dissipate.

Online spaces have very challenging attention economies, and there are always issues arising that attract people’s attention. After the initial burst of attention, over time, people forget en masse, and they move on to other issues. It seems that people’s attention on social media is “concentrated among very weak or very strong ties,” based on their needs for novelty (weak ties) and their needs to maintain close social ties with those with whom they are familiar (strong ties) (Weng, 2014, p. 73). These prior findings suggest that if an unfamiliar ‘bot shares novel information, it may still attract human attention.

Some ‘bot identifier tools result in a binary decision, either “‘bot” or “not ‘bot.” Others use a gauge scale indicating a level of likelihood of its being a ‘bot. In a mid-range, it may indicate that the account is a cyborg account, with some features of a human touch and some features of a robot. There is not absolute certitude of a social media user’s account being one or the other, usually, without some further research and validation.

Based on an article in which the author analyzed how a #releasethememo hashtag network first started, some user accounts were identified and used to test for their apparent botness. For example, the @karyn19138585 account (https://twitter.com/karyn19138585) was said to have the markers for being a bot (McKew, 2018, p. 4), but the account itself is still live, which suggests the management at Twitter do not concur. At the moment of this exploration, the account had 34,386 Tweets, 4,460 following, 3,082 followers, and 40,447 likes. The public profile for this account reads: “Deplorable island girl. Thank God for President Trump. Live in SW FL. Wife, mother and Beach Grammy! Love my country! #MAGA #RedWaveRising#ReleaseTheMemo” and is said to be based in Florida. The year of joining is 2012.

On botcheck.me, the software suggests that @KARYN19138585 is a ‘bot, with the following output: “Our model has classified @KARYN19138585 to exhibit patterns conducitve to a political bot or highly moderated account tweeting political propaganda” (Robhat Labs, 2017). (Figure 11)

Botometer enables a more complex search and exploration by enabling a light sampling of some of the followers and friends of the target account. Next to the form field with the account handle (@...) on Twitter, there are buttons for “Check user,” “Check followers,” and “Check friends.” These additional follow-on buttons enable exploration about more information about the particular social networks.

On Botometer, the interpretation is that the account is at 55% likely to be a robot, and a check of its followers suggest some humans and some potential bots, and its friends are likewise a mix of humans and potential bots (Figure 12). As a stand-alone account, it is difficult to make assertions of @KARYN19138585’s identity based on these readings, and there is not an established baseline against which to make assertions about this Twitter account.

In addition, the social media accounts captured here in Botometer are only a small number of those extant in the actual network (as compared to the numbers mentioned on the Twitter page.) Also, an account holder can choose to unfollow / unfriend others, but they do not particularly control followers (unless they control these follower accounts or are in some sort of network working together. For a more thorough investigation, it may be helpful to visit the respective landing pages of the identified individuals in the network.

EXPLORING SOCIAL MEDIA USER TYPES ON A MICROBLOGGING SITE, SOCIAL NETWORKING SITE, AND CROWD-SOURCED ENCYCLOPEDIA SITE

In review, this chapter describes exploring various publicly available elements of social media user accounts (ego neighborhoods and networks, geographical locations, and strategic messaging) to identify the core nature of the account (whether human-embodied, cyborg, or ‘bot)…and to identify whether the account is “malicious.” This exploration is being carried out in a political context, particularly the uses of Russian-created ‘bots on multiple social media platforms (Twitter and Facebook, among others). The analyses include relational structural ones, geographical patterning, topic modeling, sentiment analysis, and light content analysis, in combination.

Research Methodology

The general sequence of research is as follows: This work started with the conceptualization of the research. Then, a review of the literature was conducted, including mass media reportage of the issue and some social media postings as well. Various accounts from Twitter, Facebook, and Wikipedia were identified for this research—with known human accounts, known bot accounts, and some in-between accounts. Partial and total data from the various accounts were scraped from the respective platforms using a variety of software tools. The sizes of the datasets involved sets with over 100,000 rows of data.

The data was computationally analyzed for network analysis, geographical analysis, and strategic messaging (content, sentiment, linguistic features, and others). After these analyses, relevant data visualizations were created as a part of the analysis and as a part of reporting out the findings. Then, the collected data was fully analyzed to answer the four hypotheses, and to explore the following four points:

*   1\. The ability to identify malicious political socialbot accounts based on their ego neighborhoods at 1, 1.5, and 2 degrees;
*   2\. The ability to identify malicious political socialbot accounts based on the claimed and linked geographical locations of their accounts, their ego neighborhoods, and their #hashtag networks
*   3\. The ability to identify malicious political socialbot accounts based on their strategic messaging (content, sentiment, and language structures) on respective social media platforms
*   4\. The ability to identify and describe “maliciousness” in malicious political socialbot accounts based on observable behaviors on that account

This work theorizes some ways to validate / invalidate the sense of human-embodiment of a social media account vs. a bot-embodiment. Some initial tests involve using others’ models as instantiated in Botometer and Botcheck.me but also in methods described in mass media accounts. There were and are limits to data access for an issue that is politically controversial. And even if the topic itself were not so difficult, there are limits to the access of social data off of social media platforms even using various extractive software tools. The work here is based off of an initial analysis in a journalistic article that tentatively identified ‘bots vs. human accounts. This work does not make absolute and definitive representations of the respective accounts.

ON THE TWITTER MICROBLOGGING SITE

One of the most popular platforms harnessed for the Russian operation was apparently the Twitter microblogging site. The Russian-controlled accounts retweeted Candidate Donald J. Trump “more than two million times between September 1 and November 15, 2016, with nearly 500,000 of those coming in the campaign’s final stretch” (Silverstein, 2018). To explore the informativeness of the publicly available data, several accounts were identified from the McKew article. The analyses follow.

A Bot-Like Human-Embodied Politically-Motivated Social Media Account

In her analysis, McKew identified a human-embodied social media account that has ‘bot-like features. Queen Covfefe has the @clasimpmv as her handle. She has 48,600 Tweets, 5,884 following, 6,681 followers, 29,648 likes, and two lists. Her banner has “MAGA” (abbreviated form of “Make America Great Again”) running across. The image encapsulates a high-angle tilted-up image of Candidate Trump stage-side, with his head in lights. (There are many versions of this image online, so this may have been made available for supporters to use in their public messaging.) McKew describes the account behaviors:

In the 24 months since the account was established, Queen has tweeted 47,000 times—about 65 times per day, so about the same rate as the active ‘bot. She has tweeted #releasethememo hundreds of times in a few days. She often retweets lists of other twitter handles (sometimes hundreds of names per list)—“people” that you are supposed to follow and retweet to build your own following and influence. They are often labeled with “Follow/retweet/comment for a follow back!” Two such lists, for example, were retweeted by Queen on January 19 and February 2. Each list includes at least a few ‘bot. Some bots are amplifiers—in the simplest form, they automatically follow accounts that follow them, and retweet tweets from those accounts (sometimes, other parameters such as keywords are factored in). It is an element of automation. The rest is about network, echo chamber, fake influence and amplification. (McKew, 2018, p. 6)

Using the dedicated online bot-detectors, one could not extract sufficient Tweets to identify botness, and another identified the account as human (Figures 13 and 14).

A Controversial Human Persona in the Space

Another human account in this topical space is @RVAwonk, lauded by some as an astute analyst and called out by others as a liberal. In the same way that some newly salient issues can be a starmaker, the issue of Russian meddling in the presidential elections has made this account an important one. @RVAwonk came in at 29% on the Botometer (so: human) and also “PropagandaBot like Patterns Not Found” / human on Botcheck.me.

At the time of the data extractions, the @RVAwonk (https://twitter.com/rvawonk) account had 63,377 Tweets, 3,650 following, 277,414 followers, 64,941 likes, and 13 lists. This account was explored to capture a sense of how summary descriptive data might look like from a human-embodied social media account. At this particular slice-in-time, the @RVAwonk account’s network had a wide variety of both human and bot members in its directed graph (with outgoing links depicted only) and a fairly global reach but with geographical areas of focus (Figure 15).

Another Human?/Bot? Political Account on Twitter

Another social media account linked to the political endeavors highlighted in the #releasethememo effort is @Well\_in\_USA (https://twitter.com/Well\_in\_USA), which is described as “the second account to tweet #releasethememo…an account opened in July 2014, now largely deleted” (McKew, 2018). The geographical location of the account in the profile is “The Land of the Free.” Its profile blurb reads: “’You can fool some of the people all of the time, and all of the people some of the time, but you can not fool all of the people all of the time.’ Abe Lincoln.”

At the time of the data extraction, there were 2,000 Tweets, 442 following, 2 followers, and 1,922 likes; however, interestingly, several weeks later, the account had 1,980 Tweets, 452 following, 3 followers, and 1,896 likes. In other words there was some editing down of the available Tweets, ten additional following, one new follower, and some deleted likes. This “M2” account started in July 2014. The landing page of the account has a flag as its banner and as its account image. The site seems branded for alignment with its messaging goals and issues of interest. The title of McKew’s article lists “Twitter bots” and “Trump fans,” and it seems that this account falls to the latter group.

On Botometer, this account registers at 47%, or 7% higher than a score that might indicate “human” and suggestive of its possibly being a ‘bot. On Botcheck.me, the evaluation reads that this account “does not exhibit patterns conducive to a political bot or highly automated patterns tweeting political propaganda” (on Botcheck.me). The fact that this account still exists on Twitter after the revelation of Russian-related ‘bots might suggest that this is an individual or at least a cyborg.

Using NodeXL, the @well\_in\_usa account was mapped initially to one-degree, for the ego neighborhood of the account (the “alters” that are in announced in direct relationship to the target network). The graph metrics table shows 516 nodes in the network, with 468 unique links (Table 3). As is typical of an ego neighborhood, the geodesic distance (network graph) is only two degrees (any two nodes are two hops away from each other).
