A “Troll Farm” or Just an Enthusiastic Politico?

In the political space, activist accounts are often targets for trolling and name-calling. @MissAmericaPie (https://twitter.com/missamericapie?lang=en) is another account mentioned in the political space and suspected as a ‘bot by at least one news source. Its landing page shows a map of the U.S. divided into red states and blue states. The image of the person on the account seems to be one-of-a-kind at least in an initial perusal. Figure 25 shows an image taken from a suspected political bot account run on the Tin Eye Reverse Image Search. The results show that there were no other copies of that particular person’s image out of 25.9 billion images. Of course, there can be some lag time between when an image is put up, and it is found and archived, for comparisons. Sometimes reverse image searches show marketing endeavors as well and not ‘bots but more sock puppets backstopped by a marketing team.

| Figure 25. Using a reverse image search to check out origins of images |

At the time of the data extraction, this account was located “DeepIntheHeartO’TEXAS.” The account was set up on Twitter on April 2009. At the time of this data capture, the account had 101,993 Tweets, 18,105 following, 16,484 followers, 3,269 likes, and 36 lists. Its profile is: “Acts And they said, ‘Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved, and thy house.’ KJV” (King James Version). The website has a law and order message, with media images of the FBI, President Trump with Christopher Wray, a close-up of a fetus in utero, opinions on DACA, and others. The political messaging appeals to ideas of shared identity and shared values. In this space, the account seems to be a thought leader. @missamericapie registers 43% on the Botometer (just over the threshold into being an automated agent); however, this account is seen as a ‘bot on Botcheck.me (Figure 26).

Data From a Sensor Network on Twitter

Another type of automated account may be a “sensor”. A “sensor” network on a social media platform is a kind of automated network but not a “social” being. @beijingair microblogs air quality warnings in Chaoyang District, Beijing, People’s Republic of China, and is a tool of the U.S. Embassy. The profile description explains that this tool involves “MetOne BAM 1020 and Ecotech EC9810 monitors, reporting PM2.5 and ozone readings. Format for each: pollutant type; concentration; AQI; definition.”

The account was joined in July 2008, approximately two years after Twitter started. The @beijingair account ranks 45% on Botometer (picking up on that it seems automated), but it does not trigger any recognition as a propaganda ‘bot: “Our model finds that @BeijingAir does not exhibit patterns conducive to a political bot or highly automated patterns tweeting political propaganda” (Botcheck.me). The account actually does serve a political messaging channel from one nation-state to another. The account had 84,157 Tweets, 4 following, and 112,960 followers. The landing page of this account depicts the machine in the profile window. A social mapping of the @beijingair network shows that it is not particularly social and looks to be a bit of an isolate node (Figure 35).

Social Media User Account Identity Ambiguity

Many of the accounts explored above were culled through reading an analysis of the early steps in the unfolding of the participating #releasethememo hashtag network as defined by McKew and the New Media Frontier. This author does not want to paint any social media account by association (following a bot, being followed by a bot, retweeting a bot, replying to a bot)…or by shared issue interests (#hashtag networks, keyword searches), and so forth. Without additional information, it is very difficult to ascertain the origins of an account. Some of the suspected ‘bot accounts are still active and live, a month after their “suspicious” interactions around #releasethememo, which might suggest that Twitter may not have sufficient information to shut these accounts down. Many other identified accounts have been shut down because of their apparent “botness.”

ON THE FACEBOOK SOCIAL NETWORKING SITE

Facebook, the world’s foremost social networking site, shared that 150 million people were “reached by Russian-backed troll accounts” (Coldewey, 2017), and 675,000 Americans interacting with Russian trolls on Twitter (Burch, 2018). While the Russian-controlled accounts have since been taken down, Facebook makes available an app that allows those with Facebook accounts to know whether or not they interacted with the faux accounts. Indeed, faked Facebook events elicited “more than 60,000 Americans RSVP’d” (Silverstein, 2018). Not only did Americans RSVP, but many actually showed up to the real-space events:

Facebook, meanwhile, told the Senate Intelligence Committee last week that Russian trolls posing as American activists created 129 political events between 2015 and 2017, which were seen by more than 300,000 Facebook users and in some cases drew demonstrators to the streets en masse. About 62,500 users said they would attend one of the events and another 25,800 users expressed interest in going (Silverstein, 2018)

Many of the political ads created by these agents were seen by Americans as well:

On Facebook, social bots—accounts run by automated software that mimic real users or work to communicate particular information streams—can be used to automate group pages and spread political advertisements. Recent public revelations from Facebook reveal that a Russian “troll farm” with close ties to the Kremlin spent around $100,000 on ads ahead of the 2016 US election and produced thousands of organic posts that spread across Facebook and Instagram. The same firm, the Internet Research Agency, has been known to make widespread use of bots in its attempts to manipulate public opinion over social media. (DiResta, Little, Morgan, Neudert, & Nimmo, 2017)

For this work, it helps to get a sense of what a political landing page looks like on Facebook. The first two mapped accounts are of human-embodied political accounts on Facebook. The extractions were done with NVivo 11 Plus, which captures 100 of the most recent posts on the poststreams and related comments to those posts (some numbering in the hundreds of thousands). The data extractions are coded at the cell levels (not the sentence nor paragraph levels), given that the data is extracted in data tables and the fact that the textual communications are not in classic “sentences” or “paragraphs” (but in shorter phrases with different social media grammars).

The first one explored is the @TrumpPoliticalMovement (https://www.facebook.com/TrumpPoliticalMovement) account, with 97,031 messages captured. In Figure 38, the topic extraction to this account shows that some main issues dealt with the American people, different people groups (by race), a concern about jobs, gun ownership, laws, political identity, and some tough language (including name-calling terms).

ON WIKIPEDIA CROWD-SOURCED ENCYCLOPEDIA

As noted, Wikipedia was targeted “by Russian internet propaganda activities” (“Web brigades”, 2018). Contrary to the earlier explorations of malicious robots, the automated agents set up in Wikipedia go through a vetting process before they may be deployed on the crowd-sourced encyclopedia, and they engage in prosocial work such as ensuring proper spelling, ensuring proper grammar, undoing vandalism, resizing imagery, fixing syntax, and others (“Wikipedia:Bots,” 2017). There are bots that monitor edits from government websites (Sorokanich, 2014). On the MediaWiki platform, the robots are flagged and clearly described and linked back to their human makers.

To find a ‘bot for exploration, one can go to an article on Wikipedia, and click on the tab to “View history.” There, any user who has edited the page should be listed. These histories not only show humans but approved and flagged (self-identified) bots. Robot accounts are known as “legitimate alternative account(s)”. In a sense, such authenticated ‘bots with known creators align with Mark Meadows’ ideas of “AI bots and avatars” that are verified to enable human trust and vulnerability (Botsman, 2017, pp. 188 – 189). The User:PrimeBOT account calls itself the “destroyer of dead templates and URLs.” More information follows:

This user account is a bot that uses AutoWikiBrowser, operated by Primefac (talk). It is a legitimate alternative account, used to make repetitive automated or semi-automated edits that would be extremely tedious to do manually. The bot is approved and currently active – the relevant request for approval can be seen here. (“User:PrimeBOT,” Feb. 11, 2018)

The bot’s formal biography contains some links to its bona fides. It is written using AutoWikiBrowser (AWB). It is apparently a semi-bot. This analysis is done to provide a counter-example, a counter-factual, to the earlier political and propaganda ‘bot examples. This is set up to ask the question about how efficacious the approach may be to use social networks, geographical analysis, and content analysis to test botness.

The social network connections of a selected Wikipedia bot, User:PrimeBOT, was run at one-degree, 1.5 degrees, and two degrees (Tables 5, 6, and 7; Figures 50, 51, and 52). These bot-based article-article networks at one-degree (ego neighborhood) on Wikipedia do tend to be smaller, with fewer vertices, than topic article pages (which are often much more interconnected with other topics on Wikipedia).

Computational Text Analysis of Human and Bot Text Sets

Ideally, computational text analysis in this context would have human political Tweetstreams and identified Russian ‘bot political Tweetstreams. The text sets would also include the same for Facebook poststreams. The numbers of words in the respective texts would be relatively comparable. As it stands, the human political Tweetstreams were compared to non-political / apolitical bot accounts on Twitter and Facebook; the first set contained 530,383 words, and the latter set consisted of only 149,605. This comparison is not, colloquially speaking, apples to apples and oranges to oranges. However, what these do offer is a sense of a way forward to analyze whether or not strategic messaging may be the difference in identifying ‘bots and maliciousness. (If ‘bots meld with human populations quickly, their tweetstreams would not be particularly different than whatever people are sharing on their social media accounts).

One aspect of analyzing strategic messaging involves looking at the language used along a number of dimensions regularly analyzed using computational text analysis. The tool used in this situation is Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC). All the analytics were run, but only some of the data was selected for presentation. (The relativism features—language indicating motion / space / time –was not included, and the life issues indicators (work, leisure, home, money, relig, and death) were not seen to have significant results and were not included.

Interestingly, the Tweetstreams of the political human accounts (on Twitter) and the non-political robot (on Twitter and Facebook) seem to share some basic textual characteristics. These ranked high on analytical features in the language, fairly high on clout (power), low on authenticity or warmth, and fairly negative on tone (sentiment), in the Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC) tool (Figure 55). These auto-extracted scores are based on percentile-based assessment of features, which were built in LIWC from the study of big data text sets. This means that these text sets tend towards the relative standings as compared to text-based human communication as captured in big data text sets.

| Figure 55. Computational text-analysis summary statistics comparisons across text sets |

| ![Figure978-1-5225-5927-6.ch012.f55](i/ch012.f55.png) |
| --- |

In terms of the uses of informal language, both text sets use a fair amount of netspeak. The human-embodied accounts also showed some use of “assent.” The full options in the informal language features in LIWC include the following: “swear,” “netspeak,” “assent,” nonflu” (nonfluencies), and “filler” (Figure 65).

The bot accounts had a preference for semi-colons and dashes, which were not seen in the human-embodied social media text sets. Given the difficulty incomparability between the two text sets (topically), these comparisons are tentative only and meant to give readers a sense of additional analytics that may be done assuming cleaner samples are available. The punctuation quirks here may be a factor of the limits of the text sets used to represent the robots.

Finally, it is possible to use distant reading to extract the topics through topic modeling and then to analyze the related sentiment through autocoding…and then to run a matrix query to see what the sentiments are for the respective auto-extracted topics. The rows are derived from the high-level topic of “american” with all the descendent nodes (subtopics), and the columns are the four categories of sentiment: very positive, moderately positive, moderately negative, and very negative. This view provides a sense of what is being discussed and what is the sentiment behind the topic. Discussion

To recap, this work explored four basic hypotheses through a light exploration of a few social media accounts on several platforms known to be touched by Russian propagandists: a microblogging site, a social networking site, and an open-source crowd-contributed encyclopedia. The four hypotheses read:

*   Hypothesis 1: Malicious political socialbot accounts may be somewhat identifiable from human social media accounts by their ego neighborhoods (at 1, 1.5, and 2 degrees) on respective social media platforms.
*   Hypothesis 2: Malicious political socialbot accounts may be somewhat identifiable from human social media accounts by the geographical locations of their accounts (from the claimed location in the profile) and their ego neighborhoods (from claimed locales and messaging locales based on mobile and other apps) on respective social media platforms and from artificial #hashtag networks promoted by bots.
*   Hypothesis 3: Malicious political socialbot accounts may be somewhat identifiable from human social media accounts by their strategic and shared messaging (content, sentiment, and language structures) on respective social media platforms.
*   Hypothesis 4: It is possible to describe the “maliciousness” in malicious political socialbot accounts based on observable behaviors as differentiated from human maliciousness expressed on social media platforms.

EARLY FINDINGS

In terms of the first hypothesis, in general, the political socialbot accounts seem to follow and befriend target political and personality accounts of interest, and they meld with the human environment. They benefit from the transitive trust and affection gleaned from others’ social connections, and this suspension of disbelief by human consumers of information is a vulnerability (or “vuln”). One journalist describes the widespread relating of public figures with the Russian bots and their engagement in passing on Russian propaganda:

What do President Donald Trump, CNN anchor Jake Tapper, The Washington Post, Breitbart and Jack Dorsey, the head of Twitter, all have in common?

They and nearly 40 celebrities and politicians were all roped into retweeting or otherwise engaging with accounts created by a Russian “troll factory” to millions of followers, according to a new exclusive analysis.

Over 3,000 global news outlets also inadvertently published articles containing embedded tweets by the confirmed Kremlin-linked troll accounts in over 11,000 news articles in the run-up to the 2016 election, separate exclusive reporting shows. (Popken, 2017)

Given the thin surfaces for self-portrayal and interactions, and a culture of promiscuous and fairly indiscriminate linking and friending and responding and mentioning, many of the accounts studied seem to not be homophilous ones (of bots socializing with bots), but of bots interacting with humans. For many of the political accounts studied in the mass media, there were large followings of hundreds of thousands of people (and likely some other robot accounts). Because of this on-ground reality, it is not necessarily helpful to see the ego neighborhoods of political socialbots. (There are likely small-group socialbots that may socialize with others like it…and even isolate socialbots that engage on the periphery instead of the broad center. However, it is likely that such socialbots that fail to connect and influence by having high in-degree, high out-degree, and high graph centrality would likely not be considered valuable for influence operations. There are few benefits to being a shy socialbot).

Hypothesis 2 suggests the geographical locations of the accounts and ego neighborhoods might be insightful about a social media account’s botness. The locations of profiles can be easily faked because these are simply declared by whoever has set up the account. In the case of the Russian meddling, the servers and VPNs were established stateside to create the technological illusion of physical local-ness. Those who exchange messages on microblogging sites may block their physical locations from being captured on the platform. And once a ‘bot account has integrated with a larger network, those networks will take on the general locational characteristics of a large group of people. In other words, the ‘bot can slip into a larger population and not differentiate itself; it can emulate the human-embodied social media accounts around them.

Hypothesis 3 suggests the messaging of political socialbot accounts—the message content, the sentiment, and the language structures—may be revelatory. Based on this work, the expressed messaging contents and sentiment seem to emulate that of the crowd, broadly speaking. A closer content analysis of the messages may identify messages that originated from particular accounts and were not re-tweets or shares of others’ messages. The sentiment and tone seem structured around particular desired behavioral roles of the target audiences. The language structures, given the brevity of tweetstreams and post-streams, were not identifiably different based on a close reading. If there is an “uncanny valley” effect for humanoid ‘bots that might trigger revulsion (MacDorman & Ishiguro, 2006), suffice it to say there was insufficient difference to create this effect (for this author). Additionally, the AI in the political ‘bots did not result in these chatbots doing any fails similar to the Facebook ‘bots that started jabbering in their own made-up language (Collins & Prigg, 2017). If there was messaging discomfort, it was at the over-simplification of complex issues and politically inspired nastiness all around.

Hypothesis 4 explored the question of “malice” and whether such socialbot accounts were identifiable through their malicious messaging. This hypothesis was found to be partially true. One level of malice, the obvious and surface level, involves messaging that is mean, accusatory, angry, hostile, and nasty. There is name calling. There are derogatory assertions and comparisons. There may be the purveying of gossip. There may be the sharing of compromising information or imagery or video. This level of malice can be seen in some of the Russian bot communications. A reading of sample cases of malicious political socialbots show ad hominem attacks on politicians, various slanders, inaccurate portrayals of history, reframings of the current present, name-calling, and various forms of political nastiness; however, it was hard to assert that the messaging by the studied ‘bots were different than those between citizens about candidates. If one were to look at a “degree” or “intensity” of expressed malice, the Russian-controlled ‘bot accounts did not differentiate themselves by being more obviously malicious than other political-inspired humans.

Then, there is a less obvious or non-obvious sort of malice. This type of malice may be understood only from the limits of a particular point-of-view or lens. A propaganda bot deployed to help citizens question the legitimacy of their own democratic government may be seen as a “patriotic” bot from the side of the adversary, but to the side whose political system and polity have been attacked, the political bot is highly malicious. This is when the message comes across as neutral and factual, but is in fact deceptive and malicious. Such types of malice may generally only be understood in retrospect, with insider information, over time, and in a historical point-of-view. Some examples of these are when people share information of penny stocks or crypto-currencies in order to pump up their value, at which time the manipulator dumps their holdings with a tidy profit.

The attribution of malice to a ‘bot—whether the malice is obvious or non-obvious—is clearly referring to the controllers of the ‘bot accounts. The political masters, funders, ‘bot developers, and ‘bot controllers decide how automated agents are created and deployed, the behaviors they are given, and their resulting actions… What is relevant is not whether a social media account user is a human, a cyborg, or a ‘bot but rather who controls the account and to what nefarious ends (e.g., misrepresentation, manipulation, harassment, and other endeavors).

When people attempt to affect a particular situation maliciously and to a harmful outcome for others, and they are striving to take advantage of weaknesses in systems and in people, they are bad actors. The social media accounts, whether human-embodied, cyborg, or ‘bot, are just ways to magnify the reach of the individual or group purveying the false information. The magnification can be through low-cost human labor (think micropayments), cyborg accounts, and / or automated agents. It is important not to identify automation as a culprit (Hai-Jew, 2017). Indeed, well-designed scripted or automated agents are used in numerous contexts to the good of people.

If one were interested in designing ‘bots and ‘bot swarms to affect the American publics around particular election and hot political issues, how would one go about it? Based on the explorations so far, it seems that the ‘bots would be profiled as political Americans, with images showing their patriotism—replete with flags and political or Biblical quotes. They would hail from the heart of Texas and other red spaces. There would be a “you’re with us or against us” vibe and that sort of black-and-white binary thinking. The communications would be affirming of others’ ideas (retweets, replies), and there would be new events and new #hashtag networks to create a space for participation.

In an environment of fleeting attention and minimal characters, it is sufficiently easy to script bots that fit the bill. Search for links shared on a network, and re-share. Express support for anything shared by the respective mayors of the hashtags. Like everything that the central figures like, and dislike and dismiss anything they do not like. Use light methods to pretend to be human by activating ‘bots on circadian rhythms and based on particular personality profiles. Avoid going to mechanized speeds, and throttle these back to human speeds. Fake moods. Follow a few other ‘bots, but make the main network humanoids with political interests. Target big-name journalists.

Insufficient “Tells”

If the common human user of social media platforms, using public data, cannot use the available data to identify malicious botness or even malice with certitude, what sort of a collective defense exists? Subjective suspicions alone are not particularly helpful, and making these actionable with further queries and probes are neither scalable nor cost effective (unless it is done electronically or en masse). As this issue is developing, there appears to be four main stakeholders: government, the Fourth Estate (journalists and mass media), corporations (including social media companies and cybersecurity ones, among others), and the general public and netizens (Figure 67). These include public, private, and voluntary/community sectors.

| Figure 67. A collective defense with main stakeholders |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-5225-5927-6.ch012.f67](i/ch012.f67.png) |
| --- |

An Emergent Collective Defense Against Foreign Propaganda

In terms of a defense, government has a responsibility to ensure free and fair elections, which means blunting or stopping the manipulations of non-U.S. citizens from trying to influence elections. The foreign weaponization of social media platforms for socio-political aims serves only the interests of a few. Certainly, for the U.S. government, there is interest in ensuring that there is proper national security and the protection of citizens and of the vote. Whether national security officials can convince a skeptical public of the seriousness of a foreign government’s incursion in the U.S. vote is another factor, given the common pranking, trolling, name-calling, calling-out, remixing, memetic emulations, and common deceptions in online social spaces.

With the current reportage, the Russian playbook seems eerily like a typical social media playbook, with efforts to advance desirable messages. And who is to suggest the Russian interests should align with those of the U.S. (or vice versa)? And if everything is crowd-sourced, why wouldn’t the Russians be part of the crowd doing the sourcing? In writing about Google’s YouTube, staffer Kevin Allocca (2018) makes the point that people are consuming media in wholly non-traditional ways, without the need for narrative and often without the need for local context. Often, video watchers cannot necessarily articulate why they are attracted to a particular viral video. But the allure of the “parasocial” (the sense of media consumers that they are in relationship with media personages) is as potent as ever (Allocca, 2018, p. 291). People choose others to “follow” and emulate memetically. (Those in marketing engage in “cool-hunting” to find the alpha individuals that others see as cool and whom they would follow).

In other words, the media space has changed as well as people, so the way to address such information warfare will have to adapt. An all-of-government approach is critical because it is not just enough to attrite malicious socialbots but to address this “attack on democracy” as its respective nation-state source. According to media reports, U.S. law enforcement saw nascent signs of the Russian information campaign starting in 2014 in what looked to be initially somewhat innocent but evolving into more serious and predatory interventions. Suffice it to say that online space is not ungoverned.

The companies that provide social media services have an interest in being (and being seen as) good citizens in their respective countries and business spaces, and they do not want to see their platforms and customers manipulated. They are well positioned to identify automated agents algorithmically (even though this has been a “hard problem” for these companies for years), and ‘bot types (like political socialbots) algorithmically. As the service providers, they have access to customer account payments, Internet Protocol (IP) addresses, server locations, account histories, event logs, verifying email accounts, and other aspects that alone and in combination may indicate malicious actors (foreign and domestic).

Socialbots may not have obsessive human-typical check-ins and signs of human personality and ego (except for higher-end scripted ‘bots). They may capture the Internet Protocol addresses of multiple users to an account, and to linked accounts, and they can detect nexuses that may indicate coordination. (IP addresses can be easily faked, however.) Electronic spaces have always collected fingerprints—multiple sets—because the assumption of engineers has always been that the uses of any technology system can be for a wide range of intentions (both benevolent and malevolent and all along this spectrum) and should offer controls against misuse. The digital tracks created are permanent, and through analytical means, it is possible to reverse engineer actions and to infer intentions. Reporters have noted that Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg and others have had that “techno-optimism…crushed” (Thompson & Vogelstein, 2018), but their security staff are working to understand the threat and to address it.

One observation: the Russian agents identified those “angry and afraid” and organized them into activist groups (Roger McNamee, as cited in Thompson & Vogelstein, 2018); people’s own heightened passions were used against them and harnessed for the interests of an adversarial foreign nation-state. \[Simultaneous to these disruptions, other teams of Russian hackers were apparently conducting cyberattacks against U.S. power plants and other infrastructure (Perlroth & Sanger, 2018). Such observations punctuate the real-world facts of nation-state strife and competition and the need for the U.S. to effectively protect its many interests stateside and abroad.\]

The automated red-flagging of ‘bots on respective social media platforms likely use a combination of “tells” from big data, from machine learning (pattern identification), from human analytics, and other analytical approaches. With the identification of bad actor Internet Protocol (IP) addresses, time patterns of the St. Petersburg-based Russian trolls, their signatures and methods, there are any combination of ways to defend socio-technical systems. With sufficient surveillance, new methods can be identified fairly quickly, and these efforts may be blocked. Of course, it is important that the automated “informational sentinels” and “digital security guards” (Eubanks, 2017, p. 5) used to structure systems do not introduce bias and discrimination in blocking access to users to social media platforms and their affordances. As noted in research, American citizens can act very intensely botlike in their hyper-sharing, but their voices are important and should not be denied. Also, cybersecurity companies may play a role depending on how cyber may be harnessed / or not for political misadventures into the future.

For those who care about the Web and Internet as free spaces, there is interest in avoiding any “tragedy of the commons,” and some caretaker netizens have come forward here as well. These netizens may help inform their fellow online travelers of some of the risks and how to mitigate these. They may notify social media companies of suspected “fakes” to block such accounts. People may maintain better online hygiene and protect their own identities online (and stop mis-use of their own images, biographical details, and other features). The idea, though, is to not have people launch online vigilante actions but to work within the legal framework and corporate policies.

American citizens themselves have a role as well as volunteers and as community members. A steady stream of news reportage of government leader messaging has likely sensitized many more to the challenges of foreign election meddling and the uses of socialbots, in part, towards those ends. Optimally, people would expose themselves to a wider range of ideas beyond their own “bubbles” and “echo chambers.” They would engage more critical thinking when socializing online and create bridges with others, both in the U.S. and abroad. They would develop a clearer sense of empathy with others, so that their divides cannot be misused through tertius gaudens (“rejoicing third” in which one party benefits from strife among two others, in a term coined by Georg Simmel). They would make decisions rationally and after consideration of the accurate and relevant facts.

They would defend themselves against “social engineering” or “human hacking”—being manipulated to behave unthinkingly and without awareness of the manipulation. They would harden themselves against unthinking follower-ship and following-the-crowd and going with “social proof” that may be manufactured. Ideally, people would have a healthy skepticism about social media messaging (and the dramas of virtual friending and unfriending) and be aware of some of the technologies and enablements. This is a dynamic space, and all socio-technical systems have built-in weaknesses based on how they are designed to function. Any enablement can be used for malicious aims.

A simple example is that information systems may be used to spread information quickly, but that information may be accurate or inaccurate. Another example here is that social media platforms may be harnessed for foreign governments’ information operations, but these leave permanent digital residua and tracks, and these details may be reverse engineered back to the visible hands behind the effort (with solid intelligence work). Intelligence officers and law enforcement officers may unravel the play, which can then be disrupted and deterred against future attacks.

A much more difficult issue is to encourage people to be more intelligent about their information consumption. Calling people out for being “duped” by automated agents is a likely non-starter. (One easy work-around for the ‘bots is to connect with a high-influence and high-trust node / account and let that person spread the message. Many people do not ever track back messages to instigators. The essential nature of an “echo chamber” is that it is echoic, and reverberations can start from anywhere. No social media—or mass or niche media, for that matter—is anechoic or echo-free.) Suggesting that information snippets may have affected an entire election seems somewhat far-fetched, even though “cheap talk” may well have been mistaken for “costly signaling” by some.

It is impossible to fully disaggregate the factors that went into a particular decision. People have been found to offer post hoc rationalizations and justifications for decisions made and paths taken. And apparently, “protest votes” stemming from general disgruntlement may not be that difficult to trigger, with Americans becoming disenchanted with whatever Party has been in power in the executive branch and wanting change. These feelings may be valid or invalid, but in an open and democratic system, these are some of the chances the electorate and citizenry take.

The meta-messaging currently suggests two tracks in the interpretation of Russian meddling. One is that this is a kind of child’s play making a lot of fake accounts and using these to defame U.S. politicians and sow havoc and to troll. The counter message is that a foreign government broke election laws and committed wire fraud and contravened end user license agreements (EULAs) to launch an expensive and complex information operation against individuals and an entire populace—in order to create leverage over U.S. leaders and affect U.S. policy, for their own political aims.

FUTURE RESEARCH DIRECTIONS

This work explored whether some publicly available multidimensional information on social media accounts may indicate whether or not the original account is run by a person (or human team), a person-and-scripted agent (persons and scripted agents), or a robot (or scripted agents). The dimensions included social networks, geographical locations of the networks, and the strategic messaging (including topics, sentiment, linguistic features, and other potential “tells).

Additionally, this work asked whether or not “malice” could be identified from this public information. The initial findings are that these data and the analytical methods are insufficient to the tasks of identifying base identities of those behind a social media account…but with some insights possible in terms of malice—particularly external and obvious expressions of malice. Labeling an account as a human-embodied, cyborg, or robot account is an uncertain and fraught process, and even if the assessment is temporally correct, accounts can evolve and change. No determination is once-and-for-all. What may be more definitively determinable is who is controlling an account—based on back-end social media platform data and other more restricted data sources.

One potential augmentation to this work would be to apply these analytical approaches to the actual Russian ‘bot accounts, assuming the social media companies would release the data as public datasets for analysis. (This has not happened yet.) While some controlled access has been allowed—such as to the publicly queryable application to see if one has interacted with a Russian ‘bot account on Facebook—the underlying data is non-consumptive (inaccessible, unviewable) and restricted.

To augment this work, researchers may explore other methods of analyzing the respective ‘bot accounts, including the introduction of other dimensions, such as content analysis of the related images, the videos, and the audio files. There are other approaches that may be used as well as combinations of dimensions. One approach described here by McKew involved analyzing the first steps in the promotion of a #hashtag-based discussion and observing the behavioral roles of various social media accounts. Other approaches may involve studying disambiguated keywords to understand their usage and who is engaging in conversations around those keywords (Figure 68).

This work suggested some initial methods to confirm or disconfirm the initial assessment of social media account identity, and certainly, more work may be done in that area. Only some of the publicly available information from the respective social media platforms was used, and some available analytical methods (both human- and computational-) were deployed. For example, are there effective ways to validate existence beyond the social media platform and target user account—for actual signs of real life? Are there ways to back-track an image used in a social media platform profile to an actual individual or to some stock image company or social media account?

And beyond that verification, is there a way to verify that the actual living person account (verified on the Deep Web) is actually the individual behind a social media profile (or was that person’s identity hijacked for use by a malicious actor)? Are there ways to set effective baselines for the various details of social media accounts that may indicate identity (a unique image—as a physical biometric feature; established email account validation; verified location; non-fraud features, and others)? Is it possible to change up the social norms and practices around social media platforms to minimize the creations of fraudulent accounts (while still enabling the creation of group accounts, pseudonyms, and other value-bearing features)?

The solutions to large-scale “wicked problems” require the efforts of all stakeholders, as noted earlier (Figure 67). Perhaps there are high-level efforts that address some aspects of the issue and more unique tells and insights in particular contexts and cases. For example, other researchers have noted the uses of Russian terms (“Easter eggs” or intentional hidden messages left surreptitiously as an inside joke?) in the names of the faux Russian ‘bot accounts. Some have suggested that maybe the Russian government introduced a range of tells to lead back to themselves through electronic breadcrumbs to even sow more discord; another angle is that they were sloppy in their tradecraft. The prior working theory of a purposeful reveal by the Russian government, currently a working counterfactual, has some evidentiary support.

Perhaps there are big data solutions. After all, given how the Internet is trawled for machine learning, perhaps big data may be applied to flag non-persons and faux persons and their representations online. This would likely involve a highly noisy dataset with all sorts of common deceptions. This would not be a trivial endeavor, but the data is available, and much of this is already mapped. That said, an outside-in brute-force N=all approach is much less efficient than insider analytics using social media platforms’ big data and smart analysis.

CONCLUSION

A well-known saying about services on the Internet goes: “If you’re not paying for it; you are the product.” This truism suggests that people trade away their privacy (their thinking; their friends, their family, their interrelationships; their life patterns) in order to use free email, free online content hosting, free social media, free apps, and free everything else. There is something subtler to this dynamic, and that is that when people go online to socialize, the transactional cost includes exposing themselves to being influenced by others who have an interest in their thinking, behaviors, and resources.

In the early days of email, the channels were clogged with spam messaging and various scams; in the present day, while there are still scams, the email providers have improved in terms of being able to identify these messages and to filter them out. It is not unimaginable to think that social media platform providers will do the same regarding malicious ‘bots. In the meantime, people are still going online to relate virtually, and they are going online for accurate information (and even Truth with a capital “T”). It is difficult to imagine that users of social media will apply high levels of skepticism to the messages that they consume from the respective platforms and accounts, given the speed of communications and the demands on their attention. Every member of a population is susceptible to some types of messaging and vulnerable to some types of manipulation.

In terms of the Russian angle, ultimately, this may play out as a Russian government misadventure that will not go unpunished. It is not in the interests of peoples to clog social media spaces with malicious ‘bots, and it is risky to change up social norms about the uses of ‘bots to interfere in others’ societies. If the U.S. government handles this correctly, they may be able to deter such Russian actions into the future. They may be able to spark constructive conversations in the population and raise awareness and combat complacency. They may be able to show the close-in sense of manipulation by a “far adversary” and make the case that American citizen complacency is a dominated or losing strategy. They may be able to assert laws and social norms on the Web and Internet, which are not ungoverned spaces.

While the tones of interactions online may seem to be free-for-alls, they occur under conditions of constraints, controls, and regulations. They may be able to encourage commercial companies to take on greater responsibilities to control for malicious robots and #fakenews albeit without creating collateral damage (such as inadvertently harming the U.S. companies that provide the social media platforms). The challenge is certainly bigger than just putting out a ‘bot dragnet. Information assurance is a core value in the information sciences, but achieving this may be a “wicked problem,” which requires solving piece-by-piece, over time. As to the effects of information manipulations, conventional wisdom may suggest that messaging online may reinforce thinking and behaviors, or they may be cathartic and release in the spending of political energy in electrons (and not elections).

For robots to be even initially trusted, they “need reputations” (Meadows, 2017, as cited in Botsman, 2017, p. 190). There does exist a say-do gap in people’s behaviors. At the present moment, bots are the “hip new media,” but there are more cunning and complex tools being harnessed, such as faked videos of political figures that can be hard to differentiate from the real, and other more sophisticated hacks coming (DiResta, Little, Morgan, Neudert, & Nimmo, 2017). One account on Facebook identified as a ‘bot by a journalistic research team and a cybersecurity firm on Facebook was found to have had an account on Twitter (which was not deleted but which also had very few messages) (Shane, 2017).

The core issue of keeping elections free and fair is a foundational challenge of a modern democracy. This challenge is magnified with the impact of social media platforms themselves given the virality and quick uptake of false news on social media like Twitter, regardless of the presence of ‘bots (Vosoughi, Roy, & Aral, 2018). If a proper defense cannot be effectively raised, democracies and other targeted governments face a challenging and unforgiving future.

KEY TERMS AND DEFINITIONS

Alter: A node that is in direct one-degree connection to the target node; a member of the ego neighborhood for a target node.

Bad Actor: A malicious or harm-causing individual or entity.

Burstiness: The feature of being non-continuous but with high intensities for short periods of time (sometimes applied to communications on social media).

Consent of the Governed: The concept of a democratic government receiving its mandate to govern from the population (through levers such as voting, speech, and others).

Cyborg: A “cybernetic organism,” comprised of both organic and non-organic parts.

Degree: The number of edges connected to a vertex (with in-coming edges counted as in-degree and out-going edges counted as out-degree).

Ego Neighborhood: The one-degree direct alters connected to a target node.

Malbot: A malicious (non-beneficent, harm-intending/harm-causing) robot.

Malware: Malicious or harm-causing software.

Ngram: A contiguous sequence of n-items treated as a unit.

Personality Frame: The understanding of a particular phenomenon through the viewpoint of an individual personality.

Robot Detector: A software program that identifies scripted automated agents.

Transitivity: A relational characteristic when “an element a is related to an element b and b is related to an element c then a is also related to c” (Transitive relation, Jan. 2, 2018).

Troll: An individual or entity that posts messages in social media to cause distraction and harm.

# Chapter 13

Evidence From Romania

*   Ionica Oncioiu  
    Titu Maiorescu University, Romania
*   Anca Gabriela Petrescu  
    Valahia University, Romania

ABSTRACT

Along with the incontestable benefits for the modern society, the information and communication technology developments induce new vulnerabilities. Mobile computing devices, cloud computing, and privacy issues are just a few elements that should be taken into account when shaping the modern information security that is essential to our modern way of life. Since information security risks are rapidly evolving and taking new forms, the real benefits of information and communication technologies may be exploited only if trust is built on every layer of responsibility. This study explores of the present main information security threats faced by Romanian organizations, as well as of the attitude of Romanian organizations towards information security, as resulted from a research and detailed survey questionnaire performed by the authors. Following the results of this research, the authors propose a way to improve the security posture of Romanian organizations, as well as knowledge, capabilities, and decision making of business managers.

INTRODUCTION

Business has changed dramatically since the beginning of the 21^(st) century. Especially over the past 10 years, development of information and communication technologies (ICTs) have made their way straight to the very heart of any type of business (Ruževičius & Gedminaitė, 2007; Hadžiosmanović, Bolzoni, & Hartel, 2012; Tiago, Manoj, & Espadanal, 2014; Agrawal & Tapaswi, 2017). The cheap, real-time, easy access modality to transfer huge amounts of data all around the world has allowed companies to obtain a new geographical perspective and to develop towards regions otherwise unreachable. Contemporary globalism is built in great measure on ICT development (Andress, 2003; Hong, Kim, & Cho, 2010; Mittelman, 2011; Singh & Fhom, 2017). However, making profit from all of these advantages is feasible only if proper protection of transferred data and of network services is ensured (Willems, 2011; Stepchenko & Voronova, 2015; Malatras, Geneiatakis, & Vakalis, 2016; Lin, Lin, & Pei, 2017).

Protection implies that no access to, modification of, deletion of, or otherwise denial of access to data or network resources or services is performed by unauthorized persons or entities (Kesan & Hayes, 2012; Arukonda & Sinha, 2015; Gandino, Celozzi, & Rebaudengo, 2017). The organization’s risk management covers a wider range of risks – especially operational risks, reputation risks to the organization and, more recently, strategic risks (Hjortdal, 2011; Chen, Ge, & Xie, 2015). Moreover, within a growing number of organizations responsibilities associated with risk management are assumed by top management which generally coordinates the teams of specialists directly responsible for monitoring the risks and the risk handling measures (Yang, Wu, & Wang, 2014).

In this context, it is of major interest that managers be aware of the importance of establishing correct information security policies, commensurate with the sensitivity of the data their companies process, transmit or store in electronic format (Liaudanskienel, Ustinovicius, & Bogdanovicius, 2009; Collins & McCombie, 2012; Singer & Friedman, 2014; Friedberg, McLaughlin, Smith, Laverty, & Sezer, 2016). In the opinion of other specialists such as Landoll (2010), risk analysis is defined as an objective analysis of the effectiveness of the security measures in place to protect the interests of the organization and a determination of the likelihood of prejudice to those interests.

More specifically, risk analysis is defined by Peltier (2010) as a process of calculating risk. Algorithms for calculating risk did so as a function of the organization’s assets, threats, and vulnerabilities. Risk analysis is the first stage of risk management and is a crucial component of this process. It provides an assessment of the potential exposure to environmental threat, and the basis for the definition of the events -acceptable and unacceptable from the point of view of organization. The result of this process helps to identify appropriate measures to reduce or eliminate the identified risks. To determine the probability of an undesirable event, threats to the organization should be analyzed in conjunction with the potential vulnerabilities and security measures already implemented (Karim, 2007).

At the same time, Oncioiu (2016) agrees that no matter the field of interest, no matter the dimension or type, almost every organization today contends with much sensitive information handled in computer systems: personal data related to their own personnel or customers, commercial data and analysis, industrial patents and so forth. Regardless of the complexity of the communication and information systems, starting from simple architectures of stand-alone systems to local area networks or wide area networks, managers should be aware of the need to implement proper information security policies to build trust in their network services for both their own personnel and for business partners (Smith, 2005; Winkler, 2010; Krombholz, Hobel, Huber, & Weippl, 2015; Broadbent & Schaffner, 2016; Kurosawa, Ohta, & Kakuta, 2017).

Communication and information systems are increasingly employed on a large scale in the process of command and control of national critical infrastructures, such as energy, transportation, telecommunications, and health (Wang & Hu, 2014). Each day society becomes more dependent on these information infrastructures which become the backbone of vital information flow (Hiller & Russel, 2013; Gaidelys & Valodkiene, 2011; Okamoto & Takashima, 2015; Fischbacher-Smith, 2016). Thus, the protection of this infrastructure represents a major concern of authorities all around the world. Information security has become a top of mind issue for the public, media, and government (COM (2006) 251; COM (2008) 712; COM (2009) 149; ENISA, 2010).

Likewise, a European structure that has key responsibilities in determining courses of action regarding the security of information and principles underlying this process is the European Network and Information Security (European Network and Information Security Agency - ENISA). ENISA was established to develop a culture of safety by ensuring a high and effective level of network and information security. To achieve these objectives, the Agency contributes to increasing the capacity of the European Community, the Member States and the business community to prevent, address and respond to the problems identified in computer networks. ENISA has been a constant concern in identifying methods of risk analysis information security.

The analysis of national experts in IT security shows that since 2009 phishing incidents targeting Romanian banks resulted in three out of 10 computers being susceptible to infection with network worms because of insufficient security measures taken by organizations and individual users. The purpose of this chapter is to make radiography of the present main information security threats faced by Romanian organizations, as well as of the attitude of Romanian organizations towards information security reslting from research and detailed survey questionnaires performed by the author. To achieve this purpose, the chapter analyzes a number of problems of research.

First, this study explores the Romanian organizations’ attitude towards information technology security. Second, the protection of this infrastructure represents a major concern of authorities all around the world. As previously mentioned, the formation of security has become a key issue for the public, media, and government. Last, the chapter investigates the necessity to develop a structured process of information security risk within the organization. It must be borne in mind that, regardless of the type of organization, the field of activity or form of organization, there is uncertainty both in organization and in the environment in which it operates. Given that uncertainty is a fact of life, then uncertainty should become a permanent managerial concern.

However, collective efforts are necessary, at both the national and managerial levels of public and private organizations to ensure a safe and trusted cyber space. The awareness of potential threats and vulnerabilities is thus vital, as well as preoccupation towards cooperation in countering them by well-established rules and mechanisms created at national and organizational level. This chapter is structured as follows: the first section introduces the dynamics of the information technology security threat; in the second section, research methodology is discussed; in the third section, the results of the study and statistics analysis are shown; in the last section, the conclusions and limitations are covered.

BACKGROUND

Information technology security threats are most often defined as being “those circumstances or events that constitute potential danger to the normal state of a communication and information system, in which the confidentiality, integrity and availability of information, resources and services are ensured” (Ministry of Communications and Information Society, 2011).

The cited document classifies the information technology threats from different perspectives such as: motivational factors, impact over society, information security objectives that may potentially be affected (i.e., confidentiality, integrity, availability), actors involved, and threat sources. From the first two perspectives, the Romanian Strategy on Cyber Defense, developed by the Ministry of Communication and Information Society, defines the following types of information technology security threats: information technology attacks against infrastructures that supports public utility functions or information society services that, once disrupted, may constitute a danger for social security; unauthorized access to communication and information systems and to data they handle; unauthorized modification, deletion or alteration of data in electronic format or unauthorized denial of access to such data and services; espionage by penetrating the communication and information systems of the targeted organization; inducing patrimonial prejudice, harassment or blackmail of citizens or organizations, either public or private.

Communication and information security incidents record a significant growth during the last years, both in number and complexity (Yar, 2006). The main motivations of large scales attacks are financial profit or political supremacy. The complex cyber-attacks in 2007 on Estonia, Lithuania, and Georgia are the most widely covered examples of a general trend. The huge number of viruses, worms and other forms of malware, the expansion of botnets and the continuous rise of spam confirm the severity of the problem (Ministry of Defense Estonia, 2008).

According to a subject matter survey performed in the USA during 2010-2011 (Computer Security Institute, 2011), the threats continue to mount as attacks become increasingly sophisticated and malicious. The uncertainty may take the form of either threats or opportunities. Therefore, each manager must handle threats; otherwise, the organization’s objectives can not be met and capitalize the opportunities to the benefit of the organization, proving efficiency (McQuade, 2006; He, Chen, Chan, & Bu, 2012). Compared to the last five years, the survey illustrates a growth of the number of incidents caused by malicious infections from around 50% of the respondents in 2009 to around 64% in 2011, of password sniffing cases from 9% in 2009 to 17% of the respondents in 2011, of financial frauds, from 12% to 20%, of denial of service attacks from 21% to 29%, of websites defacements from 6% to 14%, as well as of theft of or unauthorized access to intellectual property that grew from around 9% to around 14% of the respondents.

As for the next period, it is expected the main threats confronting the communication and information systems will be targeted to system hardware and software architecture, taking the form of attacks of the peer to peer architectures, attacks directed at application level or at operating system level (Choi et al., 2014; Khan, Gani, Wahab, Shiraz, & Ahmad, 2016). Simultaneously, sophisticated attacks are expected directed to the staff users of the communication and information systems, such as social engineering attacks, correlation between offices, ISP, and home computers or mobile device attacks. State-sponsored cyber terrorism is of great concern for state authorities, as this new form of terrorism is cheap and ready available to practically everyone on each side of the world, ultimately leading to major disruptions in modern societies.

As such, concern continues to diminish the effect of unwanted influence involving a compulsory dedication of resources which, if prolonged, neglect can radically affect the overall level of resources of an organization and, therefore, the quality of its task.

Among the most important factors of disruptive impact on the activities of an organization, risk factors are by far the most significant. Risk, as defined in the western socio-economic and military environments, can occur anywhere: within the organization, structure, and decision-making process, the relationship with the external environment, the management, and policies of the organization.

Choosing an effective strategy development organization should consider the risks and vulnerabilities exposed to treatment solutions adapted to the needs of each organization’s risk and reduce costs, both short- and long-term. Meanwhile, the adoption of certain measures that contribute to risk management is conditioned by the nature of the organization and the costs incurred for these measures. To identify, analyze, and organize organizational risk assessment activities to reiterate the importance of the organizational concepts of systems theory perspective. Risk treatment is the second important step in risk management organizational stage where management organization has the key role in the adoption of the most appropriate decision in terms of the balance between the need to fulfill the performance indicators proposed and costs.

Stage security risk treatment is based entirely on the results of the risk analysis phase, the risks have been identified, and ranked in terms of the impact that their implementation can have on the organization’s mission. This is why security mechanisms must be properly designed and commensurate with the specific threats for the specific types of information (Tropina & Callanan, 2015). Organizations have to expand and deepen their current information security risk frameworks to address these key threats. This process implies a more profound understanding of the risks associated with each threat, and a better capacity of tailoring the security framework to align with the organization’s identified risks, regulatory requirements and perhaps most important – the increasing dependencies on information technology.

In addition, as previously highlighted, management vision must change radically from a passive or reactive management style to a proactive style, ready at any moment to face the challenges of achieving the objectives of the organization. Contrarily, the allocation of material and human resources in the management process can lead to non-completion of projects or even not starting them. This is where the organization’s approach is to stop the progression of the project until the risk management process. Another important aspect to note is that of a special form of risk; namely, the risk of managerial behavior in the face of organizational changes: managers hoped that the change will solve the fundamental problems of the organization; there is insufficient time for planning the implementation of change; sometimes ignore the importance of training and staff development in the context of change that will take place; change is successful only if the organization's staff change their attitude to adapt to new conditions created by the change; implementing a system with increased security personnel responsibilities.

The key to harmonizing relations between manager and staff of the organization is to understand the thinking of the latter. Through this process of understanding and developing and implementing coherent training policies, organizational management can complete the performances of the implemented security system. Otherwise, it can be concluded that substantial resources have been allocated for the implementation of the security measures system and its efficiency can not be determined.

RESEARCH METHODOLOGY

In order to obtain an image of the Romanian organizations’ attitude towards security of information they process, transmit, or store using communication and information systems, the authors performed a detailed survey using questionnaires. The research activity’s aim was to study the information security policies and mechanisms implemented within the Romanian organizations and had the following objectives: determine the level of awareness regarding the necessity of information security policies and mechanisms; determine if the managerial decision–making is performed on the basis of information security risk management results; and determine the dynamics of the security threats towards information handled in communication and information systems.

The survey was performed during the first trimester of 2016. The questionnaires were forwarded to 150 security practitioners resulting in a total of 98 responses (65.3%) being returned. We chose to receive anonymous responses to enhance the probability of obtaining more realistic responses. The proper (without recur) sample was estimated according to calculation of marginal error and this formula (Kruopis, 1993):

It is also important to note that all completed questionnaires were checked in terms of background completeness and usefulness of data and using the statistical program previously mentioned, data analysis was materialized through frequency tables and histograms for each item, and the centralization of all items.

In addition to the related tables and histograms, data analysis led to an emphasis of statistical indicators for this study, namely: the mean, median, mode, standard deviation/standard error, variance, amplitude of variance, minimum, maximum, the sum of all observations, the coefficient of asymmetry Skewness, the coefficient of vaulting Kurtosis and the calculation of quartiles.

SOLUTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS

The goal of information security is to be able not only to implement measures to detect and mitigate attacks, but also to preemptively predict attacks, deter attackers from attacking, and thus defend the systems from attack in the first place. In order for information security measures to have the capacity to deter conventional attacks, both due to aggression by external parties and those caused by internal sources, policies must be developed within each organization to parallel those developed at the governmental level. Following the interpretation of the responses, we uncovered some interesting results that are illustrative for our purpose. Most of the respondents (66%) state that the information security policy within their organizations is formally established, while 19% state that the information security policy is informal, not documented but unwritten rules are applied, 10% state that the information security policy is in course of being drafted, and 5% state that no information security rules are applied in their organizations.

However, when asked about the manner in which this information security policy is established, almost half of the respondents (46%) state this strategic document is based on “empirical” procedures, most of the time inspired from practices implemented by other organizations or from special publications advices. The remaining 54% state the information security policies in their organizations are established on the basis of a formal assessment of the information security risks specific to their organization.

Most common incidents reported by the respondents are those caused by malicious software components (42.8% of the respondents reported such kind of incidents), 9.5% reported e-mail violation, and 4.7% reported denial of service actions and the same percentage for financial frauds. Smaller percents were reported for theft of mobile computing devices and for passwords cracking. With regards to the corrective measures taken following an IT&C incident, the largest percent are associated with installing additional security software (18.9%) and smaller percent are reported for updating of information security policy of the organization, replacing of the in-use software, updates of the infrastructure, other measures (Table 2).

Table 2. Corrective actions taken after an information security incident

| Installing additional hardware components || 19.22 |
| Awareness programs || 16.51 |
| Security policy update || 10.81 |
| Hardware/software replacement || 10.41 |
| Other action || 14.15 |

Even when information security awareness programs are implemented for the personnel handling information within communication and information systems, managers are not concerned with an ex-post assessment of the impact and effectiveness of these programs. Thus, a total of 24% of the respondents state there are no information security awareness programs developed within their organizations, 28% state that information security awareness programs are applied but there are no mechanisms implemented in order to measure the effectiveness of these programs, 18% state the effectiveness of the awareness programs is estimated by the dynamics of the security incidents following the implementation of the program. Other mentioned methods are random testing of personnel, periodical written tests, and estimating the number and nature of the requests addressed to help-desk.

A superficial evaluation of the information security assembly, including security awareness, leads to the lack of feed-back necessary for the decision-making process with regard to the necessity of implementing adequate corrective measures for improving information security management. In this context, information security policies are adopted on empirical criteria, without being based on a critical assessment of the internal and external factors characteristic to the organization. The security controls framework must be established as an integrated assembly of regulatory, technical controls and awareness programs. Since all security measures have to be developed, implemented, and applied by personnel, great importance must be given to the information security awareness programs.

Specific information security awareness programs should be periodically applied at the level of organizations to consolidate the security culture of the personnel and to update it with the latest threats in the field and identified and implemented countermeasures. Policy must, therefore, aim to create rules which enable the establishment of a level of trust between organizations and to remove political and legal barriers to co-operation with a view to ensure coordinated responses to ICT incidents and attacks.

Policy must also implement a mechanism for imposing penalties for those creating or using insecure solutions both of individual “internal” systems as well as any interconnecting infrastructures. Policy must create common nomenclatures and common minimum standards of security to support the above goals. A first step in improving organizations’ behavior towards information security is to analyze the organization from the ground up to understand how data is stored, processed and transmitted. Data security and compliance framework status should be established and areas for improvement should be identified.

A second step is to protect the organization’s network and operations with layered security solutions that comply with the “in-depth security” principle of information security. Furthermore, compliance and security posture should be validated on a continuous basis, keeping the status current. Like any factor in a complex system, the benefits of information security are weighed against their total cost (including the additional costs incurred if the system is compromised). If the data or resources cost less, or are of less value than their protection, adding security mechanisms and procedures is not cost-effective because the data or resources can be reconstructed more cheaply than the protections themselves. Unfortunately, this is rarely the case.

Following the results of this research, Table 3 presents the results of several regression analyses. Organizational performance was supported, as information security awareness programs was positively associated with organizational performance (β = .27, p < .001). The benefits of information security weighed against their total cost was also supported as organizational performance was positively related to financial results (β = .33, p < .001). Finally, implementing security measures was supported as the partial regression coefficient of organizational performance reached statistically significant (β = .23, p < .001) after controlling the effect of information security awareness programs.
