# Chapter 15

The Case of Zimbabwe

*   Jeffrey Kurebwa  
    Bindura University of Science Education, Zimbabwe
*   Kundai Lillian Matenga  
    Bindura University of Science Education, Zimbabwe

ABSTRACT

This chapter is based on a study that sought to understand the threats of cyber warfare in Zimbabwe. The effects of cyber warfare, cyber intelligence mechanisms in place, and the status of the harmonization of laws and collaboration of SADC countries in efforts to address cyber threats were also covered. Qualitative research methodology was used to conduct the study. A total of 15 key respondents drawn from information technology experts, academia, top military personnel, and lawyers participated in the study. The study revealed that Zimbabwe was vulnerable to cyber warfare due to increased use of technology and failure to keep up with technological advancements. The study noted that the current legislation does not explicitly address cyber warfare threats but focuses more on cybercrime. The study recommended that Zimbabwe enact effective legislation to curtail cyber warfare in order to enhance cyber security. Investment in cyber security in terms of research and human capital development should also be prioritized.

INTRODUCTION

The threat posed by cyberwarfare through the use of computer hardware and internet related software technology by state and non-state actors has emerged as a transnational problem requiring an integrated collective security across borders in the 21^(st) century (United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, 2012). The threat of cyberwarfare has prompted the telecommunications industry, law enforcement agencies, and nation-states to improve on cyberwarfare counter intelligence mechanisms to secure their computer related network systems (Geers, 2015).

The global security debates on cyberwarfare can be traced back to the events in Estonia in 2007 following the discovery of Stuxnet, a malicious computer worm (Healy & Grindal, 2013). Andress and Winterfield (2012) highlighted that in 2007 Estonia was attacked by hackers who were believed to have links with the Russian government. Tikk, Kaska, and Vihul (2010) cited in Rid (2012, p.9) noted that, “Estonia at the time was one of the world’s most connected nations; two-thirds of all Estonians used the Internet, and 95 percent of banking transactions were done electronically.” The cyberattack brought down the websites of Estonia’s parliament, banks, ministries, newspapers, and broadcasters (Andress & Winterfield, 2012). This experience resulted in the disruption of infrastructure and economic loss thereby threatening peace and stability of the country (Nguyen, 2013 p.1127–8).

In January, 2012, Israel also experienced a wave of cyberattacks which targeted websites of Tel Aviv Stock Exchange and the national airport. The banking sector was affected by disclosure of credit cards security information and account details of Israeli nationals (United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, 2012). Internet technology in cyberwarfare was also responsible for the Russia-Georgia war of 2008. Maurer and Janz (2014) alleged that botnets and kinetic military operations were used to deface websites and to conduct Distributed Denial of Services (DDoS) attacks, which overwhelmed websites and ultimately rendering them inaccessible. The war primarily targeted the Georgian government and media websites thereby disrupting communication channels and generating confusion during the crisis.

Russia was accused of internet intrusion and hacking of the United States of America’s servers during the 2016 elections thereby determining the electoral outcome in favor of Donald Trump (National Intelligence Council, 2017). The accusations leveled against the Russian President Vladimir Putin were that he ordered an ‘influence campaign’ in 2016 designed at the US presidential election. The consistent goals of which were to undermine public faith in the US democratic process, denigrate Secretary Hillary Clinton, and harm her electability and potential to assume presidency (National Intelligence Council, 2017).

In the SADC region, Zimbabwe and South Africa have also been victims of cyberattacks. Techzim (2016) claimed that a hacker group known as Anonymous Africa was responsible for issuing Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks to critical national infrastructure (CNI) such as the national media. The Herald Newspaper of Zimbabwe was alleged to have been attacked by Anonymous Africa ahead of the country’s 2013 harmonized elections (Techzim, 2016). These cases of cyberwarfare have increased attention of scholars to research further on the implications of cyberwarfare to nation-states.

Cyberwarfare is emerging as a potential threat to state security and world peace. Governments around the world have, in response, established policies that govern interaction and collaboration among government entities, the private sector, the academia and civil society in collective efforts to mitigate cybersecurity vulnerabilities and attacks. Orji (2015, p.105) argued that some African intergovernmental organizations have also developed legal frameworks for cybersecurity.

Therefore, there is a growing consensus that nations bear increasing responsibility for enhancing cybersecurity. A related recent trend globally has been the adoption of long-term strategic plans to help deter, protect and defend countries against cyber threats. These national cybersecurity strategies outline a nation’s core values and goals in the territory of cybersecurity law and policy, from mitigating cybercrime and espionage to preparing for cyberwarfare (Shackelford and Kastelic, 2016 p. 895). Some of the legal instruments adopted in Africa include the African Union Convention on Cybersecurity and Personal Data Protection (2014), Directive on Fighting Cybercrime (2011), and Model Cybercrime Law (2011), and Model Law on Computer Crime and Cybercrime (2012).

PURPOSE OF THE STUDY

This study sought to understand the threat of cyberwarfare in Zimbabwe.

OBJECTIVES OF THE STUDY

*   1\. To establish the factors that expose countries within the SADC region to cyberwarfare.
*   2\. To examine cyber counter-intelligence frameworks available in Zimbabwe.
*   3\. To assess the harmonization of cyber laws in SADC.
*   4\. To suggest recommendations for improving cybersecurity in SADC.

RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY

The study made use of qualitative research methodology. The adoption of the qualitative research was therefore appropriate as the study made use of data that is not quantitative but relied on opinions and experiences of key informants in Information and Communications Technology (ICT) with different expertise. This study adopted the case study of Zimbabwe. A total of fifteen informants drawn from ICT experts, security sector, cybersecurity experts, legal practitioners, and the academia were interviewed. The study sample included informants from the security sector as key because it is the primary institution responsible for the maintenance of peace and stability in the country.

Therefore, it was imperative to gain an insight into their understanding and response to the emergence of cyberwarfare. In addition, considering that cyberattacks usually target critical national infrastructure, the study identified the telecommunications and banking sectors as industries with high technological use. To address the legal aspects of the research with regards to assessing the adequacy of the legal framework, the study identified the Attorney General’s Office because of its role in crafting Bills as well as independent lawyers to give their analysis of the legal framework on cyberwarfare in Zimbabwe. The study reviewed documents that focused on aspects such as cyber-related treaties, conventions, constitutions, bills, newspaper reports, and peer-reviewed journals.

LITERATURE REVIEW AND THEORETICAL FRAMEWORK

The study adopts the neo-realism by Waltz (1979) as the theoretical framework. It locates the state as the principle actor within the international arena. As Strinde (2011, p. 8) highlights, “neo-realism views state behavior as dependent on the international environment they exist in and as such look to explanations given through the limitations and possibilities of each state.” The assumption that undergirds the theory is that the state of nature is anarchy and war. Ghanea-Hercock (2012) affirms the fact that cyberspace is anarchic by claiming that the internet is now the world's digital nervous system, and suffers from parasitic and predator-prey activity, just as any biological or ecological system does. Thus, cyberspace is viewed as the new international battlefield (Petallides, 2012, p.2).

As states begin to regard cyberspace as part of their strategic interests, the neorealist theory explains the aims and interactions of states (Strinde, 2011). Petallides (2012) postulated the internet has no governing body or police force. Hence, it perfectly fits the realist security model where every state stands alone or with its allies, whom it can never fully trust, and desperately tries to build up its cyber strength and defenses while fearing that every breakthrough made by another state poses a direct threat to their security. This assertion has been evidenced by the cyber arms race which has characterized the cyberspace domain in recent years. Breene (2016) argued the USA, China, Russia, Israel, and the United Kingdom are believed to have developed cyberwarfare capabilities with Iran and North Korea being prime targets.

Furthermore, Waltz (1979), cited in Strinde (2011, p.6), highlighted self-help mechanisms by states to survive in this anarchic environment and recommends agreement between countries which will guarantee their sustained security. For a nation to achieve and sustain its safety and protection from any potential attack, it needs to develop economic, territorial and military power. Increasing military and economic influence (internal balancing) or utilization of other states’ resources through alliance formation (external balancing) is therefore critical (Strinde, 2011). Alliance formation obliges an alliance member to intervene in any warfare where an alliance is involved.

Cyberwarfare

Cyberwarfare is increasingly becoming one of the critical areas of study for academics in the field of international relations with its background entrenched in the development of more advanced technology like computer network systems connected to business transactions, governance, intelligence and the civil society (Carr, 2015). However, the definition of cyberwarfare has remained a subject of debate among scholars such as Burton (2015), Grobler and van Vuuren (2012), Rid (2012), and Tabansky (2017). Clarke and Knake (2010, p.6) defined cyberwarfare as “actions by a nation-state to penetrate another nation's computers or networks for the purposes of causing damage or disruption.” These scholars argued that cyber war has already begun, and that nations are preparing the cyber battlefield after proclaiming that the USA and several other countries possess cyberattack capabilities that can devastate a modern state.

Rid (2012) questioned the authenticity of cyberwarfare due to the domain in which it manifests as well as its impact on human life. He postulated that cyberwar has never happened in the past, that cyber war does not take place in the present, and that it is unlikely that cyberwar will occur in the future. Tabansky (2017) agreed with Rid’s assertion and further claims that cyberwarfare does not exist and that cyber events that have taken place to date cannot constitute a war because war involves threats of force and violence as vehicles to achieving a political goal.

Tabansky (2017) and Rid (2012) derive their perceptions from the assumption that there is no physical harm to human lives. Calvo (2014) argued to the contrary and claimed that it is only a matter of time before cyberwarfare can amount to an act of war. For Calvo, Rid (2012) and Tabansky (2017) base their view on Clausewitz principles of what constitutes war, which are extreme violence, instrumental violence or the threat of force to compel the enemy to accept the attacker’s will and the existence of a political goal. Dermer (2013) on the other hand questions the purported timeless Clausewitzian principles in the 21st Century by arguing that while violence, uncertainty, and rationality still accurately depict the nature of cyberwarfare, its many defining attributes and execution has definitively changed the character of wars.

Rid (2013), in contrast to Calvo (2014), maintains that cyberattacks lessen rather than heighten political violence as states engage in two kinds of aggression that do not necessarily rise to the level of war, which are sabotage and espionage. The most cited incidents of this nature that have occurred include the DDoS attacks of the Republic of Estonia in 2007 and the controversial Wiki leaks founded by Julian Assange which released sensitive government information of numerous states into the public domain (Hathaway & Crootof, 2015, p. 837).

On the contrary, Connell and Vogler (2017) hold that cyberwarfare is a holistic concept that includes computer network operations, electronic warfare, psychological operations and information operations. Burton (2015) argued that cyberwarfare is something that is happening and that it is a salient, relevant, and increasingly influential part of the contemporary security environment. He further posited that cyberspace is gradually becoming militarized, whereby cyberattacks can lead to armed conflict, and thereby posing a danger to world security. Similarly, Grobler and van Vuuren (2012) recognized cyberwarfare as the use of exploits in cyberspace as a way to intentionally cause harm to people, assets, and economies.

Forms of Cyber Attacks

The invention of cyber weapons is to launch attacks within cyberspace. According to Pool (2013, p. 300), historically, the rise of cyber weapons dates back to the Cold War. The USA founded the Advanced Research Projects Agency (ARPA) as a response to the perceived technological advantage that Russia had after the launch of Sputnik in 1957. Therefore, cyber weapons were created to maintain a competitive military edge. Hathaway and Crootof (2015) propounded that the objective of a cyberattack is to undermine the function of a computer network which is a system of computers and devices connected by communications channels. This connection exists over the Internet in most cases making it prone to intrusions. The attacks include syntactic attacks which disrupt a computer’s operating system, causing the network to malfunction, botnets and malware such as worms, viruses, hackings, and Trojan horses.

Malware is one of the most common logical weapons that can be used to launch an attack. Souppaya and Scarfone (2013) described malware as a program that is covertly inserted into another program with the intent to destroy data, run destructive or intrusive programs, or otherwise compromise the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of the victim’s data, applications, or operating system. Malware has the potential to cause widespread damage and disruption and necessitating extensive recovery efforts within most organizations (Souppaya & Scarfone, 2013, p.6). The most popular malware used in cyberwarfare include Stuxnet and Flame. According to Kushner (2013), Stuxnet is a 500-kilobyte computer worm that infected the software of at least 14 industrial sites in Iran, including a uranium enrichment plant.

Stuxnet was successful in causing damage to Iran’s nuclear facilities. It was the first attack known to cause physical destruction across international boundaries.

Therefore, Stuxnet is the harbinger of a new form of digital warfare which threatens even the strongest military powers (Kushner, 2013). Malware such as Stuxnet is a typical example of cyber weapons utilized in cyberspace. Maclean (2010) argued that Stuxnet attacks are executed by nation-states which confirms the realist notion of anarchy within the international environment and states pursuing self-help mechanisms to enhance their power. In cyberwarfare, malware is used to attack critical national infrastructure. These are services that are essential to the economic, social and political well-being of a country (Grobler & van Vuuren 2012, p. 63). Grobler and van Vuuren (2012, p. 63) listed the following as critical national infrastructure; communications, emergency services, energy, finance, food, government and public services, health, public safety, transport, and water.

Motivation of Cyber Attacks

This study argues that the risk of cyberwarfare rises with increased technological advancement. Scholarly work reviewed in this study including Andress and Winterfield (2013), Hathaway and Crootof (2015), Deibert (2012), and Orji (2015) highlighted that the interconnectedness and advancement of computer networks is the catalyst for cyberattacks. This interconnectedness inherently results in a compromise of confidentiality, availability or integrity of technological systems, and can have dramatic consequences (Grobler & van Vuuren, 2012).

Though cyberattacks are yet to directly result in loss of lives as argued by this study, they have recorded devastating effects in the past. Duncan (2007) as cited in Hathaway and Crootof (2012) highlighted that for a period stretching over a decade, analysts have speculated about the potential consequences of a cyberattack which may range from messed up financial records or harm to the stock market.

It is imperative to acknowledge that the damage caused by these attacks is difficult to quantify. Winterfield and Andress (2012) argued that there is no method to calculate the damage because it is rare that these attacks may result directly in deaths but can disrupt vital services. Subsequently, destruction to property, economic loss or impact to national security are experienced. Contrary to warfare in which there is maiming of people as a result of a battlefield skirmish, cyberwarfare tends to affect the country or critical national infrastructure sectors as a whole, by having an economic and or political effect (Grobler & van Vuuren, 2012).

The Rumin Report (2016) gives an example of the 2008 South Ossetia war in which synchronized cyberattacks crippled Georgian government websites before physical attacks. The cyberwarfare attacks were primarily executed by hackers who were well trained in exploiting the intricacies of computer networks and operated under the auspices and support of the nation-state. Rather than shutting down Georgia’s vital systems, the cyberwarfare attack intruded computer-based systems to compromise valuable data, degrading communications, impairing infrastructural services such as transportation and medical services, and interrupting commerce.

Lewis (2015) affirmed this by declaring that a cyberattack has the potential to produce results equivalent to a kinetic attack, but its primary effect, is mostly to manipulate data, knowledge, and opinion to cause a political or psychological effect rather than physical damage. These views have contributed to some scholars such as Rid (2012) and Tabansky (2013) questioning whether cyberattacks can be actually be regarded as warfare.

LEGAL FRAMEWORKS IN COMBATING CYBERWARFARE

The United Nations Charter

The United Nations Charter outlines the universal framework governing activity in cyberspace. Article 2 (4) prohibits the threat or use of force by mandating member states to refrain from the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state. Therefore military attacks are mainly for self-defense or when authorized by the UN Security Council (Waxman, 2011 p. 44). Subsequently, Article 51 of the United Nations Charter states that: Nothing in the present Charter shall impair the inherent right of individual or collective self-defense if an armed attack occurs against a Member of the United Nations. However, Waxman (2011, p. 45) argued that these two provisions raise several pertinent questions with regards to whether a cyberattack constitute a prohibited ‘use of force’ and if it has potential to give rise to the right to use military force in self-defensive response.

Wolter (2013) highlighted that governmental experts from the five permanent members of the UN Security Council and 10 leading cyber powers from all regions of the world have recognized that international law, including the principles of the law of state responsibility, fully apply to state behavior in cyberspace. As such, the right, specified in Article 51 of the UN Charter to self-defense including the use of force would apply if a cyberattack reached the level of an ‘armed attack.’ However, Hathaway and Crootof (2012, p. 840) argued that so far no state has claimed that a cyberattack constitute an ‘armed attack’ giving rise to a right of self-defense nor has any state argued that cyberattacks constitute a prohibited use of force.

In this regard, a cyberattack must rise to the level of an armed attack for a state to respond lawfully under Article 51 (Hathaway and Crootof, 2012, p. 844). Therefore, the use of the United Nations Charter for the regulation of states within cyberspace is weak since no cyberattacks have directly resulted in the loss of lives. Theohary and Rollins (2015, p. 4) argued that internationally and legally binding instruments should be drafted explicitly to regulate inter-state relations in cyberspace. Therefore, states can choose whether to comply with these provisions or not without any repercussions.

United Nations Resolutions

The study took note of four resolutions by the intergovernmental body in the fight against cyber threats and enhancement of cybersecurity. These include, UN resolution 55/63, 56/121, 57/239, and 58/199 which require states to establish legal frameworks which discourage the harboring of cyber criminals. The resolutions also protect individuals from cyber threats, combat the use of technology in committing crime, facilitate the sharing of information, creation of emergency warning networks regarding cyber-vulnerabilities, threats and incidents and the promotion of national and international research and development. However, these resolutions are not binding; hence, states are not mandated to enforce them.

REGIONAL EFFORTS FOR CYBERSECURITY

The African Union (AU), an intergovernmental body of 55 countries has also established legal frameworks to enhance cybersecurity in the region. Orji (2015) highlighted that the AU had adopted a Convention on Cybersecurity and Personal Data Protection which aims to harmonize the laws of African States on electronic commerce, data protection, cybersecurity promotion and cyber-crime control. This Convention was meant to guide the formulation of cyber legislation based on the continent’s needs and adheres to the legal and regulatory requirements on electronic transactions, cybersecurity, and personal data protection (Orji, 2015). However, Orji (2015) and Terebey (2016) noted that the Convention was finally adopted in June 2014 after a stalled process mainly caused by grievances by stakeholders such as civil society over lack of comprehensive consultation processes.

Tereby (2016) indicated that, in 2016, only eight countries had signed the Convention but had not ratified it. These were Benin, Guinea-Bissau, Mauritania, Congo, Cape Verde, Sierra Leone, and Sao Tome and Principe, despite the fact that the Convention can only come into effect if at least 15 countries ratify it. Furthermore, Terebey (2016) bemoaned that the development of national cybersecurity legislation has been relatively stagnant in the region with Mauritius possessing legislation which addresses cybercrime, e-commerce, data protection, and privacy as well as an established Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT). Both Orji (2015) and Terebey (2016) affirm that the AU is lagging behind with regards to the development of a collective continental cybersecurity policy which is essential in harmonization of cybersecurity laws and the establishment of national policy development.

SADC EFFORTS TO COMBAT CYBERWARFARE

At the SADC level, the International Telecommunications Union (ITU) in partnership with the African Union, SADC and African, Caribbean and Pacific (ACP) have established a model law called Harmonization of Information and Communications Technology Policies in Sub-Saharan Africa (HIPSSA). SADC states may use this model to craft their respective cyber laws specific to their country context. In March, 2012, SADC crafted a model law on Computer Crime and Cybercrime as a response to counter and eliminate the threats imposed in cyberspace (Orji, 2015). To date, this is the only SADC instrument that attempts to provide recourse to the threats imposed on nations through cyberspace. All 15 SADC member states either have or are crafting cyber-crime legislation to curb computer-related crimes. Grobler and van Vuuren (2012) affirmed that many countries in the SADC region have begun the process of adopting cybersecurity laws similar to those adopted by SADC.

THE ROLE OF THE STATE IN CYBERWARFARE AND CYBERSECURITY

This study sought to establish the role that SADC member states have played in the wake of cyberwarfare. The literature reviewed indicated that some countries had adopted offensive and defensive techniques to protect, defer and defend themselves from cyberattacks. Kenya and Nigeria are examples of African countries which have worked towards enhancing cybersecurity.

The Kenyan Experience

The technological environment of Kenya has vastly improved (Paganini, 2012). He further asserted that the mobile sector in Kenya is the most exposed to incoming cyber threats with over 17 million people on the Internet and 6 million of them being mobile internet users. According to Kiboi (2015), this phenomenal growth in technological advancement is attributable to the Government of Kenya’s underlying universal access to ICTs as a main objective of its economic blueprint. The fast-growing cyber threat environment in Kenya is characterized by increasingly sophisticated hackers who are launching more frequent and targeted attacks (Serianu, 2014, p. 12). The government of Kenya has been the victim rather than the proponent of the attacks (Kiboi, 2015).

The Kenyan government has introduced electronic systems within government ministries and departments such as the legal, national tax, education, immigration and integrated financial management systems (Serianu, 2014, p. 28). Additionally, Kenya has established the Government Common Core Network which is a government-wide ICT architecture. Therefore, these are potential targets for cyber attackers who may want to undermine Kenya’s national security (Kiboi, 2015). As a response to the cyber threats, Kenya promulgated the Cybersecurity and Protection Act (2017). A review of the Act indicated that it includes international cooperation mechanisms (Part IV). Furthermore, the Global Security Index (2017) reports that Kenya, provides a worthy example of cooperation through its National Kenya Computer Incident Response Team Coordination Centre (National KECIRT/CC) which coordinates at national, regional and global levels.

Within Kenya, it works with internet service providers, education, and financial sectors. The CIRT also works with counterparts through the East African Communications Organization. At the international level, Kenya works with the International Telecommunications Union (ITU) and with the United States and Japan CIRTs among other countries. In addition, Kenya is building its capacity by the establishment of the Kenya National Research and Education Network (KENET), which is the Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT) for the academic community and is licensed by the Communications Authority of Kenya. Kenya currently ranks third regarding cybersecurity as determined by the ITU (2017).

The Nigerian Experience

Nigeria is another country that is technologically advancing at a rapid pace. Osho and Onoja (2015, p. 121) highlighted there is widespread adoption of technologies in Nigeria, making it one of the main consumers of ICTs in Africa. The high rate of foreign based information technology giants establishing branches, as well as the growing amount of indigenous technology firms in the country is evidence of this.

Nigeria has experienced a series of cyberattacks. According to Baken and Mantzikos (2013), the country was attacked by Hacktivists who claimed to be members of the Boko Haram. Reports indicated that in August, 2012, the Nigerian Secret Service was hacked and the insurgent group gained access to the personnel records and databases of the organization. The Nigeria Cyber Hack-activists group orchestrated attacks that were targeted at the Nigerian government. Nigerian law Today (2013) reported that after the government announced its intention to remove the subsidy on petrol in 2012, a social media revolution began with the ‘#OccupyNigeria’ trending. Following these outcries, there were attacks on government websites including the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission’s website, the National Assembly website and the massive bombardment of phone lines of government officials. These attacks have exposed the need to enhance cybersecurity in the country.

In response to the vulnerabilities caused by widespread use of ICTs, Nigeria has established a Nigerian National Cybersecurity Policy and Strategy. According to the Office of the Nigerian National Security Adviser (2014) cited by Osho and Onoja (2015, p. 124), the initiative seeks to provide, cohesive measures and strategic actions towards assuring security and protection of the country’s presence in cyberspace, safeguarding critical information infrastructure, building and nurturing trusted cyber-community. Osho and Onoja (2015, p. 139) highlighted that the strategy included the protection and resilience of critical information infrastructure and the development of national and international partnerships.

Furthermore, the approach has provision for the creation of a Nigerian Computer Emergency Readiness Team, which will speedily respond to security incidents. Also, Nigeria has the Cybercrimes Prohibition, Prevention Act of 2015 which provides for an effective, unified and comprehensive legal, regulatory and institutional framework for the prohibition, prevention, detection, prosecution and punishment of cybercrimes in the country. The Act also addresses issues to do with the protection of critical national infrastructure and promotes cybersecurity.

DATA PRESENTATION, ANALYSIS, AND DISCUSSION OF FINDINGS

Zimbabwe Legislation on Cybersecurity

The main piece of legislation governing criminal law is the Criminal Law (Codification and Reform) Act \[Chapter 9:23\]. The Criminal Code in its present formulation does not define or create an offense relating to cyberwarfare. The law in Zimbabwe only addresses the cyber and computer-related crimes to a lesser extent. The study noted that the Criminal Law (Codification and Reform) Act creates a number of offenses that are related to intentional breaches to the computer and cyber systems. Section 162 defines some terms that are linked to some computer-related crimes as enshrined in the Act. These crimes include the unauthorized access to or use of computer or computer network as propounded in Section 163 which states that,

Any person who, without authority from the owner of the computer or computer network, intentionally gains access to; or destroys or alters; or renders meaningless, useless or ineffective; or copies or transfers; or obstructs, intercepts, diverts, interrupts or interferes with the use of; any data, programme or system which is held in a computer or computer network shall be guilty of unauthorized access to or use of a computer or computer network.

Also, there is the criminalization of deliberate introduction of a computer virus into computer or computer network in terms of Section 164 which provides that,

Any person who, without authority from the owner of the computer or computer network, knowingly introduces or causes to be introduced any computer virus into any computer or computer network shall be guilty of deliberate introduction of a computer virus into a computer or computer network.

Furthermore, the Act prohibits the unauthorized manipulation of proposed computer programmes under Section 165. It indicates that,

Any person, who fraudulently or mischievously creates, alters or manipulates any data, programme or system (or any part or portion thereof) which is intended for installation in a computer shall be guilty of unauthorized manipulation of a proposed computer programme.

A lawyer who participated in the study criticized the wording and contents of the Act. He highlighted that,

What is apparent from the wording and formulation of these crimes is that they are focused on the petty and more domestic offenses committed by hackers at a more localized level. The penal provisions do not address the emerging global, and virtual threats now referred to as cyberwarfare. This term is not used anywhere in the Act or elsewhere in domestic laws.

As a means of addressing the critical gaps identified in the Criminal Law (Codification and Reform) Act of 2004, the Government of Zimbabwe gazetted the Cybercrime, and Cybersecurity Bill. The Bill is an improvement on the legislative framework relating to cyber-related offenses. The Bill, however, still falls far short of addressing all the elements that constitute cyberwarfare. The Bill does not define nor precisely provide for the crime of cyberwarfare. Unlike the Criminal Code, the Bill attempts to explain the term cybercrime. According to Section 3 of the Bill ‘cybercrime’ means any offense under this Act. The definition is vague and hardly satisfactory as someone must go through the range of all the offenses provided for in the Bill to discern the scope and ambit of what a cybercrime is. Thus, the definition remains too general, broad and lacking in specificity. One ICT expert who participated in the study argued that,

The Bill creates several offenses that in some respect have elements of what would constitute cyberwarfare. These include offenses such as Unlawful access (Section 6), Unlawful interception of data (Section 7), unlawful acquisition of data, (Section 8), Unlawful interference with data or data storage medium,(Section 9), Unlawful interference with computer system (Section 10) Unlawful disclosure of data code (Section 11), and Unlawful use of data or devices (Section 12).

An analysis of the range of the crimes provided for in the Cybercrime and Cybersecurity Bill suggests that the term cybercrime is given a very broad and wide meaning and it may be suggested that the Bill in some respect envisages some elements of the crime of cyberwarfare without necessarily saying so. While the Cybercrime and Cybersecurity Bill do not make any reference to the specific crime of cyberwarfare it does contain a number of provisions that contemplate the crime of cyberwarfare.

An examination of the Criminal Law (Codification and Reform) Act of 2004 and the Cybercrime and Cybersecurity Bill, reveals that the legal framework in Zimbabwe does not have a crime of cyberwarfare as per the definition offered by this study. Hathaway and Crootof (2012) highlighted that the terms cybercrime and cyberwarfare are frequently used interchangeably, with little regard to what they mean. Consequently, this affects the design of a meaningful legal response when the offense. On the other hand, Pool (2013) stressed that different countries have different definitions for similar terms mostly because cyberwarfare came into existence in recent years, making it difficult to distinguish between such terms like cyberattack, cybercrime, and cyberwarfare.

Therefore, some actions that qualify as types of cyberwarfare can be offenses under the broad ambits of what constitutes cybercrimes as contemplated by the Bill. The Bill also covers offenses related to cyber terrorism and sabotage of critical infrastructure. Section 28 of the Bill states that,

Any person who unlawfully and intentionally uses computers, computer networks or information infrastructure networks; possesses, receives or makes available data, any software or hardware tool, malware, a password, access code or similar data and device, or computer data, computer device, computer network or information infrastructure network; for the purposes of committing, inciting the commission of, conspiring to commit, or attempting to commit acts of insurgency, banditry, sabotage, or terrorism defined in section 23 of the Criminal Law Code shall be guilty of cyber terrorism and liable to the penalties set out in the said section 23 of the Criminal Law Code.

In addition, cyber-related foreign and international terrorism is also addressed in Section 29 which states that,

Any person who uses any computer or information infrastructure network for the purpose of committing, inciting the commission of, conspiring to commit or attempting to commit any offense in terms of the Suppression of Foreign and International Terrorism Act (Chapter 11:21) shall be guilty of an offense and liable to the appropriate penalty in terms of the Act.

An analysis of the Bill shows that in the first instance it only caters for those cyberattacks that qualify as cybercrimes. Secondly, where the proposed law seems to contemplate the crime of cyberwarfare, it limits this to actions only initiated by terrorists’ organizations that are, by definition, not necessarily nation-states. On the contrary, Hathaway and Crootof (2012) and Strinde (2011) emphasize the role of the nation-states in acts that can be classified as cyberwarfare. Moreover, this study noted that although the proposed Cybercrime and Cybersecurity Bill creates some offenses that linked to the crime of cyberwarfare, it still falls far short of creating a specific and unambiguous offense of cyberwarfare as defined above.

Not every cyberattack would constitute a cybercrime that necessarily rises to the threshold of cyberwarfare. It is therefore critical that nation-states take the lead in promoting greater security in cyberspace because they are the main actors for motivating, if not mandating coordinated security actions (Butler & Lachow, 2012).

Zimbabwe’s Vulnerability to Cyberwarfare Threats

The informants highlighted that vulnerability to cyberwarfare was inevitable due to the interconnectedness of communication systems at the global level. In addition, Zimbabwe does not have autonomy over the information systems; hence the fact that the country is mostly a consumer of the information technology software and hardware products makes it vulnerable to cyberattacks.

A Systems Administrator from a prominent bank highlighted that,

The increased use of computers and the internet may potentially become a frontier for illegal transactions and operations, especially the computerization of all administrative processes in the government and business sector.

In the same logic, the World Bank IT Consultant resident in Zimbabwe opined that,

Telecommunications in Zimbabwe are regulated by the Postal and Telecommunication Regulatory Authority of Zimbabwe. This body assigns frequencies to telecommunication companies such as Econet, Telone, Netone, Telecel, Africom. Because of increased digitalization of systems, the companies, in turn, secure optic fiber networks which are connected to the world through underground sea cables, so they go via Mozambique and South Africa, for example, right round Africa to Europe. Zimbabwe is a consumer of these products, therefore relies on an international regulatory body for the supply and access of the systems. Attacks are thus possible as the channels can be easily manipulated or sabotaged through jamming of the networks.

The research findings concur with assertions by Andress and Winterfield (2012), Hathaway and Crootof (2015), Deibert (2012), and Orji (2015) that technological advancement increases vulnerability to cyberattacks. Orji (2015) opines that the interconnectivity and liberalization of information systems is a gateway for adversaries to attack unsuspecting targets. Therefore, the increased use of technology by countries reflects the constant desire by states to remain competitive in the international arena and the attacks that occur within cyberspace attribute to the anarchy that is characteristic of the world order.

The study thus construed that while the increased use of technology exposes Zimbabwe to cyberwarfare, the fact that Zimbabwe consumes ICT equipment and software from other countries is also a catalyst for cyberattacks. Subsequently, control and autonomy over the systems used is in the hands of the inventers and owners of such technology. The failure to keep abreast with technological advances with regards to the information systems utilized is also a factor that increases vulnerability among the least developed economies.

Politically Motivated Threats

With regards to Zimbabwe’s susceptibility regarding politically motivated cyberattacks, an Independent Cybersecurity Consultant interviewed noted that,

I don’t think Zimbabwe’s relations with other states have reached a stage where cyberwarfare can be a threat. But because we might be seen as a country that has relations with other countries, for instance, countries that are deemed to be not democratic, such as North Korea, it might be a country that might become a target because of those reasons.

On the contrary, a Colonel at the Zimbabwe Defense College argued that,

There are times when covert operations are used by belligerents in attacking each other through computer platforms like the internet. Undoubtedly, the internet is one platform that has speeded up globalization through the sharing of ideas and is therefore ideal for propaganda subversion purposes. Thus populations in SADC countries are prone to such subversion but very little can be done since the circuits in use for these purposes are open, and any attempt in restricting access would result in negative backlashes against the governments. In the government and military, it would be difficult to establish which decision-making platforms rely too much on cyber links that if attacked an enemy they would impact negatively on the security status of the country.

An IT expert opined that,

In recent years, Zimbabwe and South Africa have experienced hacktivism with political motive. There were attacks executed by a hacker group known as Anonymous Africa which has expressed some strong opinions on South African and Zimbabwean politics. The group was responsible for issuing a distributed denial of service attacks (DDoS) to national media infrastructure by attacking the Independent Online Newspaper in 2013 and South African news site SABC in June 2016 in protest over articles published titled “Mugabe hero of African liberation.” The South African websites were attacked for their support on President Robert Mugabe who the hackers called a dictator.

The Co-founder of the Digital Society of Zimbabwe also mentioned that,

Hackings are very prevalent, in June 2017 the websites of Harare Institute of Technology and National University of Science and Technology were attacked. But the attacks were mainly ransom-ware were the attackers were demanding almost 6 Billion Dollars.

From the findings, it was revealed that political factors such as regime change agents, Hacktivists such as Anonymous Africa as well as insurgent groups who use social media to challenge the status quo are a potential threat to peace and stability of the country. Similarly, Geers (2010), as cited in Grobler and van Vuuren (2012), who argued that the political nature of national security threats has not changed, but there is a new delivery mechanism which is faster and more powerful through the internet. While the hackings by Anonymous Africa did not result in dire consequences for both South Africa and Zimbabwe, such transgressions have the potential of intensification in future attacks. Similarly, the hackings of universities cited above constitute cybercrime. These incidents should not be dismissed as criminal offenses but point to the vulnerability to cyberwarfare that the country is exposed to.

The Threat of Cyberwarfare in Zimbabwe

Interviews with key respondents revealed that Zimbabwe is yet to experience a cyberattack which can be construed as cyberwarfare. In light of this, the debate by Rid (2012) and Tabansky (2017) challenging whether cyberattacks can amount to warfare in the traditional sense becomes very convincing. Hathaway and Crootof (2012) claimed that if the motive of the cybercrime is not for a political or national security purpose, it does not fit to constitute a cyberattack and is, therefore, cybercrime. However, while the attacks cited remain in the domain of criminal activity, Burmeister, Phahlamohlaka, and Al-Saggaf (2014), argued that a cyberattack can come as a disguise of cybercrime. Hence, threats should never be dismissed.

Cyber Counter Intelligence Mechanisms

The POTRAZ Head of IT was of the view that that,

The regulatory authority was very instrumental in the development of the different Bills which are currently under debate. These include the Computer Crime and Cybercrime Bill, the Electronic Transactions and Electronic Commerce Bill and the Data Protection Bill. The Authority is also currently coordinating the establishment of a Computer Incident Response Team (CIRT) in the country. The Authority also runs awareness sessions on cybersecurity from time to time.

The above assertions are consistent with Butler and Lachow (2012) who emphasized on the role of the state as crucial to ensuring their security in cyberspace. The Herald (5 August 2016) reported that the Zimbabwe National Army (ZNA) was training its officers to be able to deal with the emerging threat of cyberwarfare. This initiative to enhance cybersecurity by the ZNA is reflective of realist tendencies where states will resort to self-help mechanisms and adopt defensive capabilities to protect themselves against adversaries and maintain their sovereignty. However, there are still gaps with regards to engaging and collaborating with other stakeholders such as the corporate sector, civil society, and citizens to combat cyberwarfare.

Harmonization of Laws and Collaboration of SADC Countries

Regarding the harmonization of laws, the independent Cybersecurity Consultant opined that,

The Model Law has been implemented differently across the region. Zimbabwe as an example has not followed per se that model. South Africa didn’t follow the model and it is completely different. However, Lesotho and Swaziland have followed the model. Zambia again has a Computer Misuse Act which is also not necessarily in the same format and framework that SADC had proposed. This poses challenges for harmonization of the laws.

On the contrary, the Digital Society Co-Founder noted that,

The SADC model law itself is flawed and has ambiguous language which is the first hindrance in its integration by member states. The reason why legal frameworks for cybersecurity have been ineffective in the region is that, in some countries, it is a copy and paste of the SADC Model Law which does not fit in every country’s context.

A Colonel at the Zimbabwe Defense College highlighted that,

Every country in the world would, therefore, prepare itself for cyberwarfare according to its ‘national defense needs’, and this information is rarely shared even in close allies like NATO let alone the SADC, Zimbabwe and South Africa inclusive. Therefore, at the regional level, each country takes its precautions as far as cyberwarfare is concerned but can cooperate at that level in common user platforms in the military or police as and when necessary for interoperability.

The study recognized that the SADC Model Law on Computer Crime and Cybercrime adopted by SADC ministers responsible for telecommunications and ICT is the region's initiative to set the best practices and principles of cybercrime legislation. The harmonization of cybersecurity laws in the SADC region remains a challenge yet it is crucial to the enhancement of security. Furthermore, other forces such as state priorities and complexities exacerbate the difficulties that cyberwarfare poses with regards to law enforcement. These findings are in line with the realist position that states will put self-interests first, thus will prioritize their security above the interests of others.

The research also revealed that attribution, lack of physical boundaries, the anonymity of attackers and complications with law enforcement such as dual criminality and extraterritoriality are challenges which cyberwarfare poses and require harmonization of laws to be effective in countering cyber threats. Tabansky (2017) confirms the above scenario. He highlighted that it has become theoretically possible to exploit the properties of today’s cyberspace to attack strategic targets remotely. Furthermore, the attacker risks significantly less in cyberspace due to the widespread use of vulnerable commercial off-the-shelf technologies, the difficulty of distinguishing a glitch from a malicious action, and the challenges of identifying the attackers.

Nevertheless, The Zimbabwe legal framework has provisions for these challenges that support an interpretation that points towards the extraterritoriality nature of the crime of cyberwarfare. The emanating trend is that SADC countries are at different levels of developing cybersecurity legal frameworks. While South Africa has progressed, Zimbabwe does not have an adequate legal framework that is sufficient to address the threat of cyberwarfare, thereby increasing its vulnerability to cyberattacks.

The study deduced that the Zimbabwe legislation could be effective in prosecuting perpetrators of cyberwarfare only if SADC countries have the same laws, meaning that a crime in Zimbabwe should also be a crime in all the SADC member states. This harmonization of laws is a prerequisite to the investigation and prosecution of offenders. The non-implementation confirms Grobler & van Vuuren (2012) opinion that Africa does not follow a coordinated approach in dealing with cybersecurity, and that the various structures that have been established to deal with cybersecurity are inadequate to deal with issues holistically.

CONCLUSION

Contrary to Rid (2012) who claimed that cyberwarfare does not exist, the study concludes that the threat of cyberwarfare in the SADC region exists thereby confirming the anarchic nature of the international environment as propounded by realists. Though the study was unable to establish if attacks are experienced which can be classified as cyberwarfare as per the definition by Clarke and Knake (2010, p.6) adopted by the research, it is apparent that the technological systems can be used as weapons of warfare as indicated by Pool (2013). Furthermore, the exposure of SADC countries stems from the increased dependency and use of technology and the interconnectedness of computer networks globally in which SADC countries have no autonomy and therefore compromise control.

Additionally, the influence of politics in cyberattacks was inferred thereby affirming the realist notion of war as an extension of politics. The study also deduced there are varying definitions of cyberwarfare across the stakeholders involved. Zimbabwe’s understanding of cyberwarfare includes the use of social media for mobilization of citizens to revolt against the government which is also similar to the opinions of Shackelford and Craig (2014). These contradictions have a bearing on the actions taken to address the threat.

A common definition of cyberwarfare is the foundation of formulating strategies to counter this threat. However, this challenge is not unique to Zimbabwe or the SADC region and confirms what Burmeister, Phahlamohlaka, and Al-Saggaf (2014) observed on the differing definitions at international level which has staggered the establishment of adequate redress systems at international level. The research concluded that the legal framework in place is not adequate in addressing cyberwarfare. The absence of cyberwarfare in its precise form in both the SADC Model Law and the Cybercrime and Cybersecurity Bill in Zimbabwe reflects the gap in the legislative framework in addressing this threat. There is no specific law to address cyberwarfare but redress is found in other provisions of the law. However, this gap is similar to the findings by Hathaway and Crootof (2012) who indicated that the terms cyber-crime and cyberwarfare are often used interchangeably, therefore, the law becomes ambiguous and open to varying interpretations.

The research revealed that SADC countries are at different levels of crafting cyber laws and not all the SADC countries have adopted the SADC Model Law in its original form for domestication. Hence, this affects the harmonization of the laws which in turn affects the region’s vulnerability as cyberwarfare is transnational. These findings are consistent with Orji (2015) and Grobler and van Vuuren (2012) views that overall the legal framework is inadequate in enhancing cybersecurity in the SADC region.

Similarly, Pool (2013) affirmed that the complexities of the nature of activities within cyberspace such as the obliteration of physical boundaries within cyberspace, the anonymity of perpetrators, the remoteness of targets, the need for dual criminality, extraterritoriality, attribution, and requirements for extradition pose tremendous challenges for the persecution of offenders. The harmonization of laws is, thus, critical for the challenges to be addressed. Furthermore, the study also revealed that states tend to prioritize their interests first over common interests as postulated by realists, therefore, if cyberwarfare is not viewed as a priority by a particular state, the collaborative efforts by all SADC countries are short-changed.

Recommendations of the Study

The study recommends the SADC should facilitate the formulation of a mutual and all-encompassing definition of cyberwarfare which will guide the actions taken by nation-states in addressing this threat. This shared definition should inform the domestic and regional legal framework on cybersecurity which subsequently should include succinct provisions which specifically address cyberwarfare to avoid ambiguity and varying interpretations. These actions are fundamental in providing clarity and drawing the expectations of each SADC state to ensure that they are responsive to this emerging threat.

As such, there is need to ensure that SADC member states prioritize and expedite the finalization of domestic laws addressing cyberwarfare and harmonization of laws at the regional level. The borderless nature of cyberspace makes it impossible for any country to secure its cyber environment without the cooperation of other nations. Therefore, there is need to harness political will to address cyberwarfare and also to garner support for collaboration among the different SADC countries for the protection of the cyber domain in the region. SADC states need to play a leading role in curtailing cyberwarfare threats and enhancing cybersecurity.

There is need to engage and bring together other stakeholders such as civil society, security sector, businesses, ICT experts as well as the different arms of government, executive, judiciary and legislature in devising interventions to protect their respective countries and the region as a whole from cyberwarfare. There is also the need to conduct awareness campaigns for the general citizenry on cybersecurity, and responsible use of technology as every technological transaction is a potential gateway for intrusions.

The State Security Institutions need to recognize and acknowledge cyberspace as a domain of warfare with the potential of posing a threat to national security. Therefore, specialized training on cyberwarfare should be incorporated and a dedicated unit on cyber activity should be established. This unit should also collaborate with the cyber incidents response teams in the region to expedite the process of assessing and responding to cyberattacks if they occur. State Security Institutions should also collaborate at SADC level for skills transfer and capacity building as well as to facilitate shared responsibility and support mechanisms.

The critical national infrastructure industries such as the telecommunications industries should invest more in human capital development to be averse with emerging trends in technology. They should also ensure adequate mechanisms are put in place to secure technological systems and lower the risks of any intrusions that may disrupt service delivery. Private players need to engage more with the government which has the primary mandate of securing cyberspace to harness efforts in safeguarding the cyber domain.

Academic institutions must encourage and invest more in cyberwarfare research to enable the establishment of effective counter-intelligence mechanisms. There is need for continuous assessments and documentation of developing trends within cyberspace as well as the collation of empirical evidence of the emergence and existence of threats within cyberspace and their impact on national security. The development of homegrown and indigenous technological systems will avert the risk of vulnerabilities associated with importation. Therefore, it is prudent that academic institutions invest in the innovation and invention of local information technologies which are competitive in the global market and also encourage their uptake and adoption by government institutions and private players.

Areas for Further Research

Further research is required on the role of International Law in combating cyberwarfare and the enforcement mechanisms necessary to ensure justice delivery with regards to cyberattacks.

KEY TERMS AND DEFINITIONS

Cyberattack: Any action taken to undermine the functions of a computer network for a political or national security purpose.

Cybersecurity: The organization and collection of resources, processes, and structures used to protect cyberspace and cyberspace-enabled systems from occurrences that misalign de jure from de facto property rights.

Cyberspace: The global network of computer processing systems, interdependent information technology infrastructures, and telecommunications networks in which online communication occurs.

Cyberwarfare: Actions by a nation-state to penetrate another nation's computers or networks to cause damage or disruption.

Bryan Christiansen is the Chief Executive Officer of Tactical Systems LLC, USA in Indiana, USA. A former business lecturer at universities in Russia, Turkey, and the USA, he has traveled to 41 countries where he has conducted international business since 1985 in multiple languages and various industries with Global 500 firms and smaller. Christiansen received his Bachelor of Science degree in Marketing at the University of the State of New York in 1996 and his MBA degree at Capella University in 2003. The author of 22 Scopus-indexed Reference books on business, cultural studies, economics, and psychology, he is fluent in Chinese, Japanese, Spanish, and Turkish. Christiansen is currently working with a Russian theoretical mathematician on a new economic model for developing nations.

Agnieszka Piekarz is an independent researcher from Poland who holds a Master’s degree in Homeland Security from Pedagogical University of Cracow. Currently living in Cracow, Poland and working at one of the best technical university in Poland - Cracow University of Technology. Ms. Piekarz has held a variety of positions most recently as an Erasmus Intern at the International Relations Office at Istanbul University. Highly fluent in English as well as her native Polish, Ms. Piekarz is on the Editorial Boards of several international journals such as the International Journal of Productivity Management and Assessment Technologies.

\* \* \*

Benjamin Enahoro Assay teaches Mass Communication at Delta State Polytechnic, Ogwashi-Uku, Nigeria. He holds BA and MA degrees in mass communication from Delta State University, Abraka and University of Nigeria, Nsukka respectively. Assay is on the verge of being awarded a doctorate degree in mass communication by the Benue State University, Makurdi, Nigeria. He has published articles in scholarly journals and contributed chapter in several books locally and internationally. His research interests cover areas such as information and communication technology and national development; international communication and comparative media studies, media, democracy and good governance, population and health communication, and public relations and advertising. He is a member of several professional bodies, including African Council for Communication Education (ACCE) Nigeria Chapter, Advertising Practitioners Council of Nigeria (APCON), Association of Communication Scholars and Professionals of Nigeria (ACSPN), Nigeria Institute of Public Relations (NIPR), Association for Promoting Nigerian Languages and Culture (APNILAC), National Association for Research Development (NARD), among others.

Udo Richard Averweg is employed as an Information Technology (IT) Project Manager at eThekwini Municipality, Durban, South Africa. He entered the IT industry during 1979 and holds a Masters Technology degree in Information Technology (cum laude), a second Masters degree in Science from the University of Natal and a third Masters degree in Commerce from the University of KwaZulu-Natal, Durban, South Africa. As an IT practitioner, he is a registered professional member of the Institute of Information Technology Professionals. He has authored and co-authored more than 190 research outputs (90 being peer reviewed): some research outputs have been delivered at local conferences, some have been published in accredited peer-reviewed journals, some have appeared as chapters in books and some research findings have been presented at international conferences on all five continents. During January 2000 Udo climbed to the summit of Africa’s highest peak, Mount Kilimanjaro (5,895 metres), in Tanzania.

Sandra Blanke joined the University of Dallas – Irving, Texas in 2005 and is an Associate Professor in Cyber Security Education. She serves as the Director for the Center of Cyber Security Education and is the Ellis Endowed Chair in Management Technology. Dr. Blanke is a Certified Information Systems Security Professional (CISSP), maintains a Certification in Risk and Information Systems Control (CRISC) and her Ph.D is in Computer and Information Systems. Dr. Blanke’s research, teaching and consulting areas of expertise include Cyber Security, Risk Management, Disaster Recovery, Emerging Technologies and Cyber Insurance. She teaches courses in Cyber and Technology within the Masters and Doctoral Programs in the UD - Gupta College of Business. Blanke is a former Verizon Executive with over 20 years in Enterprise Technology and Network Operations.

Sérgio Luís Proença Duarte Guerreiro joined the Department of Computer Science and Engineering, at Instituto Superior Técnico, University of Lisbon, Portugal, as an Assistant Professor, Information Systems scientific area, in January 2017; and joined INESC-ID, IDSS (Information and Decision Support Systems Lab) as a researcher. Previously, he was a Senior IT Project Manager in Sonae.com and an Assistant Professor at ULHT (Lusófona University) and at UBI (Universidade da Beira Interior). He earned a Ph.D. degree in Information Systems and Computer Engineering at Instituto Superior Técnico / University of Lisbon (IST/UL). Before that, he concluded the Ms.C. degree and the engineering degree. Both degrees also in Information Systems and Computer Engineering at IST/UL. His research interest is located in Enterprise Engineering with the goal of finding solutions to control the business transactions operation, identifying and solving run-time misalignments. Uses the specification languages of BPMN, Archimate, DEMO, UML, SysML, WOSL, EPC; the mechanisms of Process Mining, Business Analytics; implementing solutions for Governance, Risk and Compliance.

Shalin Hai-Jew works as an instructional designer at Kansas State University (K-State). She specializes in data analytics of large-scale educational data and other data from technical systems. She has taught at the university and college levels for many years (including four years in the People’s Republic of China) and was tenured at Shoreline Community College but left tenure to pursue instructional design work. She has Bachelor’s degrees in English and psychology, a Master’s degree in Creative Writing from the University of Washington (Hugh Paradise Scholar), and an Ed.D in Educational Leadership with a focus on public administration from Seattle University (where she was a Morford Scholar). She reviews for several publishers. She has authored and edited a number of books. Hai-Jew was born in Huntsville, Alabama, in the U.S.

Jeffrey Kurebwa is a Lecturer in the Department of Peace and Governance. He is involved in teaching courses in Research Methods, Community Development and International security.

Marcus Leaning is Professor of Digital media Education at the University of Winchester in the UK. He has research interests in how the complexities of digital media are taught, how digital tools can be used in education, and developing socially aware and critical aspects of digital and information education. In 2016 he was a visiting Fellow at the University of Limerick in Ireland and in 2018 was visiting Professor at the University of Costa Rica in Information Literacy and Interculturalism. He is the author of seven books and numerous peer-reviewed chapters and articles.

Hugo Martins is developing his Master's Thesis in the context of Information and Business Systems, at Instituto Superior Técnico, University of Lisbon, in Lisbon, Portugal. A professional software engineer, his research interests are Access Control, Information Security and Blockchain-based technologies.

Kundai Matenga holds a Master of Science Degree in International Relations (Bindura University of Science Education), Post Grad. Certificate in International Election Observation & Electoral Assistance, (Basque University, Spain) and a Bachelor of Arts General Degree in English and French (University of Zimbabwe). She has 8 years’ national and regional experience in the democracy, governance and elections field. She is currently employed by the Zimbabwe Election Support Network (ZESN). She has coordinated and conducted election observation missions with ZESN, Electoral Support Network of Southern Africa (ESN-SA) and the African Union (AU). Kundai has presented papers on youth and women participation in governance and elections for the Pan-African Parliament as well as the African Governance Architecture implemented by the African Union. She has also delivered trainings on Knowledge Management, self-mastery and women’s development for the young women’s movement in Zimbabwe. She hopes to conduct further research on cyber security and elections due to the widespread adoption of technology in administering electoral processes.

Mambo Mupepi is the CEO of Grand Change Inc, an international consulting firm. Dr Mupepi's area of research include corporate organization dynamics; organizational knowledge, learning and change and their mediation/moderation by organizational design choices.

Paul Nielsen is an accomplished IT Professional with over 30 years of experience in multiple technical disciplines, including distributed computer networks, network and information security, software development, compliance, and security management. Over half of Dr. Nielsen’s experience has been managing technical people, projects and processes, while the remainder has been focused on performing technical tasks such as building and troubleshooting computer and networked systems, writing software applications, and analyzing and testing network and application security and performing security compliance assessments. Dr. Nielsen currently is a full time instructor at the University of Dallas in the Satish & Yasmin College of Business Cybersecurity program. Prior to this he worked as an Engagement Manager for Experis (formerly Jefferson Wells), a Security Consulting group. In this position he did a broad range of security work including: general security assessments, audits (PCI, HIPAA, ISO, etc.), incident response, and more. He continues to consult for Experis as an Engagement Manager and PCI Qualified Security Assessor on a part time basis. Prior to his Experis position, he worked with the Pathmaker Group, where he performed digital acquisition and forensics, penetration testing, and policy development as the Security Director. Prior to Pathmaker Group, he worked in Network and Vulnerability management for Verizon Communications where he was employed for over 12 years. Dr. Nielsen has been an adjunct instructor for the University of Dallas since 1998 with a few years off to complete his Ph.D. He has taught in both the Telecommunications Management program and the Information Assurance/Cyber Security program where he continues to teach. Dr. Nielsen’s education includes a Ph.D. in Information Systems from Nova Southeastern University. He has an M.B.A. in Telecommunications Management from the University of Dallas. His undergraduate degree is from Southwest Texas State University in Occupational Education/Business. He has extensive company sponsored technical training and maintains an active CISSP, a CCSP, and a Payment Card Industry Qualified Security Assessor (QSA) certification. Dr. Nielsen is an active participant in several professional organizations including the International Information Systems Security Certification Consortium (ISC2), the Information Systems Security Association (ISSA), the Cloud Security Alliance (CSA), the Association for Computing Machinery (ACM) and ISACA. In addition, Dr. Nielsen participates in the local chapter of Infragard.

Ionica Oncioiu holds a Ph.D. in economy and accounting. Her research interests include the development of SMEs innovation, Project Management, Accounting Information Systems, Asset Management and E-Commerce Marketing. She has had more than 10 years of experience in this area and has published 10 text books and more than 70 papers in scholarly peer reviewed international journals, also authoring eight books.

Anca-Gabriela Petrescu is born on December 8, 1980 in Bucharest. She has a triple specialization, graduating the Faculty of Economic Sciences, the Faculty of Law and The Faculty of Journalism. She has Master’s Degrees in Management, International Relation and Public Administration. She graduated multiple international postgraduate courses in management, public administration, communication and international relations. She is a member of the Body of Romanian High Civil Servants. She received her double PhD in History and Economics and she currently teaches as a University Lecturer at Valahia University of Targoviste. Her fields of interest concern management, economics, public administration, geopolitics.

Jacqueline Tanhara holds a Master of Science Degree in International Relations. Currently she is working as a Public Relations Officer at Chinhoyi University of Technology. She has published 3 Online Journals and has established a Social Media platform and a Bulk SMS/Emails platform for Marketing and Public Relations department in order to enhance Communication flow. Jacqueline Tanhara has also assisted the School of Engineering Sciences and Technology at Chinhoyi University of Technology in formulating a Graduate Tracer Study instrument inorder to keep track with former students and rate relevancy of their programmes. She is currently working on registering for her PhD studies.

Brian Wrozek is a managing executive director, executive advisory in the Office of the CISO at Optiv. In this role, Wrozek works closely with security executives to provide C-Suite advisory services to define cyber strategy, roadmaps and solutions to meet clients’ security objectives. Wrozek is the former chief security officer (CSO) for Alliance Data where he had enterprise responsibility for information security and physical security. Prior to Alliance Data, he was the IT security and privacy director at Texas Instruments where he managed all facets of electronic data and system security worldwide. Wrozek earned his Bachelor of Science in computer science from Michigan Technological University. He earned his MBA and Cybersecurity Certification from the University of Dallas. Wrozek is an adjunct professor at the University of Dallas teaching graduate-level cyber security courses in the Satish & Yasmin Gupta College of Business. Wrozek received the 2008 Central Region Information Security Executive of the Year award from Tech Exec Networks and the 2010 Information Security Executive of the Year award at the Texas Regional Infrastructure Security Conference.

Winfred Yaokumah is the Dean of the Faculty of Engineering, Science and Computing at the Pentecost University College, Accra, Ghana. He obtained his PhD in Information Technology with specialization in Information Assurance and Security at the Capella University, USA. He has published extensively in several international journals, including the Information Management & Computer Security, Information Resources Management Journal, International Journal of Technology Diffusion, Journal of Information Technology Research, International Journal of Technology and Human Interaction, International Journal of E-Business Research, International Journal of IT/Business Alignment and Governance, and the International Journal of Information Systems in the Service Sector. His research interest includes cyber security, cyber ethics, e-services, IT governance, cloud computing, technology diffusion, information security governance, and IT leadership.

İsmail Yıldırım is an associate professor of finance at Hittite University, Department of Finance, Banking and Insurance, Corum, Turkey. He received PhD in Finance with his thesis titled “Stress Testing in the Risk Measurement of Insurance Companies: An Implementation in Turkish Insurance Sector”. Has the title of associate professor in the field of insurance.
